#306. Breaking: Forget Expensive Ribeye: A Cheaper Cut For Delicious Beef Stroganoff

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (553 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foodrepublic

Breaking: Forget Expensive Ribeye: A Cheaper Cut For Delicious Beef Stroganoff

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (553 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that indulgently and immensely comforting, beef stroganoff is one of those low-effort meals you make when you just want to feel good.
  • It has been revealed that while it may not satisfy the purist, and might even horrify a Russian (the dish's country of origin), we'd argue that ground beef is a worthy alternative to any traditional whole cut of steak.
  • Another reason ground beef works so well here is its cooking time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that indulgently and immensely comforting, beef stroganoff is one of those low-effort meals you make when you just want to feel good. But one thing that might not lift your spirits is the price. Classic stroganoff starts off with strips of thinly sliced beef, with cuts like ribeye being among the best picks. We're not here to fault ribeye, which has earned its price for a reason, but if you want to knock a few dollars off your next batch, try swapping in ground beef instead.

It has been revealed that while it may not satisfy the purist, and might even horrify a Russian (the dish's country of origin), we'd argue that ground beef is a worthy alternative to any traditional whole cut of steak. The texture is bound to be different, and you'll need to adjust how you cook it, but good-quality ground beef still has the rich, beefy flavor that pairs so well with the tang of sour cream, earthy mushrooms, and the sweet depth of cooked-down onions, all at a significantly lower cost.

Another reason ground beef works so well here is its cooking time. Traditional beef stroganoff relies on expensive cuts that are prized for their tenderness and quick-cooking nature. Cheaper, tougher cuts like chuck or round usually need hours of braising to soften, which doesn't suit a dish that's meant to come together quickly. Ground beef, however, is often made from those same economical cuts, and the grinding process does all the tenderizing mechanically. That means you're getting all that mouthwatering flavor without the waiting, guaranteeing a tasty, Boomer-approved meal.

If you make the switch from ribeye to ground beef, you'll want to do a few things differently. First, check out the numbers on your ground beef packaging. You're looking for a blend that doesn't shy away from fat, something like an 80-to-20 lean-to-fat ratio, or even 70-to-30. Like ribeye, these fattier blends are packed with rich flavor, and the fat that'll render out will elevate the sauce, just in a different format. Go any leaner and you risk dry, chewy beef pebbles floating in your sauce.

Recent findings suggest that with ribeye, standard practice is to slice the beef ultra-thin, give it a quick sear, then let it simmer in the sauce for a few minutes. The process for ground beef is similar, albeit with a few caveats. For starters, there's no slicing, so you're already saving time. Like ribeye, you want to get the meat nicely browned. Our personal advice is to add the beef to the pan in small handfuls and flatten each one with the back of a spoon, which allows it to brown without overcrowding the pan.

It has been revealed that remove the beef from the pan once it's seared, which isn't usually done with ribeye. Even in a fattier blend, ground beef has far more exposed surface area than your average slice of steak, so it risks drying out if it's left to simmer for too long. For the most tender results, build your sauce first, then add the beef back in and stir once you're just about ready to serve. Don't worry about the flavors not melding, since the fat and fond left behind from searing will be doing most of the heavy lifting.

#305. Breaking: Cranberry Crackle Salad

Breaking: Cranberry Crackle Salad

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (683 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cranberry crackle salad combines crunchy and creamy textures with sweet and tangy flavors.
  • I live in cranberry country (aka northern Wisconsin), and when fresh cranberries hit store shelves, there’s a good chance you’ll find me in the kitchen baking with them.
  • According to recent reports, crackle salad is a variation on retro fluff salad that combines cream cheese, whipped topping and fruit mix-ins with a crunchy, candied “crackle” topping (made with crushed pretzels, chopped pecans, brown sugar and melted butter).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recipe by Susan Bronson, Rhinelander, Wisconsin.

Tested by Taste of Home Test Kitchen.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Cranberry crackle salad combines crunchy and creamy textures with sweet and tangy flavors. It's a retro-style dessert with a hearty dose of seasonal cheer.

I live in cranberry country (aka northern Wisconsin), and when fresh cranberries hit store shelves, there’s a good chance you’ll find me in the kitchen baking with them. One sweet treat that often finds its way onto our holiday brunch menus is a loaf (or three) of cranberry-orange bread. There’s just something so cozy about the combination of tart cranberries and sweet, bright orange juice—the inspiration for this cranberry crackle salad recipe.

According to recent reports, crackle salad is a variation on retro fluff salad that combines cream cheese, whipped topping and fruit mix-ins with a crunchy, candied “crackle” topping (made with crushed pretzels, chopped pecans, brown sugar and melted butter). In this holiday-inspired crackle salad, the cream mixture is flavored with whole-berry cranberry sauce and orange zest. Fresh orange juice in the crackle adds a subtle citrus flavor, too. This recipe makes enough for a small crowd, and is perfect for sharing at a Thanksgiving potluck or as a fun throwback side dish at holiday gatherings.

Recent findings suggest that preheat the oven to 400°F. Line a 15x10x1-inch rimmed baking sheet with parchment paper or a silicone baking mat.

In a large bowl, stir together the broken pretzels, chopped pecans and brown sugar. Stir in the melted butter and orange juice to coat.

Recent findings suggest that spread the pretzel mixture in an even layer on the prepared baking sheet. Bake it for five to eight minutes or until it’s bubbly. Let it cool completely on the baking sheet before breaking it into pieces.

Editor’s Tip: Keep your eye on the crackle as it bakes; it can easily burn if baked too long.

In a large bowl, beat together the softened cream cheese and vanilla. Stir in the cranberry sauce until it’s combined. Gently fold in the whipped topping until it’s incorporated.

Fold in the orange zest. Cover the bowl and refrigerate the mixture for at least one hour.

It has been revealed that just before serving, stir in half of the pretzel mixture. Top the salad with the remaining pretzel mixture to serve. If you like, add sugared cranberries as an additional garnish.

Editor’s Tip: Avoid adding the crunch to the salad too early, as it will soften up over time.

Recent findings suggest that leftover cranberry crackle salad should be stored in an airtight container in the fridge. It will last for up to three days in the fridge. The crackle will soften over time once added to the salad.

Any extra crackle topping should be stored in an airtight container at room temperature to keep it crunchy. It should keep for up to one week.

You can make the cream mixture and crackle up to two day in advance. Store the salad and crackle separately, and don’t combine them until just before serving the salad.

If you want to dial up the crunch factor even more, allow the baked crackle to cool thoroughly before using it. This will ensure it has the crunchiest texture.

Industry observers note that fresh cranberries are a great option when they are in season. To make this cranberry crackle salad with fresh cranberries, you’ll need a 12-ounce package of whole cranberries. (You could also use frozen whole cranberries, but they need to thaw first.).

In a food processor or blender, pulse the berries until they’re finely chopped. Pour the berries into a large bowl and stir in 1/2 cup of granulated sugar. Cover and refrigerate them for at least one hour or overnight. Use the fresh berry mixture in place of the canned cranberry sauce in this recipe.

This cranberry crackle salad will fit right in with any holiday potluck spread. It’s also a fun retro dessert salad to share at a holiday meal alongside classic savory offerings such as roasted turkey, mashed potatoes and green bean casserole.

#298. Alexis Nikole Nelson, aka the Black Forager, Makes Nature Her Buffet

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Saveur

Alexis Nikole Nelson, aka the Black Forager, Makes Nature Her Buffet

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2004 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is Amused Bouche, SAVEUR’s food questionnaire that explores the culinary curiosities of some of our favorite people.
  • Alexis Nicole Nelson’s life mantra is simple: “Don’t put things in your face hole unless you know what they are!” This mostly applies to foraging wild foods, something she has been doing since she was a kid with her mom and has since turned into a flourishing career and community.
  • Recent findings suggest that nelson’s journey to becoming the Black Forager started with an interest in vegetarianism as a 5-year-old, which, at the time, was discouraged by her family.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is Amused Bouche, SAVEUR’s food questionnaire that explores the culinary curiosities of some of our favorite people. This interview series will dive deep into their food routines, including dinner party strategies, cherished cookbooks, and the memorable bites they’d hop on a flight for.

Alexis Nicole Nelson’s life mantra is simple: “Don’t put things in your face hole unless you know what they are!” This mostly applies to foraging wild foods, something she has been doing since she was a kid with her mom and has since turned into a flourishing career and community. She has showcased her adventures and recipes as @blackforager since 2018 (with millions of curious followers across Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube) and now in her debut cookbook, Happy Snacking, Don’t Die! This comprehensive guide to finding and cooking with ingredients from your backyard or nearby forests and fields is organized by season and anchored by Nelson’s vibrant personality and boundless energy, encouraging readers to get out of their comfort zones and educate themselves on edible plants hiding in plain sight.

Recent findings suggest that nelson’s journey to becoming the Black Forager started with an interest in vegetarianism as a 5-year-old, which, at the time, was discouraged by her family. “You have to finish growing first!” Nelson recalls her mom saying. Nelson ate meat products to keep from wasting food her parents prepared until she was 12, when she decided to start packing her own lunches. “It was a lot of undressed Boca burgers and French fries. It was a bleak time,” she admits with a laugh. She went fully vegan at 24 and hasn’t looked back.

I am not a very outdoorsy person, but I was captivated by the whimsical way Nelson goes about foraging and sharing online, and even more so after chatting with her on a recent Zoom call. When I asked for easy gateway foraging ideas, she immediately suggested field garlic or onion grass: “I am a biased party, because that is the first forageable that my mom taught me. Once you notice it, you see it everywhere, and it has a foolproof test, which is the smell test. If you break it and it doesn’t very fragrantly smell of onions and garlic, you have the wrong plant. Easy, easy!” She recommended looking for little purple flowers or round pink spiky balls, and on my next walk with my dogs, I spotted some. I haven’t picked and cooked with any yet, but now I’m on the lookout (and smell-out) for this abundant allium and plan on pairing it with the maitake bacon recipe from her book. Nelson suggested making a “BLT-adjacent sandwich with whatever mild greens are in season, a slice of tomato, and maitake bacon on toasty sourdough.”.

Sources indicate that whether you’re a foraging beginner or an expert, Nelson’s edition of Amused Bouche will be equally eye-opening and mouthwatering. Read on for her adventures and misadventures in the fields and in her home kitchen.

If you could only eat one thing 24/7/365, what would it be?

In a recent development, I love a tofu scramble and mixing in whatever is in season, and I bring home mushrooms, greens, and aromatics. In the springtime, it’ll be ramp leaves and oyster mushrooms. In the summer, it’s chanterelle and bicolor bolete with some nodding onion flowers from my front yard. As we move into winter, I’m thankful that we get enoki mushrooms pretty consistently all throughout the season in the woods. I do a combo of firm silken and super-firm tofu because I want the best of both worlds. Eggs don’t just have one texture; the whites and yolks are different, and I always want to try to get as close to eggs as I can with my tofu textures. I’m perpetually on a search for a forageable legume that I can make my own tofu with. One of my friends, Jesse Akozbek (@feralforaging), makes tofu with black walnuts.

What’s the first thing you learned how to cook?

The first thing that I remember cooking is baking cakes with my dad—usually just a basic frosted vanilla cake. My mom used to be a cool head-honcho character at Procter & Gamble, and she would be gone for two or three weeks at a time for work. We’d bake the cake the night before [she got back], frost it, and then just before she came home, we’d leave the cake out and hide.

How about your latest kitchen adventure?

According to recent reports, I broke out my food mill because I went a little overboard harvesting cornelian cherries with my fiancé this year. They’re fun to harvest, and we brought a step stool to reach more and ended up going home with a couple gallons of fruit. It’s all fun and games until you see them all on the counter and realize they’re gonna go bad so I gotta figure out what I’m doing with all of this. I thought of doing a glacé cornelian cherry like I’ve done with chestnuts before, but the water content of the cherries is so high that when I simmered them in a sugar syrup, they just disintegrated and disappeared. I tried to stir it carefully, but it all just turned into goo. I fished them out with my little spider, put them in my food mill, and ground it. They have substantial ol’ pits on the inside, and I am not trying to eat any of those. It was an applesauce consistency in the end, but like what if applesauce had dreams? What if applesauce was the star of a Studio Ghibli movie? I made cornelian cherry shortcakes with it, and my fiancé was like, “So I’ve had three…” and we realized that when you eat a lot of fruit and fiber at once, you remember it later. I also saved the flavored syrup that was created after straining out all of the goopy fruits, and I am saving it specifically for making Shirley Temples!

What’s your treat-yourself splurge?

Recent findings suggest that my favorite way to treat myself is getting dinner with my fiancé at Agni, an amazing Bengali American fusion restaurant here in Columbus, led by my friend, chef Avishar Barua! They have these french fries that take three days to make, and I—no joke—dream about them sometimes.

What’s your most cherished cookbook?

According to recent reports, marie Viljoen’s Forage, Harvest, Feast is the cookbook that demonstrated me as a recent college graduate that foraging, the weird thing I’ve been doing since childhood, could become such elevated cuisine. It’s absolutely stunning, and she is a recipe and photography genius—she does it all! I remember checking that book out from the library for the first time and my jaw dropping at how she used foraged foods in ways I had never even let myself consider. She gets shouted out in my cookbook because I used a few of her recipes as a jumping-off point then over time I started changing things to make them my own. A decade later, it becomes something different but still has the heart of that original recipe, like my milkweed nectar is definitely the child of her milkweed cordial! Her book was eye-opening for me even before I knew this was what I was going to end up making my career, back when it was something I just did because I loved it and I was a poor recent grad. A really great way to spruce up a 59-cent pack of ramen is wild greens and mushrooms!

Is there a cooking disaster that made you swear off a dish forever?

I keep doing this thing where I start fermenting drinks and then travel, which is dumb. Don’t do that! My most explosive ferment was actually not mine, it was a gift from fellow foraging friend Gabrielle Cerberville (@chaoticforager). She very kindly brought me a bottle of her wild plum wine, and I did not put it straight into the fridge because I was not using my noggin. Three days later, I went to open it to pair with dinner, and it was like my world was in slow motion and it was just a geyser everywhere! Wine on the ceiling, wine on the walls, a lot of wine on the floor, a lot of wine on me. I cleaned it up sadly, shooing my pets away. No drunk pets! I also had a milkweed cordial explode, which meant I had to scrub sticky pink off every single thing in the refrigerator. Do not recommend it.

Which nostalgic foods from childhood bring you the most comfort?

Industry observers note that I grew up in the Cincinnati area, so there will be a soft spot in my heart for Cincinnati chili forever. It’s just ingrained within me. Thankfully Skyline has vegan rice and beans using the same spices that you can also put onto pasta like a wild Ohioan. That will always taste like a Friday evening with my dad, because my mom is from New England and famously hates Cincinnati chili. I think calling it a chili was maybe its biggest downfall—when you learn about the history behind it and how it’s actually the child of a Greek meat sauce, suddenly the spice palette makes so much more sense. I think people would be so much cooler with that, but everyone’s expecting Tex-Mex chili, and that is not what you are signing up for!

When you’re playing dinner party DJ, what’s spinning?

In a recent development, there was a podcast I was obsessed with called The Dinner Party Download a decade ago, and I named my playlist after that. It has been evolving throughout the past 10 years and has Mitski, which I know feels sad for a dinner party but it’s mellow, some alt-J, Bill Withers, The Contours. A lot of Motown-era music, like The Supremes, Stevie Wonder, The Four Tops, Staple Singers. And then Janelle Monáe, Kate Nash, “Rhapsody in Blue” by George Gershwin is thrown in there. I go all over the place, but I think it creates a general buzzy atmosphere. I don’t want it to necessarily be as dancey as a dance party, but I also don’t want people to fall asleep, either.

What is your biggest entertaining flex to impress guests?

Sources indicate that I really love plating things and cutting things into fun shapes and making them look pretty. I took a cooking class in Japan with Elizabeth Andoh, a very prolific cookbook writer, a couple of years ago, and after my fiancé and I walked out of it, we were just like, “Dang, our food’s real ugly!” A huge part of her class was how much presentation matters and how the first way that you are consuming the food is with your sight, with your eyes, so why not make it look cute?

Tell me about a meal so good you would hop on a flight to relive it.

In a recent development, while my fiancé and I were in Florence for a friend’s wedding, we knew that Italy, historically, was not the easiest place to be vegan. You can find things but maybe not that many things, and maybe not the things that look as good as the things everybody else is eating. So I was significant sad the entire time until we stumbled into a tiny hole-in-the-wall vegan restaurant called Il Vegano. We found it on Google by searching “vegan restaurants near me,” and it had the best pasta with tomato sauce and tiramisù that either of us have ever had. Mind you, my fiancé is not vegan and very much could still eat real tiramisù and did on that trip. And the night ended with us essentially begging in broken Italian for the head chef to write a cookbook. We waddled back to our hotel saying it was the best meal we’ve ever had.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Breaking: Skip Gruyère: This Norwegian Cheese Boasts Nutty Flavor & Fewer Calories

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (591 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that cheese is one of life's greatest pleasures, but no two varieties are quite the same.
  • Jarlsberg is instantly recognizable thanks to its large, round holes, and while traditional Swiss Gruyère might lack these holes, it matches Jarlsberg's intensely nutty flavor — although how the two cheeses develop their respective flavors is very different.
  • Despite sharing a similar taste, their nutritional profiles tell a different story.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that cheese is one of life's greatest pleasures, but no two varieties are quite the same. Knowing your way around your mozzarella and parmesan is a useful skill that won't just impress your dinner guests but will also transform the way you use cheese in the kitchen. Take Gruyère, for example. If, say, a French onion soup recipe calls for it, and you've had no luck finding it at the store, any cheese connoisseur will tell you that Norwegian Jarlsberg makes an excellent substitute. The two share a similar nutty flavor and melt beautifully, with Jarlsberg also serving a lower-calorie option.

Jarlsberg is instantly recognizable thanks to its large, round holes, and while traditional Swiss Gruyère might lack these holes, it matches Jarlsberg's intensely nutty flavor — although how the two cheeses develop their respective flavors is very different. Jarlsberg gets it from a proprietary bacterial culture called Propionibacterium shermanii, a sub-sect of Propionibacterium freudenreichii. During fermentation, this culture consumes lactic acid to produce propionic acid and carbon dioxide. The acid contributes to the cheese's nutty profile, while the carbon dioxide becomes trapped in the cheese, creating those large holes. Gruyère takes a different approach, developing its signature flavor through a combination of factors, including the unique composition of the high-altitude Alpine milk, its bacterial cultures, and a longer aging process.

Despite sharing a similar taste, their nutritional profiles tell a different story. Jarlsberg contains around 100 calories per ounce, compared with up to 120 calories for Gruyère. That's a modest saving of 20 calories per ounce, which can quickly add up if you're using a generous amount in a grilled cheese or fondue. So if you're looking for a slightly lighter alternative to Gruyère without sacrificing flavor, Jarlsberg makes for a wonderful swap.

In a recent development, as is the case with Gruyère, one of Jarlsberg's biggest selling points is its versatility. You can always enjoy it as is, pairing it with grapes, crackers, and cold cuts as part of an elegantly presented charcuterie board, or keep things simple and serve it alongside a glass of wine; Jarlsberg goes particularly well with chardonnay and sweet rieslings, as well as low-tannin reds like pinot noir. While there are plenty of ways to enjoy the cheese without cooking it, we think the best way to get the most out of Jarlsberg is to take advantage of its meltability.

Jarlsberg's flavor is comparatively milder than that of sharper Gruyère, making it an excellent substitute if you're after a nutty, creamy cheese that won't overpower everything else, which makes it a great contender for a grilled cheese. If you still want some of Gruyère's intensity, simply combine the two. Their complementary flavor profiles mean neither cheese should overpower the other, giving you a nutty filling with plenty of depth. In a nod to Jarlsberg's Norwegian roots, add in some fresh dill, pickles, and a generous helping of cold-smoked salmon for a Scandi-inspired twist.

Sources indicate that another great way to put Jarlsberg to work is as a pizza topping. Its mild, buttery flavor and excellent meltability make it an obvious fit. Rather than tomato sauce, pair it with mushrooms, caramelized onions, and fresh thyme to let the cheese shine. If white pizza isn't your thing, swap the dough for Danish rye bread to create your own smørbrød, a charming Scandinavian open-faced sandwich. Simply take the buttered bread and add your toppings of choice, layer the Jarlsberg on top, then blast it in the broiler until creamy and gooey.

It has been revealed that we tested some of the best subscription boxes to find the ones truly worth gifting. Whether you’re shopping for a woman who has everything or treating yourself to something special, these thoughtfully curated subscriptions make it easy to discover newly introduced favorites and enjoy a delightful surprise each month.

In a recent development, looking for more inspiration? Explore our 2026 Holiday Gift Guide for gifts she’ll love.

It has been revealed that bloomsyBox is your one-stop shop when it comes to flower and plant subsctiption boxes. The brand offers a variety of eco-friendly blooms spanning seasonal bouquets, roses, tropical flowers and even houseplants for gifting. Choose from classic arrangements, large, mixed bouquets or collections of roses in monthly, weekly or bi-weekly deliveries.

Madi Koetting for Taste of Home.

“My BloomsyBox arrangement featuring red and white roses arrived expertly arranged, although I swiftly trimmed the stems for maximum freshness and plopped them in a clear glass vase,” notes tester Madi Koetting. “Despite the less-than-ideal winter weather, my bouquet remained intact for a whopping two and a half weeks. BloomsyBox is another go-to for show-stopping flower delivery.”.

Recent findings suggest that I re-tested BloomsyBox in 2026 to ensure quality and consistency. My Garden Soirée bouquet arrived via next-day delivery, with all 30 stems fresh and perfectly intact. BloomsyBox delivery is turly one of the freshest, fullest and most well-preserved flower delivery boxes I’ve ever received, and it would make a wonderful subscription gift for anyone who loves fresh blooms.

Industry observers note that A candle subscription that’s affordable, flexible and totally giftable may seem too good to be true, but we found an option that has it all. Vellabox offers flexible subscription options, and each candle comes from a different candlemaker, so there’s no limit to the number of scents and brands she’ll get to try. Plus, regardless of size, each box comes with a curated gift to accompany the candle.

KATIE BANDURSKI FOR TASTE OF HOME.

In a recent development, deputy Shopping Editor Katie Bandurski has been a Vellabox fan ever since trying them for her Vellabox review. She has received a number of candle companion gifts, from lip balms to an eco-friendly scrub brush. “I’ve received many Vellabox boxes over the years, and they’re all high quality. I’ve found so many amazing scents, and I love to give them as gifts,” she says.

According to recent reports, for the price point, we find Vellabox to be an incredible value for gifting, enjoying and exploring upcoming scents. They’re also very well packaged to prevent breakage, and each comes in a pretty fabric pouch, sure to feel extra special to giftees.

Our best chocolate box winner offers our favorite chocolate subscription box, too. I tested the Compartés Chocolate of the Month Club box in February—and it wowed from the moment it arrived. Inside were two chocolate bars and a box of assorted chocolates.

Recent findings suggest that the assortment featured strawberry cream and crème brûlée–filled chocolates. The strawberry cream was exactly what you’d expect—fruity and delicious. The crème brûlée, however, was a surprise, capturing the rich, warm vanilla flavor of the classic dessert with impressive accuracy.

February’s box included two chocolate bars: California Berries, a vegan dark chocolate full of dried berries, and Strawberry Shortcake, a white chocolate bar packed with strawberries and airy, crunchy shortcake pieces.

While the subscription does require a minimum of three deliveries (discounted to $180 from the $225 value), it would make a thoughtful gift, especially if you have a series of gifting occasions, like the holiday season aligning with someone’s birthday month.

After trying the most popular charcuterie clubs, we found that Appy Hour charcuterie kits offer a convenient, curated solution that takes the guesswork out of building a board—a perfect gift for casual hosts and aspiring entertainers alike.

It has been revealed that an average subscription box from Appy Hour typically contains up to five cheeses, two meats, cracker packs and two or more accompaniments like dried fruits, olives, candied nuts, chocolate, spreads or pickled items. Tester Paul Rankin’s box included four packets of cured meats, three hard cheeses, one jar of sheep and goat cheese in oil, one sweet lemon ricotta, a box of artisan crisps, a bag of pralined pecans, a bag of dried cherries and, lastly, a tiny jar of blackberry balsamic jam.

Sources indicate that “This entire box was exquisite,” says Paul. “I’m already a huge fan of a charcuterie board, so this was an easy winner. Each meat was different and delicious; the dried cherries and candied pecans tasted amazing. But the cheese, the cheese! The cheeses were the star, particularly the sweetened lemon ricotta, which was absolutely stunning.”.

The ease and quality of this kit are hard to beat, and buying each item separately would likely cost more than the price of the box, making it an excellent value for giving and receiving alike.

If fruit is her snack of choice, The Fruit Company offers a wide selection of fresh fruit for delivery. There are multiple different monthly fruit clubs that include everything from pears and apples to more exotic choices like star fruit and champagne mangos. And you can choose different packaging options, from ribbons and bows to beautiful baskets.

It has been revealed that “This is a solid fruit basket,” notes Katie Bandurski of her Simply Organic Fruit Basket. “It’s beautifully arranged, shipped without any damage to the fruit and has a nice variety.”.

In a recent development, you can choose from four different subscription options: HarvestClub Americana (oranges, peaches, pineapples, cherries), HarvestClub Medley (a mix of hard-to-find fruits and familiar favorites, like Rainier cherries and Fuji apples), HarvestClub Organic (seasonal organic fruit) and HarvestClub Exotica (exotic fruit, like champagne mangos and star fruit). All boxes ship free and are available on 3-, 6- and 12-month-long options.

In a recent development, looking for the perfect gift for an experienced baker? Crumble Crate offers monthly boxes that include pre-portioned dry ingredients, a recipe, at least one quality baking tool and a QR code that leads to instructional videos, shopping lists and extra tips.

It has been revealed that katie Bandurski tested the apple rose tart, which arrived with a tart pan and pastry cutter, along with specialty ingredients like almond flour. Some basics, including apples, butter, eggs and lemon juice, needed to be supplied separately.

KATIE BANDURSKI FOR TASTE OF HOME.

Industry observers note that even as an experienced baker, Katie found the project challenging. Forming the apple roses took some patience, and she had to reread a few of the more involved steps. Still, the finished tart looked impressive and tasted excellent. She described the experience as equal parts baking project and art project.

Crumble Crate may be frustrating for a true beginner, but if you’re gifting to a baker who already knows her way around the kitchen, it makes every delivery feel like a worthwhile challenge.

Winc is one of the best-rated wine clubs out there, and the subscription wine club includes diverse selections with a little bit of everything, from sake to rosé.

Industry observers note that you can select individual wines or fill out a survey to have bottles specially curated for you. While it doesn’t come with tasting notes or other supplemental information in the box, all of that is easily available on their website.

According to recent reports, tea Runners is a top pick when it comes to tea subscriptions. Each box includes four sampler pouches of tea, 10 tea bags and a postcard with some basic info about the club, tea origins and steeping instructions.

KATIE BANDURSKI FOR TASTE OF HOME.

In a recent development, the Original Box is a great gift for her to start experimenting and figuring out what types of tea she likes. If she already knows what kind of tea she likes, she can choose from four box options: Black, Pure, Herbal or Original.

Sources indicate that inside Katie’s box, each tea impressed with its freshness and flavor. She likens Moonlight Jasmine to “a warm summer night,” whereas Floral Nectar Black wowed with its subtle finishing florals. Even the Majestic Earl Grey impressed Katie, who isn’t a major fan of Earl Grey. “It was so delicious—much fresher than any Earl Grey I’ve had before,” she says.

We adore Jeni’s ice cream, and our rave review of Jeni’s Pint of the Month Club may just convince you that this is the food subscription box you need to get her.

In a recent development, katie notes, “I was impressed with the wide array of flavors in my ice cream subscription box. The mix had a little bit of everything—chocolaty, fruity, salty and even savory. Plus, many of these were flavors I would not have picked out myself. Talk about a great way to widen your ice cream palate!”.

Katie Bandurski For Taste of Home.

This one is definitely on the pricier side, but our editors absolutely love it.

The Partners Coffee Roaster’s choice subscription is one of the best ways to stay on top of the latest coffee. I tried Partners for the first time this year, and was blown away by the fresh, delicious flavor and quality of the brand’s whole bean coffee. The beans truly took my home latte to another level. Katie, who has also tried the brand, loves Partners for their bold packaging and both Newly introduced York- and global-themed brews.

Katie Bandurski for Taste of Home.

Each 12-ounce bag is hand-selected by a member of the Partners team. You’ll receive both single-origin beans and blends, depending on the month. Enjoy delivery every one, two, three or four weeks, starting at $20 a bag. As an added bonus, you get free shipping with the coffee subscription.

Let’s just say, I have Partner’s Coffee on my personal Christmas list this year, and I’m hoping Santa comes through!

Sources indicate that any bookworm will appreciate this curated book box. Choose between a 3-, 6- and 12-month subscription, and your giftee will receive a specialty-bound read each month for the duration of the subscription.

KATIE BANDURSKI FOR TASTE OF HOME.

It has been revealed that plus, Book of the Month is totally customizable. They’ll get to choose one book out of a selection of five or six books each month, and can even skip a month if they need some more time to read their last pick.

Sources indicate that I needed a gift for the family member who ‘has everything’ and also loves books—and BOTM was the perfect find. With BOTM, she can choose books she doesn’t already own from a curated list. Buying a subscription as a gift is super easy too. I opted for a physical card, which I tucked in a little gift basket with other goodies.

Industry observers note that jiggy is a puzzle tech giant that focuses on partnering with artists through the Jiggy Puzzle Club. Members get an exclusive 500-piece puzzle each month, plus VIP perks like early access to latest products and opportunities to interact with Jiggy artists. Each puzzle also comes with a reusable drawstring bag, making it highly giftable.

KATIE BANDURSKI FOR TASTE OF HOME.

#294. I Chewed 7 Popular Gum Brands Until They Lost Their Flavor—Here's Which Lasted The Longest

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (941 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Delish

I Chewed 7 Popular Gum Brands Until They Lost Their Flavor—Here's Which Lasted The Longest

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (941 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that chewing gum can be incredibly frustrating.
  • So I decided to put seven popular gum brands to the ultimate test.
  • I judged each gum on the intensity of its spearmint flavor, how pleasant it was to chew, and, most importantly, how long that minty taste actually lasted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that chewing gum can be incredibly frustrating. You unwrap a fresh piece expecting a burst of minty flavor that'll last a while, only to find yourself chewing flavorless rubber five minutes later. And most of the time, it doesn't even make it that long.

So I decided to put seven popular gum brands to the ultimate test. I would chew each piece until the flavor completely disappeared, timing exactly how long it took before I was left with nothing but a rubbery wad of disappointment.

I judged each gum on the intensity of its spearmint flavor, how pleasant it was to chew, and, most importantly, how long that minty taste actually lasted. And after spending a frankly ridiculous amount of time chewing gum, I have some thoughts (and jaw pain). Here's how all seven brands ranked, from shortest-lasting to longest-lasting.

It has been revealed that I quickly knew Pür wasn't going to be a strong contender. Of all seven brands, this had the least flavor right from the beginning. While the other gums delivered at least some noticeable burst of spearmint, Pür barely gave me enough to enjoy before the taste started disappearing.

Sources indicate that but the bigger problem was the texture. Almost immediately, the gum became tough and waxy, making it unpleasant to chew even before the flavor was completely gone. Instead of that soft, satisfying consistency I want from gum, it felt like I was working way too hard for very little reward.

By the time I hit one minute and 36 seconds, there was absolutely no reason to keep chewing.

Recent findings suggest that considering the packaging literally advertises long-lasting flavor, I had pretty high expectations going into this one. Unfortunately, the results were anything but impressive.

According to recent reports, the spearmint flavor disappeared after just two minutes and one second, making Extra the second shortest-lasting gum in the entire test. When a brand makes longevity such a prominent selling point, I expect to get more than two minutes of enjoyment out of a piece.

Sources indicate that I'm not saying I need my gum to taste fresh all afternoon, but two minutes feels like a pretty low bar. I don't like liars, Extra. And you’re not extra, you’re underwhelming.

Trident managed to outlast Extra and Pür, but not by a particularly impressive margin. The biggest thing I noticed was the texture. This gum leaned more toward the waxy side, which isn't exactly my favorite quality in something I'm supposed to be chewing for an extended period.

The spearmint flavor lasted two minutes and 30 seconds before fading away, putting it firmly in the bottom half of the ranking. While it held on slightly longer than Extra, the difference wasn't enough to make Trident feel particularly long-lasting.

And considering how much better the top four performed, this one simply couldn't compete.

Orbit immediately impressed me with a very strong burst of mint flavor. Compared with the previous three brands, the initial taste was much more noticeable, making the experience more enjoyable from the start.

Even after the flavor began to fade, Orbit remained soft and pleasant to chew. It never developed that tough, waxy consistency that made some of the lower-ranked gums so unpleasant.

The mint flavor lasted four minutes and seven seconds, which was a significant improvement over Trident.

It has been revealed that if we're judging these gums purely on how intense the flavor is when you first start chewing, 5 Gum wins. This had the biggest, boldest burst of spearmint flavor in the entire lineup. The initial mint sensation was noticeably more powerful than anything else I tried, making it an excellent choice for someone who likes their gum to pack a punch.

And thankfully, the flavor wasn't just strong for the first few seconds. It lasted an impressive seven minutes and six seconds before finally fading away, putting it among the longest-lasting gums in the test. The only thing keeping 5 Gum from the top spot was that two other brands held on just a little longer.

Ice Breakers delivered one of the most interesting experiences of the entire taste test because its intense cooling sensation and overall mint flavor seemed to have two different lifespans.

For the first two minutes and seven seconds, the gum delivered a powerful cooling effect that made my mouth feel especially refreshed. But even after that initial cooling sensation faded, the spearmint flavor kept going. In fact, I was able to chew it for another five minutes and two seconds before the flavor finally disappeared, bringing the total to seven minutes and nine seconds.

That's just three seconds longer than 5 Gum, making this an incredibly close competition.

Industry observers note that I have to admit, Eclipse surprised me more than any other gum in this ranking. Going into the test, I wasn't expecting it to outlast every other brand, especially after experiencing the intense initial flavor of 5 Gum and the cooling sensation of Ice Breakers.

Sources indicate that the spearmint flavor lasted an impressive seven minutes and 33 seconds before finally disappearing, making it the longest-lasting gum of the seven I tested. While 5 Gum delivered the strongest initial flavor and Ice Breakers impressed with its cooling effect, Eclipse ultimately won the competition that mattered most: longevity.

According to recent reports, it outlasted Ice Breakers by 24 seconds and 5 Gum by 27 seconds. Those aren't enormous differences, but when you've spent this much time counting every second of mint flavor, they certainly count. Eclipse might not have been my most anticipated winner, but the numbers don't lie.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature.
  • It has been revealed that ina Garten has made her position on Thanksgiving dinner quite clear.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Recent findings suggest that even Ina isn't making everything from scratch this year. Her newly revealed side dishes include some surprisingly simple shortcuts.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

It has been revealed that ina Garten has made her position on Thanksgiving dinner quite clear. The turkey may be the centerpiece, but the side dishes are the real stars. “Thanksgiving is one of those meals where I care more about the sides than the main event!” she recently shared with her followers.

It has been revealed that in a recent Instagram post, Ina revealed that she’s especially excited to make several new dishes from her latest cookbook, Simply Ina. There are familiar Thanksgiving favorites with a few clever twists, along with some store-bought shortcuts that prove even the Barefoot Contessa knows when to let someone else do part of the work. It’s a reassuring approach to a meal that can demand a lot of time in the kitchen.

Here’s a look at the six recipes Ina shared, along with similar Taste of Home dishes you can make for your own Thanksgiving dinner.

Sources indicate that ina’s combination of caramelized butternut squash and dried cranberries makes particularly good sense for Thanksgiving. Roasting brings out the squash’s natural sweetness, while the tart cranberries provide some welcome contrast. It’s a colorful alternative to the sweeter squash dishes that tend to find their way onto holiday tables, but one that wouldn’t look out of place next to a generous helping of Ina’s sausage and herb stuffing.

Try a Taste of Home version: Butternut Squash Jumble.

It has been revealed that ina has always been a champion of making Thanksgiving easier, and her new turkey gravy takes that philosophy a step further. She’s starting with canned turkey gravy, then dressing it up for a richer, more homemade flavor. It’s a practical shortcut for someone who’s spent years teaching us how to make gravy from scratch. And as Ina points out, nobody wants leftover turkey without gravy, either. Making enough for Friday’s sandwiches is simply good planning.

Try a Taste of Home version: Make-Ahead Turkey Gravy.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

Industry observers note that mashed potatoes are practically guaranteed a place on the Thanksgiving table, but Ina’s addition of garlic gives this familiar favorite a welcome savory kick. Ina actually starts with Bob Evans prepared mashed potatoes, then dresses them up with garlic confit, butter and half-and-half. With so many sweet, rich dishes competing for space on the plate, garlic mashed potatoes offer a little balance without sacrificing any of the buttery comfort everyone expects.

Try a Taste of Home version: Garlic Mashed Potatoes.

Brussels sprouts have come a long way from the boiled vegetables many of us remember from childhood, and Ina’s version pairs them with pecorino, a salty, sharp sheep’s milk cheese. The combination makes sense: The cheese adds richness and a savory bite that complements the sprouts’ slightly bitter flavor. It’s the sort of side dish that might even persuade a few longtime Brussels sprouts skeptics to reconsider.

Try a Taste of Home version: Brussels Sprouts with Garlic & Goat Cheese.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

In a recent development, here’s where Ina’s fondness for a good shortcut really comes into play. Her Chunky Cranberry Conserve starts with canned whole-berry cranberry sauce, which she dresses up with grated Granny Smith apple, orange juice and zest, raisins and pecans. The result has more texture and complexity than the contents of the can alone, without requiring you to start from scratch.

Sources indicate that there’s something reassuring in knowing Ina Garten is perfectly content to open a can of cranberry sauce on Thanksgiving. If it’s good enough for Ina, the rest of us can probably stop apologizing for it.

Try a Taste of Home version: Cranberry-Apple Chutney.

Industry observers note that sweet potatoes are a Thanksgiving staple, but Ina’s combination of maple syrup and chipotle gives them a welcome change of direction. The maple enhances their natural sweetness, while the smoky heat of chipotle keeps the dish firmly on the savory side of dinner.

And there’s another shortcut hiding in this dish. In a recent interview with Cup of Jo, Ina revealed that she uses prepared mashed sweet potatoes from Trader Joe’s, adding chipotle powder, maple syrup, butter and seasonings to make them her own. She figures nobody would know she hadn’t roasted the sweet potatoes herself, and with everything else that needs cooking on Thanksgiving, that’s a shortcut (and a great Trader Joe’s find) worth stealing.

Try a Taste of Home version: Hot Honey Sweet Potatoes.

How a Newly introduced Restaurant Injected Retro “Latin Soul” Into a New-Build Space

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1002 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eater

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bar Nuestro on private dining nooks, vintage sourcing, and more﻿.
  • It has been revealed that opened at the end of October, Bar Nuestro is Washington, D.C.’s newest bistro serving European- and Latin-inspired dishes and drinks.
  • Pre Shift: Tell me about the design concept for Bar Nuestro.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bar Nuestro on private dining nooks, vintage sourcing, and more﻿.

It has been revealed that opened at the end of October, Bar Nuestro is Washington, D.C.’s newest bistro serving European- and Latin-inspired dishes and drinks. Founder Daniella Senior and designer Shawn Hausman (whose firm worked on iconic spaces like the Chateau Marmont and the ’80s club Area) collaborated on the project, ensuring that the space captured the same retro vibe as the menu. I especially hope their mini-private-dining room concept catches on.

Pre Shift: Tell me about the design concept for Bar Nuestro.

In a recent development, daniella Senior: We wanted the space to really feel—even though it’s a new buildout—that it’s been there a long time. I’m kind of tired of the same aesthetic going around, one that’s almost too clean, too new, too matchy-matchy. I think that doesn’t, at times, help you communicate what the food is trying to communicate. For us, the food and the space work together. We wanted it to feel very Old World. We took a lot of inspiration from Vienna’s old corner cafes, which have been institutions for a while. We wanted a “We’ve been here a minute” type of feel.

It has been revealed that from our furniture to our tiles, [the Bar Nuestro team and designer Shawn Hausman] sourced a lot of vintage pieces, about 25 percent of the furniture. We have chairs that came from Austria and Italy in the ’30s and fabric with vintage patterns. When Shawn was traveling through Europe, he’d send pictures of things he found, and I sourced accent pieces—like the credenza in our garden room, vases, menu holders, a vintage phone—in local vintage shops.

It has been revealed that it’s definitely loud. And it was definitely fun to see it come together. But don’t get me wrong, there were times where I was like, “I’m not sure how these things are gonna go together.” Now I’m thrilled with the result.

Industry observers note that it seems like there are many different kinds of spaces within the one restaurant. Was that intentional?

Industry observers note that I love the feeling that, even within the same space, you’re able to get different vibes. We have a cafe side that we transition into an aperitivo room, which has all these textures and shades of blue. The paint job in there is insanity. It took over two weeks to paint this 300-square-foot space because of the level of detail. Then the main dining room is bright and feels very cozy, and there’s the garden room, which is primarily green, and it’s got stripes throughout the ceiling and the walls. And then we have the patio, which is a little more zen. Each room has a different personality, which I love.

Some of the tables in the main dining room are also sectioned off like semi-private dining nooks. Can you tell me about that design decision?

Sources indicate that even though the space is relatively large, we didn’t want it to feel that way. We wanted that feeling of coziness and warmth that you can’t get from a big open space. So we have three of these “mini private rooms”—they only seat about five people—but in them, you feel like you’re in your own world. Those were inspired by a cafe in Vienna.

Also, we wanted Bar Nuestro to be for everyone, and that includes kids. I have a young child myself, and I know you can get nervous sometimes in nicer restaurants if your kids are being too loud or disruptive. These rooms allow us to give that privacy to those who want it, while you still get to be part of the action of the dining room. [A mirror trim around the space] provides continuity. It helps the guests in the mini dining booths feel more connected to the rest of the dining room, and it helps with service. Without being intrusive and having to check from a super close distance how your guests are doing, staff can see where diners are within their meal.

Sources indicate that I love how many hooks there are in the space. Restaurants never have enough hooks for purses and coats!

Industry observers note that thank you. Being comfortable within the dining experience has a lot to do with the lighting and the music, but things like hooks aren’t often paid sufficient attention to. I come from a culture where putting a purse on a floor is a no-no, so a lot of the restaurants back home have purse chairs that they bring over. We didn’t quite have space for that, but we wanted there to be sufficient hooks so that people could relax even more.

According to recent reports, do you have any tips for other restaurant operators about working with a designer? How do you communicate your vision effectively?

It has been revealed that we wanted a very unique design, and when I was thinking about other spaces that I really enjoyed, I realized that Shawn had been the designer. So that made it, for us, a very natural decision. From there, it’s all about being very clear about expectations. Understanding costs and having a clear budget from the start is incredibly important.

Bar Nuestro opened just a few weeks ago. How has it been going so far?

So far it’s going great. We’re very happy and we’ve been well received by the neighborhood. We’re excited to keep building it. Opening a restaurant is kind of like a camel’s back: There’s the first hump of opening the location itself, and then you have the second hump which is really building the community around it. A lot of people only see that first hump, but it’s a two-part thing. This second part has been challenging and rewarding. It’s like, “Now the space is set, let’s work on what our day-to-day looks like.”.

#289. Where’d You Go, Crêpes Suzette?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1160 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Saveur

Where’d You Go, Crêpes Suzette?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1160 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, there’s something simultaneously comforting and dazzling about setting a dessert on fire: Candles atop a birthday cake; the meringue encrusting a baked Alaska; the caramelized fruit in a classic bananas Foster.
  • It has been revealed that crêpes Suzette is a surprisingly simple dish considering its decadent, theatrical reputation.
  • For such a famous dish, though, its appearance on restaurant menus is increasingly rare.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, there’s something simultaneously comforting and dazzling about setting a dessert on fire: Candles atop a birthday cake; the meringue encrusting a baked Alaska; the caramelized fruit in a classic bananas Foster. But chief among them is one whose very name promises something different, something with French sophistication and an air of mystery that demands a moniker all its own: crêpes Suzette.

It has been revealed that crêpes Suzette is a surprisingly simple dish considering its decadent, theatrical reputation. The drama comes from the flames—thin, traditional French crêpes are drenched in a sauce made of orange liqueur, which is then set ablaze (typically tableside in many restaurants), causing the spirits to simmer and the sugars to caramelize. French chef Andrea Calstier, of Michelin-starred La Bastide in North Salem, Newly introduced York, grew up eating them with his family, and in the brasseries of his home country.

For such a famous dish, though, its appearance on restaurant menus is increasingly rare. And for such an iconic French dessert, well, it may not technically be French at all. So where did these flaming pancakes come from? Where did they go? And isn’t it about time we bring them back?

Industry observers note that while there are conflicting reports about the original creator of crêpes Suzette, the top candidate is Henri Charpentier, chef at the Café de Paris in Monte Carlo, Monaco, in the late 1800s. But while multiple roads lead back to Charpentier, the path gets murky, contradicted by both general plausibility and Charpentier himself.

In a recent development, originally, Charpentier claimed credit for the iconic dish in his autobiography, Life à la Henri: Being the Memoirs of Henri Charpentier. In this 1934 volume, he suggested that the dish was a happy accident, tinged with drama. He alleged that as a young man working at the Café de Paris, he had been carrying a platter of crêpes to the Prince of Wales (the future King Edward VII) and stepped too near a chafing dish, setting the crêpes on fire, to the shock and delight of the prince, who proposed naming the newly created dish after his dining companion, a young woman named Suzette. (Frustratingly little information is available on who this Suzette may have been, if she was a real person at all.).

The story has the right theatrical touches for the dish, but it is almost certainly apocryphal, not least because Charpentier himself, in an interview with American writer Elsie Lee for the 1950s “Compleat Imbiber” series, said that he had developed the dish by taking a beloved childhood fruit crêpe and adding the then-fashionable touches of a liquor-based sauce and, presumably, a flame.

Wherever it came from, though, and whatever Charpentier had to say about it, Suzette’s unwitting legacy has endured for more than a century—her crêpes have remained a household name, even if they have fallen somewhat out of style. While chef Calstier notes that they’re still “served in many restaurants” in his native Marseille and that “French customers…are accustomed to seeing crêpes Suzette in any brasserie,” he admitted that “here in the U.S., they are more difficult to find.”.

Recent findings suggest that part of the reason may be that, as with many dishes that predate the Edwardian era, it simply went out of fashion. But according to Lucile Plaza, executive chef at Benoit New York, it’s a result of the dish’s inherent service requirements: “True tableside service requires high staffing levels and precise choreography that a busy modern kitchen can’t always support daily,” she says. In London’s West End, fine-dining heavyweights Savoy Grill and The Ritz take this showmanship to the extreme, with portable burners and bottles of Grand Marnier on wooden trolleys.

But while there are complications to adding an edible spectacle to a restaurant menu, there are benefits, too. Chef Plaza notes that for the kitchen, “Suzette is brilliant because it is the ultimate way to use leftover crêpes. The intense bathing in the hot, rich citrus sauce revives the starch perfectly.” But not every restaurant that serves crêpes Suzette does so with a tableside flourish: In London’s St. John’s Wood, Oslo Court Restaurant, which is famous for its retro menu of classics like steak Diane and sole Veronique (two more of Edward VII's girlfriends, perhaps?), crêpes Suzette are brûléed with a torch in the kitchen rather than set aflame at the table. Adding crêpes Suzette to a menu may only be as hard as a restaurant wants it to be.

Sources indicate that A burst of blue-tinged flame may not be necessary for the dish to achieve its signature caramelization, but it is key to the show—and a major point in favor of the dish’s present-day revival. As the old saying goes, “we eat with our eyes first,” and it’s truer than ever today. In fact, for many diners in the age of social media, it’s the phone that eats first, and that’s where crêpes Suzette has real potential for a modern renaissance. Nearly 400,000 viewers have watched a YouTube video of the tableside crêpes Suzette service at the London Ritz, and more than a million have viewed a TikTok of crêpes Suzette being prepared tableside at Switzerland’s five-star Suvretta House in Saint Moritz.

Spectacle is cool again, and whether dining out or cooking at home, we want to feel astonished and excited by the foods we eat. While a tableside flambé may prove logistically complicated at a restaurant scale, the feat is significantly easier to pull off at home—all it takes is a lighter or a match and a little confidence. Chef Calstier, for one, indicates that crêpes Suzette are a favorite of his wife, Elena, adding, “You can prepare everything in advance and do the flambé in front of your guests to wow them.” Plus, he says, “they don’t require many ingredients, beyond that bottle of Grand Marnier that we all have stashed away somewhere. They’re quite simple to make.”.

Moreover, as delectable as classic crêpes Suzette are, they lend themselves well to upcoming takes and customizations. Chef Plaza’s version at Benoit has a cherry twist: “Replacing Grand Marnier with kirsch is a natural match,” she notes. “The dry cherry distillate brings an incredible aroma to the tableside without adding cloying sugar.” Meanwhile, at La Bastide, chef Calstier dishes up a twist that uses French toast instead of crêpes while sticking to the classic flavors and flambé. We asked one of our favorite pastry chefs, Caroline Schiff, author of Daily Desserts: Treats on Repeat, to develop a savory version for us, which she describes as “a cheeky little twist” on the classic. In her take, inspired by French onion soup, crêpes layered with caramelized onions and nutty gruyère are set ablaze with a splash of sherry. “They are at once a novelty and a nod to the classic,” she says.

Charpentier, one imagines, would approve.

#288. Why Did My Pumpkin Pie Crack and How Can I Fix It?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (906 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tasteofhome

Why Did My Pumpkin Pie Crack and How Can I Fix It?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (906 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here's how to avert dessert disaster before it strikes—with tips for hiding it just in case.
  • In a recent development, most cooking mistakes are fixable.
  • Pumpkin pie will crack when the eggs are overbeaten, when the filling is overbaked, and when the pie experiences rapid temperature changes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Here's how to avert dessert disaster before it strikes—with tips for hiding it just in case.

In a recent development, most cooking mistakes are fixable. When it comes to baking, though, one wrong move can ruin the whole recipe. It’s extra frustrating when you’re trying to make a Norman Rockwell-worthy pumpkin pie for Thanksgiving, and a huge crack splits right through the center. Yes, you can still eat a cracked pumpkin pie, but if you can avoid the crack (or cover it up), all the better. The eyes eat first, as they say!

Pumpkin pie will crack when the eggs are overbeaten, when the filling is overbaked, and when the pie experiences rapid temperature changes. Not to put the blame on one single ingredient, but it all comes down to the eggs—or, rather, how you treat them.

Industry observers note that pumpkin pie is technically a baked custard (like cheesecake), and eggs are thickeners in custards. Overbeating the eggs aerates the filling, which causes it to inflate during baking, then deflate and crack as it cools. Overbaking the filling will tighten the eggs and cause the filling to crack, too. And even if you pull the pie out at just the right moment, the filling can still crack from a rapid temperature change that makes the eggs contract. Ugh. It seems like there’s a lot working against you, but taking preemptive steps reduces your chances of ending up with a cracked pumpkin pie.

These are all the steps I take as a professional baker to reduce the risk of cracking, as well as a few tricks to cover up cracks if they appear.

Sources indicate that seasoned bakers know that whipping eggs aerates them. That’s usually a plus when you want structure in baking recipes, but in pumpkin pie, it’s the catalyst for a cracked filling. The pie’s filling will puff up in the oven, then promptly collapse as the eggs deflate. That structural change causes the filling to crack. It’s the same problem that leads to a cracked cheesecake!

Room-temperature eggs blend into custards much more easily, so take the eggs out of the fridge 30 to 60 minutes before starting, depending on the kitchen temperature. Once you add the eggs to the filling, mix them just until they’re combined.

Even if you use a reliable pumpkin pie recipe with tons of five-star reviews (cough, cough: our pumpkin pie recipe) and follow it to the very letter, it may be the oven that betrays you in the end.

In a recent development, ovens often have miscalibrated internal thermometers, so even if you set your oven to the recommended 350°F, the real temperature may be significantly higher. Before you realize it, the pumpkin pie is overbaked and already cracked.

Buy an oven thermometer and hang it from one of the oven racks for all your bakes going forward. They usually cost about $10—totally worth the investment!

Recent findings suggest that have you ever read a recipe with specific oven rack placements? They’re not there as a suggestion; oven rack placement significantly affects your bake. Ovens produce heat from the bottom, and this creates zones as that heat rises: hotter on top and cooler down below.

Since you want your pumpkin pie to bake relatively low and slow, the bottom oven rack is best. The filling cooks evenly, and the pie crust browns beautifully—no cracks and no soggy bottom.

Sources indicate that the best way to avoid an overbaked (and therefore cracked) pumpkin pie is to know the signs of doneness. The edges should dome a bit, but the center should be wobbly like Jell-O, not rippling like an ocean wave. The pumpkin pie will continue to bake from the residual heat once the oven is off.

Sources indicate that this is where your oven light comes in handy. Don’t open the oven door until you see the edges start to dome, or cool air will rush inside before it’s supposed to. Only when you see the dome should you check for a wobbly center.

According to recent reports, even after meticulously following every single step to avoid a pumpkin pie crack, a rapid change in temperature can undo all that hard work. The shock of removing a pumpkin pie from a hot oven and setting down in a cold November kitchen (or, worse, a 32° fridge) will cause the eggs to contract, leading to a crack.

According to recent reports, once the pie is done baking, turn the oven off and leave the door slightly ajar. If the oven door doesn’t stay open on its own, prop it open with a wooden spoon. Keep the pie in the oven until it’s completely cooled.

So, your pumpkin pie did crack. That’s OK! It happens from time to time, even when you follow all the rules. The good news is that the pie still tastes great. Even better? You can cover up the crack with homemade whipped cream. Pile it in the center or pipe it in a decorative pattern. Use stabilized whipped cream if you want to add the topping a day ahead of time. You can even grate fresh nutmeg on top for dimension.

According to recent reports, you can do the same with Swiss meringue. Spread it simply, or pipe it on top for a big, showy decoration. Toast the meringue so it’s beautifully golden brown.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ever since Starbucks started co-opting seemingly every street corner and strip mall and multiple waves of coffee snobbery (laudatory) have risen in direct opposition to mass market espresso, it’s safe to say the average consumer has changed what they expect from a cup of coffee. Just look at the coffee maker aisle in any big-box store and, along with single-serve and pod machines and other barista-replacing gadgets, you’ll find a slew of coffee makers that promise to make you dozens of drink styles, froth up some milk, and bring you “instant” cold brew. But sometimes the simplest way to make coffee is still pretty darn good. What we’re saying is don’t discount the drip coffee machine.

The cliché of bad drip coffee from a cheap piece of plastic doesn’t apply anymore. And even lots of cheap coffee makers are so much better than they used to be. If you’re in the market for a lot of coffee with little effort, your options are now legion. Companies like Breville, Fellow, Oxo, and Ratio have joined the original king of drip, Technivorm, in making quality appliances that better control factors like water temperature, flow rate, and bloom time, several of which brew coffee that’s almost as good as what you can get with a kettle and a pour-over setup.

Our writers and editors have tested more than three dozen coffee makers over the years, and below we get into the ones that make a good cup of coffee, the ones that make a great cup of coffee, and the unfortunate ones that just can’t keep up with today’s coffee-brewing arms race.

It has been revealed that newly introduced in this upgrade: We tested two new coffee makers with plastic-free brewing systems from Caraway and Simply Good Coffee. We also tested the new Braun OptiBrew Pro, which includes an onboard milk frother among other features.

Capacity: 10 cupsCarafe style: ThermalDimensions: 8.9" x 8.9" x 12"Weight: 9.6 lb.Features: Adjustable brew water ratio; adjustable temperature settings, flavor profile settings, programmable 24-hour timer; Wi-Fi connectivity; cold-brew capable; SCA Golden Cup capabilitiesWarranty: 3 years.

The Aiden is as close to a perfect drip coffee maker as we’ve tested because its designers considered nearly every need. But even with all its bells and whistles, the Aiden still has to make coffee that tastes good. And it does. Senior editor Noah Kaufman compared it side-by-side to carafes of pour-over and found both hit fruity and caramel notes, with real nuance and depth of flavor.

What we love: The Aiden is customizable across so many parameters you might lose track: You can set water temperature (anywhere between 122°F and 210°F); the time and number of pulses of water (think of them as the individual water pours if you were making pour-over coffee); and bloom time that helps get rid of gasses that can make your coffee taste sour. This machine can also make a smooth pot of cold brew by slowly dripping water over the course of several hours. (Machines that claim they can make cold brew in minutes don't usually live up to their own hype.).

And even though you can tweak your coffee in all the ways outlined above, you can also just use the Aiden like a basic one-button drip coffee maker. The Instant Brew option will use however much water is in the tank, brewing at water temperatures recommended by the Specialty Coffee Association (SCA) in its Golden Cup standards, which mark water temperature and coffee-to-water ratios for ideal flavor. To paraphrase Fellow’s founder, who visited us in the Test Kitchen, he wanted the machine to work for both coffee connoisseurs and total noobs.

Industry observers note that the Aiden also features a slew of carefully considered, where-have-you-been-my-whole-life details. Its two filter baskets—one for three cups or fewer and one for more than three cups—have spring-loaded seals to prevent drips when you remove them to empty the grounds into the garbage. It doesn't have a warming plate because it doesn't need one—the included thermal carafe kept coffee hot on the dining room table for around two hours. And the removable side water tank is easier to fill than either a built-in tank or one on the backside of the machine.

Recent findings suggest that during the testing, we also tried Fellow’s Drops program. It’s not exactly a coffee subscription—you order via text on demand—but it gives you access to various rare and small-batch beans from Fellow’s roaster partners. The Aiden comes preloaded with specific brew settings for recent Drops offerings, adjusting water temps and pulse cycles beyond the standard light/medium/dark profiles and the resulting coffee produced using the Drops settings was truly excellent. Brewing the same beans with both the Drops settings and the regular settings make a real difference. It’s one of the closest ways to recreate that “rare pour-over at your favorite café” experience at home.

What we’d leave: Compared to most of the drip coffee makers you’ll find at a significant-box store, it’s somewhat expensive. However, within the recent wave of better-quality drip coffee machines, it falls right in line with average pricing we’ve come to expect from a daily coffee workhorse that produces this level of coffee.

In the long run: Noah has used the Aiden about five times a week for over two years, and it has lived up to its early promise. The coffee has remained consistently good, and we’ve had no concerns with the interface, plus the removable side water tank has continued to prove its convenience.

It has been revealed that the Aiden is a precision machine, and regular maintenance matters. Noah found this out the hard way after too many months of skipping descaling, which eventually produced a loud noise that sounded like the pump might be on its last legs. To get an unfiltered read on customer service, he reached out as a regular customer rather than identifying himself as a Bon Appétit editor. Fellow responded within two days, pointed him toward descaling as a fix, and after he sent a video of the machine in action, offered to replace it entirely. They also recommended descaling monthly going forward, which felt a little aggressive, but the clear instructions were appreciated.

Ratio has been trying to limit the plastic across its whole lineup and offers up this stainless steel dripper as an add-on to the Ratio 6, which ensures no hot water or coffee touch plastic during the brewing process.

The Fellow Aiden is a great coffee maker, but it has a lot going on. We know that some people’s ideal drip coffee maker is one you load up with coffee, turn on, and leave to do its thing. The Ratio Six (which is actually an 8-cup coffee maker, don’t let the name fool you) lets you do just that without compromising on the quality of the brew.

What we love: It’s got one button that begins the brew process. There is no water temperature to set, no flavor profiles to adjust. The resulting coffee is absolutely delicious and takes no effort on your part. The Ratio Six (Series 2) includes a thermal carafe that outperformed all the others we tried (the Fellow was a close second), keeping coffee hot for over two hours.

What we'd leave: The Ratio's fixed water tank at the back of the appliance is a real bear to fill. The brew basket also sits on top of the carafe instead of being attached to the body in any way. That made it easy to empty, but it was a little precarious to set up until we got the hang of it.

In the long run: Ratio’s 5-year warranty is longer than just about any other coffee maker you can buy (Technivorm’s Moccamaster is the only other one with a warranty that long), and it’s clear why the manufacturer felt comfortable making such a long offer. However, the things we found a little irritating about the Ratio’s design at the beginning did not get less irritating over time though.
