    Season 1¼ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (4–5) all over with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

    Heat 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large pot over medium. Add 1 tsp. crushed fennel seeds, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. ground cardamom, and ¼ tsp. ground cloves and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 20 seconds. Add chicken, one 1" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth or chicken stock, and 3 cups water. Bring to a simmer over medium-high heat. Partially cover pot, reduce heat to medium-low, and simmer until an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part of a thigh registers at least 165°, 15–18 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board and let cool slightly. Reduce heat to low and cover pot. Using 2 forks, shred chicken.

    According to recent reports, melt 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 cup orzo and cook, stirring often, until golden brown and fragrant, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

    Recent findings suggest that scrape orzo mixture into pot with broth. Increase heat to medium and simmer broth, uncovered, until orzo is just al dente, 8–10 minutes. Remove soup from heat and add shredded chicken, 5 oz. baby kale or spinach, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice. Stir until greens are just wilted. Taste and season with more salt if needed.

In the last 24 hours alone, Baraghani has been busy beating out creative director Terrence O’Connor for a Best Body prize at the podcast How Long Gone’s inaugural “Goneies” Award Show, (Baraghani was asked to remove his blazer to reveal a formfitting Dario Vitale–era Versace pink tank top) before running into David Tanis while shopping for groceries.

    Industry observers note that when Baraghani unveiled he would be opening a restaurant this fall near Union Square with restaurateur Michael Silber, publications began tripping over themselves to cover the news. Still, he says, few have pushed him on the true meaning of the name Ditto. Perhaps they were too busy trying to keep up.

    Baraghani takes a seat on one of the iron stools beside the prep table and there is a rare, brief silence, which is broken almost immediately by the tinny opening notes of a techno song emanating from the crew performing a renovation on the lower floor. I inquire about his cortisol levels as he juggles opening Ditto a few blocks away, the second cookbook he has just shot in this apartment, and now the remodel below us.

    Baraghani grins. “I feel calm,” he insists. “If something goes wrong, I can fix it, because I feel pretty clear on what I want to achieve.”.

    He has spent the last 10 years peppering his recipes with caveats. “I know that my food may be a touch too lemony for some,” he writes in The Cook You Want To Be. “And that I use what has been called a ridiculous amount of herbs.”.

    In a recent development, his background too. Years ago, he penned an essay for this magazine about growing up Iranian in a post-9/11 America; he started to go by Andy instead of Andisheh and bought an “Italian Stallion” T-shirt. He wrote about learning to accept his sexuality in restaurant kitchens, where he rarely encountered other gay men, and in his family life. He grew up in the Bay Area, the son of parents who had emigrated from Iran to Berkeley in 1977. The piece ended with an admission: “So as nice as it would be for this story to end with that Iran feature or getting my dream job at Bon Appétit, the truth is that I’m still trying to figure things out. It’s not always steady progress.”.

    Since I had a baby six weeks ago, I have been walking around floored that the adults in my life could have ever been children, but with Andy, I don’t have to work too hard to picture it. He has a particularly cheerful sense of wonder. When I ask about it, he says it comes from his upbringing. His parents were political activists. Andy’s mother worked as an aesthetician (yes, he established his famous skin-care routine early). He grew up surrounded by a diverse community of immigrants who would invite his family to their celebrations and into their homes, where a young Baraghani got to taste dishes from far-flung places. After he landed in Upcoming York, he would take respite in stints abroad, traveling from hostel to hostel so he could eat his way across Vietnam, Lebanon, and Turkey.

    In a recent development, now, though, Baraghani notes he is done footnoting his vision. In the intervening years since that essay, Baraghani has written and cooked and tasted at warp speed. He was bound to self-actualize in the same timeframe it took the rest of us to figure out how to style barrel-leg pants. Or perhaps it’s the reality of having to reckon with what he can’t change: In 2024, after a battle with small-cell lung cancer, his beloved father passed away. Baraghani tells me that before it was stagnancy, his greatest fear was losing a parent. He has since learned that loss isn’t something to solve, but a tremendous void one must learn to live with.

    “There’s an explicit confidence you’ll see [at Ditto,]” he says. The dishes will weave together all of the threads of Baraghani-ism: seasonal vegetables prepared deftly with Persian flourishes, blending tart and sour and aromatic with a firm point-of-view. If the specifics seem hard to picture, I think that might be the point. Baraghani has thrived historically by taking a straightforward-seeming dish and twisting it just off-kilter, so it is a few degrees punchier and much more beautiful than you were expecting. The result is food that is as much about the people and places evoked by the flavors as it is about aesthetic provocation. (That Italian Stallion shirt, he tells me, is long gone.).

    Industry observers note that literally speaking, Ditto will be a revival of the sort of counter-service restaurant Baraghani has long adored, from Gjusta in Los Angeles to City Bakery in Latest York. He and Silber sprang for a shiny rotisserie oven, for what they’re calling a “beyond chicken program,” with intends for spit-roasted porchetta, romanesco, and cabbage.

    It has been revealed that the goal is dishes that are palpably human, in a space Baraghani hopes will seem accessible to everyone. It was important for both owners to find a space in a hub neighborhood. With the storefront they chose, a former Agnès B. on 16th Street, Greenmarket shoppers can stop by for a selection of California-ish sides and salads displayed Yotam Ottolenghi–style, counter pastries, or just to peruse marketplace provisions: tahini, harissa, dates (and, for now, no tinned fish). Maybe, one day, they’ll stay open for dinner service, but for now the proposal is breakfast and lunch.

    Suddenly Baraghani is moving again, reaching for his phone to show me a photo of a dish he would have loved to serve, had Con Ed turned on the gas in time for a September opening: a mound of spicy tuna salad piled perkily in a blanched tomato with a turret of scallion greens.

    The sight makes me hungry, and I realize we still haven’t gone out for that cream. Ninety minutes have passed and I have yet to ask any of the questions I’d prepared for Baraghani, who keeps surprising me with disclosures. (Such as: He did not speak until he was three years old.).

    Suddenly, it is time to head to Ditto for a tour, cream and scones be damned.

    As we walk over, I ask about the restaurant’s name. He asks if I’ve seen the movie Ghost. I have, but not for a while. “It’s another way to say ‘I love you,’” he states simply, before disappearing to join a meeting.

    It has been revealed that later I dig up that scene Baraghani mentioned and press play. In it, Whoopi Goldberg tries to convince a frustrated Demi Moore that her recently deceased boyfriend has returned as a ghost. Moore jumps up in disbelief to flee the restaurant as Patrick Swayze, the boyfriend, scrambles to find a way to prove to her that he’s right there. “Tell her ‘ditto,’” he urges Goldberg, who screams “ditto” after Moore as she bolts. “Ditto!” It’s their code word for “I love you too.”.

    Moore stops in her tracks and turns, her gaze connecting with a man she misses, who she isn’t totally sure is there.

    In a recent development, and for the first time in a while, she is no longer in motion. She is still.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that this creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

    In a recent development, note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, promptly empty the contents into a new pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

    Find more Rachel Gurjar recipes here.

    To a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

    Scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, since The Great British Bake Off premiered in 2010, countless talented contestants have shared their passion for puddings, tarts, and everything in between with the world. But only the very best dominated biscuits, perfected their pastries, and showed off their cake skills to get crowned the winner.

    But where are those GBBO champs now? From authoring cookbooks to welcoming children, they have kept busy. Some made baking their full-time career, while others stepped away from their ovens. Wherever they ended up, one thing’s for sure: Once a star baker, always a star baker.

    Recent findings suggest that “The boy who bakes” paved the way as the first-ever winner of The Great British Bake Off, or The Great British Baking Show as it’s called in the U.S. and Canada. The former debt collector has since focused solely on his writing, cookbooks, and television appearances, often contributing to magazine columns and appearing on demonstrates such as Sunday Brunch and Good Morning America.

    Jo Wheatley is one of the few Bake Off champions to have stepped away from their cooking career. Since her season of the show, she has written two cookbooks and even run her own cooking school for a time before retiring and moving to Portugal with her husband. She still shares the occasional recipe on social media and on her blog, but for the most part, keeps it to “sunny snaps & padel in between,” according to her Instagram bio.

    Sources indicate that since winning the show, Whaite graduated from Le Cordon Bleu and opened his own cooking school. He also started a bakery and a snack brand. He has appeared on Steph’s Packed Lunch and Strictly Come Dancing, where he finished as the runner-up. He has authored six cookbooks and a memoir, and married his longtime partner in 2024.

    Recent findings suggest that the winner of Season 4, Quinn continues her work as a creative consultant, food artist, and designer, and has authored a cookbook. She also holds the Guinness Book of World Records for making the largest Jaffa cake and Jammie Dodgers. She previously hosted a YouTube baking series and creates custom cakes, shares recipes online, and makes occasional media appearances.

    Sources indicate that nancy Birtwhistle wasn’t a one-and-done after her 2014 GBBO win—she also participated in The Great British Baking Show: Holidays. Since appearing on the franchise, Birtwhistle has penned a few books on both baking and sustainable living. The GBBO alum also regularly makes appearances on TV and radio reveals.

    Industry observers note that since dominating Season 6, Nadiya Hussain has become one of the UK’s most prominent celebrity chefs. She has hosted numerous TV indicates, including Nadiya’s British Food Adventure, Nadiya Bakes, and The Chronicles of Nadiya, and was even the subject of the documentary Nadiya: Anxiety and Me. The star baker also wrote over 10 cookbooks, plus fiction and children’s books, along with an autobiography.

    Recent findings suggest that A year after her 2015 win, Hussain was even commissioned to bake the birthday cake for Queen Elizabeth’s 90th. And in 2020, the chef received an MBE, or Most Excellent Order of the British Empire, for her work in the culinary and broadcasting industry.

    Since winning Season 7, Candice Brown has opened her own pub, The Green Man, with her brother in England, as well as Margo’s, a restaurant and deli. She has also penned two cookbooks and written food columns for local newspapers. Brown has also made appearances on numerous other demonstrates, including Dancing On Ice, Loose Women, Pointless Celebrities, and Celebrity Mastermind. She also played a role in the movie Love Sarah.

    Since winning Season 8, Faldo has founded her own wedding and specialty cake business: Sophie Faldo Couture Cakes. In addition to her day job, she teaches baking classes in person and online. Plus, she returned to the Bake Off kitchens in 2023 and won The Great Christmas Bake Off.

    It has been revealed that things have only gotten busier for Rahul Mandal after his Season 9 win. Since the show, he has released a cookbook and continues baking in his downtime and sharing his creations on social media. He also returned to the franchise and won The Great Fresh Year Bake Off special in 2021. However, the champion still works full-time as a research scientist and engineer at the University of Sheffield. Mandal has also gotten married and had a child.

    Industry observers note that david Atherton balances his baking with everyday life. The Bake Off winner works as a practice nurse and health advisor by day, and continues his baking pursuits by night, so to speak. Since his win, he has written a series of children’s and adult cookbooks, writes a regular food column for The Guardian, and shares home cooking and baking tips on social media. Additionally, Atherton teamed up with fellow Season 10 baker Michael Chakraverty to launch the Sticky Bun Boys baking and pop culture podcast.

    Industry observers note that peter Sawkins made history in 2020 when he became the youngest baker to win GBBO at just 20 years old—and that wasn’t the end of his time on the franchise. Sawkins returned and won The Great Fresh Year’s Bake Off in 2025. Meanwhile, Sawkins has graduated from college and completed pastry training at the Amaury Guichon Pastry Academy. He has also published two cookbooks and frequently shares recipes and baking tutorials online. Additionally, Sawkins works part-time in sports fundraising and plays competitive badminton.

    It’s been five years since Giuseppe’s Season 12 win, and he’s upped the ante on his culinary career since. In the past half-decade, Dell’Anno has authored two cookbooks and contributed to a third. He also runs a successful cake business, teaches baking classes in person and online, and frequently shares his baking insights on broadcast television and in food columns. Like some of his fellow winners, he’s also made appearances at local festivals.

    Known for recipes featuring bold Malaysian flavors, Syabira Yusoff continues to feed her love of baking by sharing tutorials on social media, hosting online culinary workshops, and judging baking competitions herself. Impressively, she does all this in her free time while continuing her career as a cardiovascular researcher and bioinformatician at King’s College London. Most recently, she unveiled her engagement to her longtime partner just this past July.

    Matty Edgell has stayed busy, both professionally and personally, since winning Season 14. The former high school teacher resigned after the show and now focuses on creating recipes on his website while also sharing baking tutorials on social media. He also tied the knot and welcomed his first child. Edgell publishes a Substack newsletter and has made appearances on TV shows and at local food festivals.

    Since her 2024 win, Grasso has kept plenty busy. Not only does the winner post weekly recipes to her Instagram account, but she also released two digital cookbooks earlier this year: Cooking Therapy and Baking Therapy. She has made appearances at local food events such as the Gloucester Quays Food Festival and recently opened up about her bipolar 2 diagnosis.

    In a recent development, as the most recent winner of GBBO, Jasmine Mitchell has only a year behind her in the culinary spotlight, but she’s exploded onto the scene with gusto. Since her time on the show, Mitchell has appeared as a guest on numerous talk highlights, appeared as a judge on Danish Bake Off, and currently has a cookbook in the works. She’s doing all this while finishing medical school!

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • “I don’t have time” should never be an excuse to skip breakfast.
    • Using an unsweetened soy or nut milk will keep the pudding more pumpkin-forward than dairy milk (and keeps the recipe vegan, of course), but any milk you have on hand will work here.
    • Recent findings suggest that healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    “I don’t have time” should never be an excuse to skip breakfast. Take this overnight oat–chia pudding hybrid, which comes together in barely 10 minutes. (I’m betting that’s less time than it takes to stand in line at the grocery store to buy a container of worse-tasting, more expensive oatmeal!) Grab a can of pumpkin and some baking staples, mix it up, then pop the bowl in the fridge. The next morning you’ll be rewarded with a lightly sweet, mousse-like treat that’s actually good for you—don’t forget to finish each bowl with a dollop of yogurt for a pumpkin-pie-with-whipped-cream vibe. Self-care rarely tastes this good.

    Using an unsweetened soy or nut milk will keep the pudding more pumpkin-forward than dairy milk (and keeps the recipe vegan, of course), but any milk you have on hand will work here.

    Recent findings suggest that healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares nourishing, craveable recipes that you can pull off in 10 ingredients or fewer.

    20 minutes (plus 8 hours for chilling).

    Whisk one 15-oz. can pure pumpkin purée, 1½ cups unsweetened milk of choice, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, ¼ cup pure maple syrup, and ½ tsp. ground cinnamon or cardamom in a large bowl until smooth. Add 3 Tbsp. chia seeds and whisk to combine. Let sit 10 minutes. (Doing this gives the seeds a head start on hydrating and prevents them from sticking together. But if you can’t spare the time, just give the mixture a good stir before serving.).

    Stir chia mixture again, then add 1¼ cups old-fashioned oats and mix well to combine. Cover oat mixture and chill at least 8 hours.

    Spoon oat mixture into bowls and top with plain whole-milk yogurt, unsalted roasted pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or granola, maple syrup, and cinnamon as desired.

    Do Ahead: Oat mixture (without toppings) can be made 4 days ahead. Keep chilled.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will.
    • Sources indicate that slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness.
    • To a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

    Sources indicate that slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

    Find more Rachel Gurjar recipes here.

    To a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz. [170 g]), leaves and stems, 1 bunch mint (about 2 oz. [55 g]), leaves and tender stems, 6 green Thai chiles or 2 serranos, stemmed (more if you want it spicier), ½ cup (120 ml) lime juice (from about 5 limes), 2 tsp. cumin seeds, 1½ tsp. fine sea salt, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. chaat masala. Pulse for a few seconds in intervals until the ingredients are pulverized into a smooth paste. Transfer to an airtight container and store until ready to use, up to 1 week in the refrigerator or 1 month in the freezer.

    Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

    Sources indicate that drizzle the sheet with extra-virgin olive oil and place 1½ lb. (680 g) Japanese or Korean sweet potatoes, ends trimmed, halved lengthwise, cut-side down. Bake for 60 to 70 minutes, until golden and caramelized on the cut side and cooked through and tender; a knife inserted into the center of the potato should slide through easily.     To a small bowl, add ½ cup (120 g) plain whole-milk yogurt or sour cream and ½ tsp. fine sea salt and whisk to combine. If you’re using sour cream, thin it out with a little water.

Sprinkle with 1 medium red tomato (5 oz. [140 g]), finely chopped, 1 small red onion (7 oz. [200 g]), finely chopped, 2 Tbsp. chopped cilantro leaves and tender stems, 1 tsp. chaat masala, 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, thinly sliced, and crispy sev and serve immediately.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated.
    • I’m not going to tell you that breakfast is the most key meal of the day.
    • Throughout the 19th and 20th centuries, advocates for breakfast cereal used religious rhetoric and maternal guilt to fuel their marketing efforts, while public relations executives at a pork company convinced doctors to recommend a heartier breakfast of bacon and eggs for sustained energy, aimed at working families.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week.

    I’m not going to tell you that breakfast is the most key meal of the day. Humans have been on the planet for hundreds of thousands of years and our ability to thrive simply isn’t rooted in whether we eat first thing in the morning. In fact, the cliché is barely a century old, stemming not from nutritional science but good old-fashioned advertising.

    Throughout the 19th and 20th centuries, advocates for breakfast cereal used religious rhetoric and maternal guilt to fuel their marketing efforts, while public relations executives at a pork company convinced doctors to recommend a heartier breakfast of bacon and eggs for sustained energy, aimed at working families.

    Yet today breakfast is one of the most commonly skipped meals. So instead of wagging my finger at you about missing something so “crucial,” I think it’s worth asking: Why did you miss it in the first place?

    Recent findings suggest that on a jam-packed holiday like Thanksgiving, there are plenty of reasons. You have a turkey to roast. The table has to be set. Someone needs to pick up the wine. And oh, there’s still the pie dough to roll out! Maybe you even want to “save room” for the glorious feast you’re putting so much effort into.

    Recent findings suggest that but skipping this meal does come at a cost. Even if you aren’t ravenous, it’s metabolically valuable to eat in the morning. Breakfast stabilizes energy, and studies have shown that forgoing it leads to a reduced consumption of important nutrients like fiber, potassium, iron, and calcium, often found in morning staples like fruit, whole grains, and dairy. Without some food to start the day, you risk an energy dip, brain fog, and downright hanger. Which, let’s be honest, we don’t need in a kitchen overflowing with dirty dishes and extended relatives.

    According to recent reports, I have an easy solution. Making breakfast on Thanksgiving (or any day, really) doesn’t have to be a last-minute hassle. It can be quick to assemble and still feel special—like you’re really taking care of yourself, because you are. Take this overnight oats–chia pudding hybrid, which comes together in barely 10 minutes the night before you plan to eat it.

    Sources indicate that open up a can of pumpkin purée—odds are you bought extras that didn’t become a pie. Mix it with oats, maple syrup, and whichever milk you have in the fridge. A scoop of chia seeds adds bonus nutrition and prevents the oats from turning gluey as they hydrate overnight.

    Sources indicate that the next morning you’ll be rewarded with a lightly sweet, mousse-like treat that’s actually good for you. It’ll keep you full and firing on all cylinders for a day of turkey roasting, potato mashing, and vibe managing. It may not be the most important meal of the day—at least on Thanksgiving—but it will be delicious.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that mayonnaise is the thick and creamy matrix that disperses all the other flavors in your pasta salad, coating the noodles and giving the dish a great texture when cold.
    • It has been revealed that feta is a crumbly, tangy cheese with plenty of fat and salt, making it intensely flavorful but also creamy under the right circumstances.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that mayonnaise is the thick and creamy matrix that disperses all the other flavors in your pasta salad, coating the noodles and giving the dish a great texture when cold. But if you want more of that tangy, rich flavor, plus a decent boost of calcium, try blending feta with vinaigrette next time for a tasty result.

    It has been revealed that feta is a crumbly, tangy cheese with plenty of fat and salt, making it intensely flavorful but also creamy under the right circumstances. When you blend it with a premade vinaigrette, you create a beautifully bright condiment that pairs quite well with just about any type of pasta, from whole wheat to semolina. Unlike mayo, it combines the smooth decadence of dairy fat with fermented complexity and has a thinner texture that sinks into the nooks and crannies of different noodle shapes. While tasty, the ingredients still pair quite well with other pasta salad secret ingredients, from curry powder to various vegetables, so you won't need to switch up your recipe too much.

    Recent findings suggest that daily recommended calcium intake varies quite a bit based on age and other factors, but it starts at around 1,000 milligrams a day for most adults. Getting this much can be a challenge, but feta has about 270 milligrams per 60-gram serving, or about half a cup. Compared to the practically zero milligrams found in mayonnaise, this is an easy way to convert pasta salad into something not only more flavorful, but also more nutritionally complex.

    According to recent reports, pasta salad is a pretty flexible recipe, with no real standard ingredients outside of the carb in its name and a dressing. This means you don't have to choose between flavor and nutrition, and there are plenty of ingredients that can check both boxes quite easily.

    The false assumption everyone makes about milk is that it's the be-all and end-all of calcium-rich foods, but there are plenty of vegetables rich in the nutrient. A single cup of cooked spinach can add a whopping 240 milligrams of calcium and tastes fantastic with a feta-vinaigrette dressing. It's also quite an unobtrusive vegetable that has little effect on your dish's flavor profile, adding subtle grassy notes that make the end result more complex. If you want to bulk out the texture instead, a cup of cooked broccoli adds about 60 milligrams of calcium and creates a deliciously chewy texture when left a bit crunchy.

    Sources indicate that pasta salads are all about selecting the right pasta shape for your dressing. Since this vinaigrette is a bit runnier than mayo, you'll want to stick with varieties that are short and curly, creating enough surface area for it to cling to. While varieties made with traditional ingredients only have about 18 milligrams of calcium per 100 grams, whole grain pasta has 28 milligrams and a more rustic flavor. This can help balance out the acidity of the dressing, giving the dish a great mix of brightness and earthiness.

    A substantial, billowing cloud of meringue tops this crimson beauty and acts as a sweet reprieve from the tart cranberry curd. The vibrant filling is made even more sour with a generous amount of lime juice. Think lemon meringue pie but holiday-ified. Use our Perfect Pie Crust as the base to create a sturdy-flaky foundation, and be sure to start the pie the day before you proposal to serve it, as the curd requires several hours of chilling to set into a sliceable texture. Cut into it too soon and it will run onto your plate, creating a messy—albeit delicious—slice.

    We never make pie dough without a metal bench scraper. Our favorite is from Gestura. Use the scraper to cut butter, fold dough and nudge it into shape, transfer it from counter to plastic wrap, trim edges, cut strips, and, sure, scrape flour off your counter.

    3 hours (plus 30 minutes for freezing and 5 hours for chilling).

    Whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

    Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

    Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour and dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more rice flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

    It has been revealed that let dough disk sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Roll out dough on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1½" overhang. Fold overhang under so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Set pan on a rimmed baking sheet and prick bottom and sides of crust with a fork in several places. Freeze, uncovered, at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours.

    Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 400°. Line crust with a sheet of parchment paper and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake crust, tenting edges with foil if browning too promptly, until edges are set and look dry, 20–25 minutes. Carefully lift out parchment paper and weights and continue baking crust, gently pressing bottom and sides occasionally with a flat-bottomed measuring cup if puffing up, until bottom looks dry and is golden, 20–25 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let crust cool.

    Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

    Bring 1 lb. fresh or frozen cranberries, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, and ¼ cup water to a boil in a large saucepan, then reduce heat to medium and simmer, stirring often, until cranberries soften and burst and most of the liquid has evaporated, 10–15 minutes. Let cranberry mixture cool.

    Sources indicate that transfer cranberry mixture to a blender; reserve pan. Add ⅔ cup fresh lime juice and ¼ cup (32 g) cornstarch and blend on high speed until smooth. Scrape purée back into pan (not over heat) and add 3 large eggs, 2 large egg yolks, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Place over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture bubbles and thickens to a pudding-like consistency, about 4 minutes. Remove pan from heat. Add ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, and whisk until melted and combined. Strain curd through a fine-mesh sieve, pushing with a rubber spatula, directly into crust. Smooth into an even layer and cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Chill pie at least 4 hours and up to 1 day.

    Recent findings suggest that just before serving, beat 6 large egg whites, room temperature, ¼ tsp. cream of tartar, remaining 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until foamy and sugar is dissolved, about 5 minutes. Increase speed to high and continue to beat until stiff peaks form, about 3 minutes more.

    Spoon meringue over filling and swirl decoratively as desired. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue if desired.

    Here’s how to make Legoland’s legendary apple fries, complete with the cinnamon sugar coating, caramel drizzle and vanilla whipped cream dip.

    Sources indicate that legoland’s most popular food isn’t the usual lacy funnel cake or plate of chicken tenders. Look around for the longest line, and you’ll find it at Granny’s Apple Fries, where deep-fried apple sticks are coated in cinnamon-sugar, drizzled with caramel sauce and served with vanilla whipped cream. Thankfully you don’t need to wait in line (or buy a ticket to the park) to enjoy these legendary apple fries. Here’s how to make a copycat version of Legoland’s apple fries right at home, down to the homemade whipped cream and caramel sauce drizzle.

    It has been revealed that peel and core the apples. Using a sharp knife, carefully cut the apples into 1/2-inch sticks.

    Allison Cebulla For Taste Of Home.

    Place the cornstarch in a large bowl. Add the apple sticks, a few at a time, tossing to thoroughly coat them. Shake off the excess.

    Allison Cebulla For Taste Of Home.

    In an electric skillet or deep-fat fryer, heat the oil to 375°. Fry the apple fries, a few at a time, until they’re golden brown. Drain the oil from the apple fries by placing them on paper towels.

    Industry observers note that in a small bowl, stir together the granulated sugar and cinnamon. Immediately sprinkle the mixture over the hot fries. The sooner you sprinkle, the better the mixture sticks.

    Editor’s Tip: Never, ever overcrowd your skillet or deep-fat fryer. Doing so may cause a dangerous boil-over. Always work in small batches.

    Allison Cebulla For Taste Of Home.

    Industry observers note that in a small, chilled glass bowl, use chilled beaters to beat the heavy whipping cream until it begins to thicken. Add the confectioners’ sugar and vanilla extract, and beat until soft peaks form.

    Industry observers note that serve the apple fries warm with the vanilla whipped cream. If desired, drizzle the apple fries with warmed caramel sauce.

    Allison Cebulla For Taste Of Home.

    It has been revealed that allow leftover apple fries to cool completely to room temperature, then store them in an airtight container. They can last in the fridge for up to four days.

    Yes, you can freeze apple fries. Allow them to cool to room temperature, then transfer them to an airtight container with pieces of parchment or waxed paper between them. Freeze them for up to two months. Reheat them in a 400° oven until they’re crispy and warmed through.

    Allison Cebulla For Taste Of Home.

    It has been revealed that to cut apples for apple fries, peel and core the apples, then cut them into fourths. From there, cut the apple into 1/2-inch slices lengthwise, then turn each slice on its side and cut it in half lengthwise. You should be left with apple matchsticks.

    If your apple fries are soggy, the oil temperature was likely too low. When the oil isn’t hot enough, it will soak into the cornstarch and make it soggy rather than crisping the fries. It’s a common deep-frying mistake, so make sure to keep a close watch on the oil’s temperature.

    According to recent reports, serve apple fries immediately while they’re still hot. We love to finish them with salted caramel sauce and dip them in the vanilla whipped cream. Serve your apple fries with hot apple cider or homemade hot chocolate to make your treat extra decadent and sweet.

    Sources indicate that salmon's rich intensity also means it generally has more calories, which can mean different things based on someone's dietary needs. If you're conscious of this and still want something that cooks up swiftly (and deliciously), try flounder, a leaner, lower-calorie option that never lacks flavor.

    In a recent development, exact calorie amounts can vary quite a bit, especially when it comes to wild versus farmed salmon, but even the leanest ones usually sit between 130 and 200 calories per three-ounce serving. Flounder populations, however, have a more uniform lifestyle and consistently clock in at around 100 calories per three-ounce serving. That brown or gray layer of fat may help a salmon migrate and survive cold waters, but flounder are sedentary ambush predators that don't have nearly the same energy requirements. On your plate, this means a fillet of flounder is lean, clean-tasting, and quite mild compared to a richly marbled piece of salmon.

    Sources indicate that because flounder is often thinner and far less fatty than salmon, that also means it cooks exponentially quicker. While a skin-on fillet can widen your margin of error, it's still much easier to render your tender fish into a dense, rubbery mess. Your best bet is to treat it like a lean steak and use a hot and fast cooking method, letting a bit of carryover cooking finish the center rather than trying to reach the perfect temperature in a pan or on the grill.

    Flounder is delicate, light, and can easily lose its natural flavor if seasoned too heavily. While it's not exactly a beginner-friendly fish, the best ways to cook it are often straightforward and focus on timing and temperature, not technique. Hands-off methods that require little manipulation or rely on a sauce for flavor are usually ideal and keep your meat moist and tender.

    Sources indicate that if you haven't tried making a meunière yet, it's a classic seafood dish you should try at least once. Made by combining browned butter, lemon, and parsley, it's just flavorful enough to elevate your flounder without overwhelming it. Just about any French butter sauce, from beurre blanc to béchamel, is great with flounder because it adds a bit of richness and is a great vehicle for other tasty seasonings. Plus, they're flavorful enough that you'll only have to pan-sear each side of your fish, reducing the chance that it'll fall apart or overcook.

    Flounder grows more delicate the more it's cooked, so preparation methods that rely on you only handling it when raw are also quite ideal. Baking is a precise method, and you only have to move the fish once to transfer it to a plate. On the other hand, flounder is fantastic when deep-fried, and the breading helps it hold its shape. You'll still want to use a large, slotted tool and a delicate hand when fishing it out, but all you need to do is batter and drop it into oil for a great result.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

    No one wants to waste perfectly good food—I’m more likely to eat something slightly past its expiration date than throw it out prematurely—but some pantry items are just taking up space.

    Industry observers note that dusty canned foods, old spices, expired baking ingredients, and more past-their-prime goods serve little to no culinary value. Getting rid of them will actually help you identify the pantry items that you can still use before they go bad. But how can you keep your pantry organized more regularly, and what exactly should you throw away?

    Go through every item in your pantry at least twice a year, recommends Nicole Gabai, professional organizer, founder of B. Organized, and author of The Art of Organizing: An Artful Guide to an Organized Life.

    Recent findings suggest that if a twice-yearly check-in feels too daunting, consider a weekly five-minute check-in to discard expired goods, claims Shaniece Jones, professional organizer and founder of Closet Therapy. “Organize by accessibility and intention,” she says. “Keep your daily go-tos at eye level, heavy items like large cans of oil and bottled water on lower shelves, and seasonal or rarely used items up high.” Labels, Lazy Susans, and drawer dividers are some of her go-to tools for organizing the pantry.

    As you start cleaning, check off the following items—these are some of the most common pantry items our organizing experts find past their prime.

    While many shelf-stable foods, such as canned goods, are still safe to eat past their expiration date, you should still check for signs of spoilage. “You can tell canned goods have spoiled if they are rusted, or if you see the cans bulge or dent,” Gabai indicates.

    Labeling pantry items helps you check how long they’ve been open. For opened packages and bulk goods you’ve decanted into containers, write the date on the label so you know when you opened them.

    Industry observers note that spices that have lost their smell? Time to go. “If it smells flat or just not aromatic, then it needs to be replaced since it will add very little, if any, flavor to what you’re cooking,” Gabai indicates. She also notes that ground spices typically last one to two years, while dried herbs can last up to three years.

    “Baking ingredients like flour, baking powder, and baking soda can lose their effectiveness over time,” states Meaghan Kessman, founder of Meaghan Kessman Home Organization.

    In a recent development, eventually, flour will go bad, but how long it takes to get rancid depends on how it’s stored and the type of flour. In general, Gabai indicates it will last at room temperature for six to eight months. She recommends storing it in an airtight container in the fridge or freezer.

    “Check for expiration dates and any signs of spoilage, such as clumping or an off smell,” Kessman states. “If you’re unsure, test baking powder by adding a teaspoon to hot water—if it bubbles, it’s still good to use.”.

    We often buy cooking oils in bulk, but keep in mind that they eventually go bad. “Oils and fats, such as olive oil, vegetable oil, and shortening, can become rancid if stored for too long. Rancid oils have a sour or off smell,” Kessman notes. “Always check the expiration date and store oils in a cool, dark place to keep them fresh longer.”.

    Gabai recommends storing oils in a cool, dark place and disposing of them properly; freeze in a zip-top bag, then toss in the trash (never pour down the drain).

    These pantry staples are oil-rich, so they spoil faster than you might think. “They can last about 6 months at room temperature, but if you freeze them, they can last a year or more,” Gabai indicates.

    According to recent reports, “Snacks and cereals can go stale promptly once opened,” Kessman says. She recommends checking expiration dates and signs of staleness, like an unusual smell or texture.

    According to Gabai, grains, rice, and beans can last about one to two years, but brown rice and other whole grains will not last as long because of their higher oil content.

    Industry observers note that “Condiments like ketchup, mustard, and salad dressings often get pushed to the back of the pantry and forgotten,” Kessman says. “Check for expiration dates and any signs of separation, discoloration, or off smells.”.

    Honey is the rare exception that probably isn't spoiled. The National Honey Board states that honey has a shelf life of approximately two years, although it can last much longer if stored correctly in a sealed container.

    “Honey was found in the tombs of kings and royalty as far back as 3,000 years in Egypt—and it was still edible!” Gabai notes.

    If you notice crystallization, Gabai recommends gently heating the honey container in a pot of water.

You'll get eggs with a dark red color and a warm dose of spice, making a dish with a lot of flavor yet not much fuss.

    "Store-bought is fine" carries a little more weight when Ina tells you exactly which pasta sauce to buy.

    Recent findings suggest that I can happily spend an entire afternoon making dinner. Give me a little music, a glass of wine and something to braise, and I’ll settle in without much concern for when it all reaches the table. It’s a lovely way to cook when I have the time, but leisurely cooking isn’t always practical for busy parents. On most days, dinner needs to fit into my family’s schedule, and my kids don’t want to hear that dinner is still achieving notable levels of depth and complexity as it enters its sixth hour on the stove.

    But having less time to cook shouldn’t lower our expectations for dinner. A simple plate of pasta can be every bit as satisfying—provided the ingredients involved are worth eating. It’s why I’m particular about store-bought sauce. I’m happy to buy it, but I want to enjoy it as much as anything I spent time making myself.

    Industry observers note that ina Garten seems to have arrived at a similar conclusion. Her signature “store-bought is fine” reassurance comes with some excellent recommendations, including the marinara from Rao’s Homemade, a brand I’ve been loyal to for years. It’s a small thing to have in common with Ina, but until I acquire a Parisian apartment of my own, I’ll gladly take it.

    “Why make your own marinara when Rao’s marinara sauce tastes homemade?” Ina has stated. It’s a reasonable question, particularly coming from someone with very little left to prove in the kitchen.

    According to recent reports, she’s equally decisive on her website. When a reader asked her favorite jarred marinara, Ina answered, “That’s easy! Rao’s Marinara Sauce.” It also appears among her recommended ingredients in the site’s shopping section.

    It has been revealed that her advice to an incoming college student gives the recommendation some practical context. When asked which staples to have on hand, Ina suggested keeping pasta and Rao’s marinara around for a ten-minute dinner. That’s useful advice at any age, particularly once you discover that graduation doesn’t necessarily leave you with more time to cook.

    Industry observers note that ina’s comment about homemade flavor gets at why I’ve continued to buy it, too: Rao’s has the richness and depth I want in a sauce, even when I’m serving it with nothing more elaborate than bucatini and Parmesan. I actually look forward to that dinner. The fact that it comes together swiftly is just a bonus.

    According to recent reports, lately, I’ve been especially impressed with the brand’s newly introduced creamy roasted garlic sauce (so much so that I gave it a Taste of Home Award). The mellow roasted garlic and the richness of mascarpone have made it a favorite in my house.

    Ina’s explanation of “good ingredients” offers a useful starting point. In Modern Comfort Food, she writes, “They don’t have to be expensive, but they need to be chosen thoughtfully.” Her emphasis is on flavor and choosing ingredients because of what they contribute to the finished dish.

    When it comes to Rao’s, she points to slow simmering and good tomatoes, basil, garlic and oregano. That makes the ingredient label a sensible place to begin when comparing jars. The marinara label lists whole peeled Italian tomatoes, followed by olive oil, onions, salt, garlic, basil, black pepper and oregano—and no added sugar.

    Recent findings suggest that for a classic marinara, look for that familiar foundation of tomatoes, oil, aromatics and herbs. If you prefer a more savory sauce, keep your eye on the added sugar, too. These are useful details to compare across brands, although the label can only tell you so much about how well the ingredients have been cooked and balanced. In this case, I’m happy to let Ina’s recommendation settle the matter.

It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried).

    For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

    In a recent development, whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

    Turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

    Recent findings suggest that do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

    When dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside.

    Melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

    Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine.

    Sources indicate that unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet.

    Spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.).

    Bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

    Recent findings suggest that do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.

    #143. Industry News: The Traditional Kitchen Knife Bobby Flay Recommends Is On Amazon

    📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (589 w)
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foodrepublic

    Industry News: The Traditional Kitchen Knife Bobby Flay Recommends Is On Amazon

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (589 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
    • Whether you're an amateur home cook or a seasoned chef, a high-quality chef's knife is one of the three knives you need in your kitchen arsenal.
    • Before getting into the knife's many selling points, there's one thing we have to address.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

    Whether you're an amateur home cook or a seasoned chef, a high-quality chef's knife is one of the three knives you need in your kitchen arsenal. However, with so many options out there, choosing the right one can promptly become overwhelming. You'll want something versatile enough to finely chop vegetables, break down a chicken, and handle just about everything in between. Durability matters, too. A good knife should last for years, if not a lifetime, with the right care. And, of course, it needs to hold its sharp edge. Luckily, Food Network star Bobby Flay has a recommendation that takes some of the guesswork out of the process (per The Kitchn): the Shun Classic 8-inch Western Cook's Knife, available on Amazon.

    Before getting into the knife's many selling points, there's one thing we have to address. At $163.95 (which is the sale price — it's normally around $205), it's certainly not a budget-friendly buy. But there are plenty of reasons why we think it could be worth the investment. At its core, knife steel is a blend of iron and carbon, with manufacturers adding other elements to improve its performance. It's these added elements that set Shun knives apart from the rest.

    The Shun Classic 8-inch Western Cook's knife uses a proprietary blend called VG-MAX, which is specifically formulated to resist corrosion and wear while maintaining a sharp edge. It also has a high carbon content, helping the blade achieve the hardness needed for excellent edge retention. The combination of elements in VG-MAX gives the Shun an advantage over many more affordable knives made with lower-grade steel, which have the tendency to lose their sharpness far more promptly with regular use. In other words, you're paying for a knife that's designed to stay sharp, rather than one that needs constant maintenance to keep it performing.

    If the name didn't give it away already, Shun is a Japanese knife brand, and all its knives are handcrafted in Seki City, a region renowned for centuries of sword and knife making. Any kitchen nerd knows that Japanese knives are up there with German ones when it comes to quality, so just by looking at the place of origin, you can expect a considerable degree of craftsmanship to have gone into this blade.

    Interestingly, despite its Japanese origins, the Shun Classic 8-inch Western Cook's Knife doesn't adopt the traditional santoku shape, often considered Japan's answer to the Western chef's knife. Both blades are versatile, all-purpose kitchen knives, but they differ in their blade profiles and the way they're typically used. Neither is necessarily better than the other; that distinction largely comes down to personal preference and preferred cutting style.

    While the blade might not have a traditional Japanese shape, the handle certainly draws on Japanese craftsmanship. It's made from Pakkawood, an engineered composite created by stacking thin hardwood veneers and infusing them with phenolic resin, which is then bonded together using high heat. The result of this admittedly complicated process is a durable, moisture-resistant material that's less prone to warping and cracking than ordinary wood. This makes it easy to keep clean, although that doesn't mean you should put the knife in the dishwasher or leave it to soak in the sink. Even quality materials can't protect even the most durable blades from the harsh detergents, water, and high temperatures, which will inevitably cause rusting and damage over time. Hand-washing and drying your knife promptly remains the better option.

    Best Kitchen Scales, Tested Over a Decade of Baking (2026)

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I’ve been an avid home baker for well over a decade (my first stint in “food media” was a baking blog I started in middle school!), and I can confirm that there is no single tool quite as important to the outcome of your baked goods as a simple kitchen scale.
    • In a recent development, another bonus of a kitchen scale?
    • Scales aren’t just for bakers, either.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I’ve been an avid home baker for well over a decade (my first stint in “food media” was a baking blog I started in middle school!), and I can confirm that there is no single tool quite as important to the outcome of your baked goods as a simple kitchen scale. Bon Appétit’s Test Kitchen team agrees, which is why you’ll see gram measurements in the baking recipes on our site.

    In a recent development, another bonus of a kitchen scale? In most cases, you can kiss measuring cups and spoons goodbye, which means far fewer utensils to clean once your bakes are in the oven.

    Scales aren’t just for bakers, either. They make portioning burger patties and meatballs easier, streamline meal prep, and keep your Sunday morning pancake routine cleaner.

    I’ve tested 16 models over several years and consulted Shilpa Uskokovic, former BA senior Test Kitchen editor and co-owner of Hani’s Bakery, to find the best kitchen scale for home cooks. The winner is just $27.

    In a recent development, upcoming in this upgrade: I tested the new version of the Oxo Good Grips 11-Pound Digital Kitchen Food Scale. While it was easy to use and I appreciated the pull-out display, it was less accurate than the Escali—and over double the price. You can read my full review below.

    Size: 8.5 x 6 x 1.5"Capacity: 11 lb.Gradation: 1 gAuto shut-off: 4 minutes 30 secondsPower: AA batteries (included).

    This Escali Primo has held the top spot in our testing for over six years and has been a favorite in the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen for far longer than that. “This scale has been with me for more than a decade of my career, staying faithfully by my side through 12-hour shifts in pastry kitchens, bouts of religious recipe testing, and weekly sessions of casual baking,” says senior Test Kitchen editor and resident baking whiz Shilpa Uskokovic.

    It’s durable, accurate, intuitive to use, and affordable—pretty much everything we could ask of a kitchen scale.

    Recent findings suggest that what we love: The Escali Primo is lightweight, comes in a variety of fun colors, and has a simple two-button interface to turn it on, tare it, and toggle between ounces, pounds, and grams. In testing, it was responsive and precise, quick to tare, and delivered accurate readings every time. Its 4.5-minute auto shut-off is among the longest of any model we tested, so you won’t lose your measurements mid-bake. Plus, its 11-pound capacity is large enough to accommodate any task a home cook might ask of it.

    Performance aside, the Escali Primo has several design features that helped it stand out. For one, the fact that the weighing platform is elevated and offset from the base means you can easily read the display or use the buttons even when measuring into a large, wide mixing bowl. The plastic body and sealed control panel make it a breeze to wipe down after a floury baking session and also keep stray crumbs from getting stuck in any crevices. Another detail we like? The four rubberized feet keep it stable on your kitchen counter.

    It has been revealed that the Escali Primo has proven quite durable as we’ve continued to test it long-term, another reason why it’s a perennial favorite among our Test Kitchen editors. Shilpa again: “It’s compact and easy to store, it’s easy to wipe clean, it toggles between grams and ounces seamlessly, and it’s reliably accurate.".

    What we’d leave: The Escali can only measure in 1-gram increments. While this was typical of most scales we tested, those looking to use their kitchen scale for dialing in their coffee routine will want something more precise (though coffee scales are kind of their own thing). Unlike some pricier models, the Escali’s display is not backlit, but we didn’t find this to be an issue. It’s also worth noting that the Escali is not a touchscreen device, so you’ll need to use a bit of pressure on the buttons.

    Size: 8.3 x 7 x 1.3"Capacity: 11 lb.Gradation: 1 gAuto shut-off: NAPower: AAA batteries (included).

    In a recent development, amazon Basics products are not consistent across the board, but this scale is a certifiable hit. At about half the price of the Escali, it’s a good option if you’re not positive about this scale thing and want to spend as little as humanly possible to do so.

    What we love: There are a lot of similarities between the Amazon Basics scale and the overall winner. The Amazon Basics scale has the same two-button setup, a similar elevated weighing platform that makes it easy to see the display, and the same 11-pound maximum capacity. It’s made of plastic with a stainless-steel platform that’s easy to wipe down and is just a touch larger than the Escali at 7 inches across.

    Industry observers note that in testing, I was impressed by the Amazon scale’s accuracy, considering its price point. It responded to weight addition or removal almost as swiftly as the Escali and provided an accurate readout about 99% of the time. That 1% weight change inaccuracy happened when someone repeatedly added weight or switched back and forth between units of measurement, and when it did happen, the reading was off by a minor amount. The problem could be fixed by removing what was on the scale, taring it, and starting over. For $10 (at the time of writing), you’d be hard-pressed to find a better model.

    Recent findings suggest that what we’d leave: Unlike the Escali, the Amazon scale’s buttons lack any kind of laminated sealing to prevent crumbs or liquid from entering the crevices around them. As mentioned, this scale isn’t quite as accurate as the winner and it tended to overshoot an item’s actual weight at first (before correcting itself relatively swiftly). And last, the stainless-steel platform is more prone to scratching or smudging than Escali’s plastic one.

    You’ll notice there aren’t any other scales marketed as coffee scales on this list, and that’s because the Fellow Tally was the only coffee scale we thought could plausibly work as an all-purpose model too.

    Recent findings suggest that what we love: The Fellow Tally is one of our favorite coffee scales (especially for pour-over) thanks to features like a built-in timer and a “brew assist” that directs you on the proper ratio of coffee to water—but its 5.5-pound maximum capacity means it works for most home baking projects too. If you’re the kind of person who likes to nerd out over your brewing and baking techniques, this is your best bet unless you want to invest in two separate scales.

    In testing, we quite liked the Tally’s design for its tactile controls and easy-to-read OLED display, and appreciated its ability to measure grams, ounces, pounds, and milliliters (that milliliter measurement is calibrated for water, so one milliliter equals one gram; if you're measuring a heavier liquid like milk it will be slightly off). The elevated 6-inch platform is large enough to comfortably hold a mixing bowl while allowing easy visibility of the display.

    Calibration weight accuracy test.

    Recent findings suggest that to find out how accurate each scale was, I used a set of calibration weights. I tested each scale’s ability to give an accurate reading for the minimum amount of weight it claimed to be able to accommodate (usually 1 or 2 grams), and its ability to detect small changes when there was already weight on the platform. I also placed weights in various places on each scale’s platform to determine whether they could give an accurate reading regardless of whether the weight was in the center or at the edge.

    I coated each scale in a mixture of flour, water, and oil and let them sit overnight. I cleaned the residue off and noted which scales were easy to clean and resistant to any scratching or staining.

    I distributed winning scales to staffers to see how they fared after long-term use in our homes and in the Test Kitchen and added any long-term testing notes to reviews as they came in.

    I looked for consistently accurate measurements and a short response time when adding and removing items of varying sizes and materials from each scale. I took into account how weight distribution affected the readings, looking for scales that delivered spot-on results regardless of where on the platform we placed the weights. I also took note of how precise each scale could be in its measurements, but found our favorite all-around options tended to measure in 1-gram increments.

    I looked for scales that were intuitive to use without picking up a manual.

    I tested scales with weight capacities ranging from 1.65 to 16 pounds, but found that a maximum capacity of 11 pounds was more than enough for the tasks one might try to accomplish in a home kitchen.

    I wanted a scale that felt durable, well-made, and stable on the counter and was also designed to be easy to clean.

    Unlike a stand mixer, a scale isn’t the kind of kitchen gadget most home cooks are looking to keep permanently on their counter. Lightweight, compact models that could be easily stashed in a cabinet were better.

    I took into account the relative price of each scale. After years of testing, we’ve found that you really don’t need to spend much to get a high-quality, highly accurate kitchen scale, so any models that were pricey needed to wow us with their design or extra features.

    These scales didn’t quite make our list of top picks, but they still impressed us in testing and might fit your needs depending on what you’re looking for.

I liked it a lot, but found it was often off by 1 gram, especially when the weight was placed in one of the platform’s corners.     Etekcity Luminary Smart Nutrition Scale.

    Cuisinart KML-KO3B Precision Chef Bowl.

In testing, I found this to be true—readings were rarely accurate to the exact tenth. After testing the scale in his home kitchen for several weeks, senior commerce editor Noah Kaufman also noted that readings came in on the slow side, which made measuring ingredients that pour out quickly (like flour or liquids) tricky. I did appreciate the detachable display (helpful when using a large, wide bowl that might otherwise obscure the screen), but it wasn’t enough to outweigh the negatives—and besides, I’m of the opinion that there’s no reason for the average home cook to pay $120 for a scale when a $25 one performs incredibly well.

    We also tested the Ozeri Pronto, Etekcity Multifunction Food Kitchen Scale, and GDealer Tempered Glass Kitchen Scale, all of which have been discontinued.

    How do you use a kitchen scale?

    To use a kitchen scale, you’ll have to familiarize yourself with the concept of “tare.” Taring a scale allows you to reset the weight back to zero when you already have something on the weighing platform. This is particularly useful if you want to measure ingredients into a bowl (just place the bowl on the platform, click the tare button, and go on adding your ingredients), or if you want to measure multiple ingredients into that bowl without needing to add or subtract the existing weight in your head.

    What should you use a kitchen scale for?

    It has been revealed that baking is the obvious answer here, but the use cases for kitchen scales go far beyond the world of flour and butter. Use a scale to perfectly portion out meat for meatballs or burgers, aid in your meal prep for the week, or for any recipe where precise quantities are of the utmost importance.

    According to recent reports, alaina Chou: Alaina has been testing products at Bon Appétit for over three years, which means she’s used dozens of air fryers, toasters, rice cookers, and—you guessed it—kitchen scales.     #139. Skip Regular Butter And Oil: Roasted Potatoes Are 10x Crispier With This Ingredient

    📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (502 w)
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foodrepublic

    Skip Regular Butter And Oil: Roasted Potatoes Are 10x Crispier With This Ingredient

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (502 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A mistake everyone makes with crispy roasted potatoes is using the wrong cooking fat, which tends to burn under the high heat required for great texture.
    • High-smoke-point oil is great for roasted potatoes because it lets you use high heat to crisp the exteriors.
    • The biggest difference between ghee and clarified butter is taste and color.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A mistake everyone makes with crispy roasted potatoes is using the wrong cooking fat, which tends to burn under the high heat required for great texture. Regular butter and oil each have their strengths, but neither gets quite the same result as ghee, a type of clarified butter with Indian origins.

    High-smoke-point oil is great for roasted potatoes because it lets you use high heat to crisp the exteriors. However, it doesn't add much in the way of flavor, so you're missing out on an opportunity to layer on more depth. On the other hand, butter is great at making a hearty side dish, but the milk solids tend to burn at temperatures above 350 degrees Fahrenheit. Ghee, however, has virtually no milk solids and very little moisture, making it the perfect middle ground. With a smoke point of around 450 degrees Fahrenheit and a rich flavor, it's the perfect way to achieve great texture without sacrificing taste.

    The biggest difference between ghee and clarified butter is taste and color. The former comes "pre-toasted," giving it a deep golden hue and an intense nuttiness that essentially kick-starts the roasted flavor of your tubers. Even if you don't use the various tricks to increase surface area, your potatoes will taste like they have more crispy outsides than usual. A small amount helps them develop the perfect color, giving you a showstopping presentation that tastes great, looks amazing, and still lets you use your existing favorite recipe with only one ingredient substitution.

    Recent findings suggest that ghee's flavor is more pronounced than butter's or oil's, but it's still just as versatile. Rather than switching up seasoning, it's best to focus on how to increase the "roasted" factor of your potatoes. Increasing their surface area, ensuring they have as little surface moisture as possible, and using the correct type of pan are easy ways to improve their flavor.

    Industry observers note that there's an easy British trick for roasted potatoes that makes them exponentially crispier: roughing up the exterior. By parboiling them, then shaking them in a colander, you transform the smooth outside into one covered in tiny little ridges and bumps. These have a far greater surface area, which means your ghee has more room to help brown the exteriors, so you end up with more crispiness than normal. Not only does this improve the flavor, but it also speeds up the roasting time since you aren't cooking a raw vegetable.

    Recent findings suggest that moisture is the enemy of crispiness and can prevent even ghee from creating a great texture. If you parboiled your potatoes, letting them steam-dry for a bit makes them easier to work with and removes excess water. If cooking them raw, it may help to pat the pieces dry first to remove excess surface moisture. Either way, a heavy-bottomed pan, preferably cast iron or stainless steel, holds more heat and can develop far better color and flavor than something that is thin, flimsy, or nonstick.
