    #135. 10 Protein-Packed Substitutes For Mayo In Chicken Salad

    📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2390 w)
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foodrepublic

    10 Protein-Packed Substitutes For Mayo In Chicken Salad

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2390 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that chicken salad is like edible Americana, a comfort food that's beloved for its taste, nutrition, and versatility.
    • But the foundation of any respectable chicken salad is its creamy binder.
    • In a recent development, yogurt has a long and storied reputation as a health food, so long, in fact, that its beneficial properties are documented in Indian Ayurvedic medicinal writings from more than 7,000 years ago.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that chicken salad is like edible Americana, a comfort food that's beloved for its taste, nutrition, and versatility. You can find it in the prepared section of your local supermarket or on the menu of your favorite diner. Trying to cut down on carbohydrates? Have a scoop on a salad. Want a light and easy lunch? Have it as a club or between two pieces of toasted whole-grain bread. More importantly, though, chicken salad is like a ball of clay ready to be shaped by your taste preferences. You can take it in infinite directions: Mediterranean, Southwest, Spanish, French, Indian, Vietnamese. Have some extra sprigs of cilantro or half a bag of red grapes lying hanging around the fridge? Add 'em. Don't know what to do with those leftover pecans or knob of fresh ginger? You can throw those in, too.

    But the foundation of any respectable chicken salad is its creamy binder. In that regard, mayonnaise is the undisputed classic, turning your basic diced chicken breast into something moist, savory, and luscious. However, plenty of other ingredients deliver that signature smoothness — just with more protein. From tzatziki to silken tofu to labneh, there are tons of options that deliver both texture and an added pop of flavor. Whether you're minding your macros or just looking for a new spin on a classic dish, this list of protein-packed mayo substitutes is for you.

    In a recent development, yogurt has a long and storied reputation as a health food, so long, in fact, that its beneficial properties are documented in Indian Ayurvedic medicinal writings from more than 7,000 years ago. Today, it's seen as a better-for-you breakfast option, loaded with beneficial probiotics, calcium, and, of course, protein. Yogurt, especially the more thoroughly strained Greek variety, has an excellent calorie-to-protein ratio (about 16 grams of protein per 150 calories when made with whole milk), which is why it has become so popular with bodybuilders and wellness influencers.

    In a recent development, however, Greek yogurt still has a place in ordinary kitchens, and it's especially useful for people looking for a healthier alternative to mayonnaise, cream cheese, or any other creamy, high-fat, high-cholesterol product, which is why it makes such a great addition to homemade chicken salad. Even when prepared with mayonnaise, chicken salad is a relatively nutritious lunch option, typically made with low-fat chicken breast, fresh herbs, diced veggies, and maybe some nuts or sliced grapes. Whole milk yogurt, which is creamier than low-fat options, builds on that by adding extra protein, moisture, and the richness synonymous with a good chicken salad. It also adds a little tang that complements the subdued nature of poultry and plays well with other common chicken-salad additions, like mustard, dill, or curry powder.

    Recent findings suggest that it feels like every week there's another article or study being published identifying the benefits of gut health. This increased focus on the gut microbiome and the trillions of microorganisms that occupy it has brought all sorts of fermented dairy products, which are packed with probiotics and other useful bacteria, back into the nutritional spotlight. In this department, Greek yogurt is king (at least in the United States), but other styles are slowly making their way to the supermarket dairy aisle. One of them is skyr, also known as Icelandic yogurt.

    It has been revealed that technically classified as a cheese because its proteins are coagulated with rennet (a naturally occurring enzyme), skyr is dense, almost custard-like, with a mild sweetness and less assertive bite than Greek yogurt. Nutritionally, the two dairy products have an almost identical profile, although skyr is typically slightly higher in protein per serving due to a more rigorous straining process. But it's that straining — and subsequent thicker texture — that makes skyr such a terrific mayo substitute, delivering the same full creaminess without the more forward lactic tang of typical yogurt. How you use it in your chicken salad is a personal preference. If you like your chicken salad on the more unctuous side, use it as is; if you like it a little looser, thin your skyr with a tablespoon or two of milk, which may also help coat each ingredient more evenly.

    It has been revealed that on a per-calorie basis, cottage cheese is hard to beat among high-protein foods, with (on average) 12-14 grams of protein per 100-calorie serving. Unlike yogurt, which is fermented with bacteria, cottage cheese is made through acidification. As milk becomes more acidic and the pH level drops, the proteins denature, clump, and coagulate into tiny little curds. Although the process is simple, there's a lot of variability between brands. Some are saltier or creamier or contain larger curds.

    Recent findings suggest that but the most influential factor, especially regarding your chicken salad, is the fat content. While low-fat cottage cheese has fewer calories per serving, it lacks the richness needed to rehydrate dry chicken. Beyond extra unctuousness, full-fat cottage cheese adds salinity, clean milky notes, and a very mild cheese flavor. However, there's one major difference between cottage cheese and mayonnaise: Texture. Straight out of the plastic tub, cottage cheese can be, well, lumpy. This may not bother you in the slightest, but if it does, there's an easy workaround: Whipping the cottage cheese. You can do this with a hand mixer, mini food processor, or even just a substantial fork; the goal being to break those curds into a finer texture similar to ricotta. You can use the same technique to incorporate this high-protein food into smoothies, dips, and even macaroni and cheese.

    Hummus was the "it" food product of the early 2000s, but in the years since, it has faded in popularity. Maybe we were just given too much, too fast: Beet hummus, carrot hummus, lentil hummus, chocolate hummus — each variation obfuscating the beauty of this simple, timeless, life-sustaining food. Hummus, the type made from chickpeas, sesame paste (tahini), and olive oil, is an ancient form of plant-based protein foundational to Mediterranean and Middle Eastern cuisines. When blended, the ingredients make a velvety emulsion that — depending on how much ice water or oil you use — can be spread or scooped over everything, from bulgur wheat to falafel wraps.

    Recent findings suggest that it's also a great addition to salads — including ones made from chicken. Here, hummus provides an extra protein boost as well as some much-needed fattiness. Its blend of Middle Eastern spices — cumin, sumac, garlic, za'atar — contributes a warmth and brightness that cuts through the inherent blandness of cooked chicken breast. If using hummus as the foundation of your chicken salad, consider adding other Mediterranean ingredients, like capers, olives, walnuts, almonds, fresh tomato, or cucumbers. You can use your favorite supermarket brand, or just rapidly whip up delicious hummus at home.

    Probably the most underrated ingredient on this list, silken tofu is a centuries-old, plant-based protein with limitless applications. Like other forms of bean curd, silken tofu is made from soybeans, but it's worlds different from soft, medium, or firm varieties. While it comes in similar packaging, silken tofu is hardly solid; it's more like a pudding or flan that will fall apart if you try to pick it up with a fork. However, it's precisely this loose creaminess that makes silken tofu such a terrific substitute for mayonnaise in your next chicken salad.

    It has been revealed that besides being a great protein source — containing around 20 grams per 16-ounce package — silken tofu can easily be made smooth and pourable. When blended, it becomes something akin to Alfredo sauce, with a velvety consistency that's ideal for coating chicken. Another advantage of silken tofu is its taste — or lack thereof. You're dealing with a blank canvas here, one that will promptly absorb whatever seasonings, herbs, or sauces you mix with it. It may need some doctoring to get the texture right, but just use this as another opportunity to add flavor. Try adding cilantro and lime, tarragon and sherry vinegar, or hot sauce, for a Buffalo wing-inspired chicken salad.

    Sources indicate that there are only so many ways to add creaminess to food without relying on dairy, a fatty emulsion, or some complicated form of food chemistry. Adding a can of blended beans is one of them. Legumes, like black beans, kidney beans, and butter beans, have a starchy center that turns smooth and pillowy when blended. Most commercial varieties you find at your typical supermarket are good for cooking, but some have a more distinct flavor than others.

    Recent findings suggest that when making chicken salad, it's best to use beans with a clean, neat taste and not too much earthiness. For this, white, cannellini, or Great Northern beans are best. They won't overwhelm the other ingredients in your chicken salad, but they also aren't entirely neutral-tasting, either. The key to using these legumes is to purée them with different spices, herbs, and condiments, like Worcestershire sauce, miso, or a splash of vinegar. To achieve a texture that's similar to mayonnaise, you'll likely need to add some liquid or fat. Olive or another neutral oil works, but adding a heavily seasoned broth will give you an even better result. To do this, make a quick pan sauce with sautéed aromatics, seasonings, and stock; add it to your beans, then blend everything in a blender or food processor.

    This one is a little sneaky. Egg yolks are inherently fatty, but they also contain natural emulsifiers that turn into a creamy paste when blended. That means you don't have to add a drop of mayonnaise (which, ironically, is made predominantly from egg yolks) to achieve a luscious texture. But egg salad brings more to the party than just creaminess. If you've ever watched a TikTok nutritionist worth their creatine, then you're probably frustratingly aware that egg whites are one of nature's purest protein sources.

    This combination of smooth, fatty yolk and protein-rich white makes egg salad an incredible substitute for mayo. It's a tongue-in-cheek pairing, for sure, but this whimsical culinary mashup also delivers on taste. Because eggs are a tad sulfurous on their own, season them generously with ingredients like Dijon mustard, capers, lemon juice, smoked paprika, or even a few shakes of curry powder. However, the key to achieving a natural creaminess is proper egg cookery, which essentially boils down to not overcooking your hard-boiled eggs. The answer: A quick dunk in the ice bath for about 10-15 minutes to halt cooking and preserve those fluffy yolks.

    It has been revealed that want the nutritional upside of yogurt with an added burst of refreshing Mediterranean flavors? Sounds like it's tzatziki time. The yogurt-based dip is most closely associated with Greek cuisine, serving as a cooling counterpoint to robustly seasoned grilled meats, fried zucchini, and platters of pita. And, while its protein content isn't on the same level as skyr or cottage cheese, it isn't negligible, either, which is why it's another smart mayo substitute for your next chicken salad.

    Tzatziki looks simple, but it delivers a chorus of complex flavors that few condiments can match. It's all things smooth, rich, tangy, and fresh, thanks to a blend of fresh herbs and other aromatics. Besides yogurt, the predominant ingredient is cucumber. Paired with fresh mint, dill, and garlic, this creates a clean, powerful taste profile. It instantly elevates ordinary chicken into something moist and tender. Slip your tzatziki-coated chicken salad into a pita and top with shredded lettuce, tomato, black olives, and sliced red onion for a memorable lunch. While tzatziki is popular, it can be difficult to find good options in your average supermarket. Thankfully, a quality tzatziki sauce is easy to put together; just remember to squeeze the moisture out of your cucumbers. Otherwise, your sauce will be too wet and separate.

    In a recent development, labneh is made by straining Greek yogurt in cheesecloth until you remove the remaining liquid whey. This not only creates a denser product, but it also concentrates the flavor. It's traditionally made with goat's milk, which is a little grassy on the palate and has a slightly tangier finish than a cow's milk cheese or yogurt. Unlike yogurt, though, which you typically eat with a spoon, labneh is more of a dip, perfect for crudités, pita, lavash, or even grilled fruits. It has a decadent mouthfeel and is decidedly more savory, especially when dressed with olive oil, making it a nice way to rejuvenate an otherwise tired chicken salad.

    But there's no reason to pigeonhole this spreadable yogurt as savory or sweet; it works beautifully with both taste profiles. You can roll it in za'atar, sumac, and fresh mint, or crust it with pistachios and drizzle it with honey. Since it's the thickest yogurt-based product on this list, when using it for chicken salad, you'll likely want to add a splash of milk or a non-dairy alternative to loosen it up. If you can't find labneh in stores, you can literally just add Greek yogurt to a cheesecloth, hang it above your sink, and let it drip for a few hours until it's firm and extra creamy.

    Like most dairy products, feta is a solid protein source, with about 4 grams per 2-ounce serving; however, it differs from other cheeses because it's brined in a salt-water and whey solution rather than traditionally aged. This process helps preserve the cheese while also imbuing it with its signature salinity. If you've been lucky enough to try quality feta, you know that this soft, crumbly cheese packs a punch. In the mouth, it has a clean, fresh cream flavor and mild tang, making it a natural partner for grilled meats like beef, lamb, or chicken.

    It has been revealed that feta isn't spreadable, nor does it melt, but you can easily transform its texture by dropping a few chunks into a blender or food processor and "whipping" it until smooth. The result is smooth, salty, and spoonable — and perfect for chicken salad. When using whipped feta, consider both its salt content and mild acidic bite. These are strong flavors that should be balanced with other sweet and savory ingredients. Try pairing it with starchy, nutty, or mildly sweet foods like roasted butternut squash, pistachios, dried cranberries, or nectarines.

    Is It Safe to Eat Raw Cranberries?

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This holiday star rarely turns up in the fruit bowl.
    • Most of us have likely eaten cranberries without ever trying one on its own.
    • According to recent reports, I live near Bandon, the Cranberry Capital of Oregon, where enthusiasm for the fruit extends well beyond Thanksgiving.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

    This holiday star rarely turns up in the fruit bowl. Could you eat cranberries raw if you wanted to?

    Most of us have likely eaten cranberries without ever trying one on its own. The fruit is familiar enough to be indispensable at Thanksgiving, but rarely considered when we’re in the mood for a bowl of berries to snack on.

    According to recent reports, I live near Bandon, the Cranberry Capital of Oregon, where enthusiasm for the fruit extends well beyond Thanksgiving. Cranberry bogs are part of the landscape, and local berries fill jars of jam and syrup at roadside stands. This fall, my family attended the annual cranberry festival, where a friend of ours was crowned Cranberry Queen. (It’s a small town.).

    Even here, though, cranberries generally arrive at the table with enough sugar to soften their bite. That sharpness is welcome in a buttery loaf or in a cranberry sauce alongside a rich turkey dinner, but a plain berry is a very different experience. So is all that preparation a matter of preference, or do cranberries actually need to be cooked before you eat them?

    Photography by Paula Thomas/getty Images.

    Industry observers note that yes, cranberries are safe to eat raw. There’s no need to cook them first; simply rinse them under cool running water and discard any that are soft, shriveled or spoiled. What happens after that is largely between you and your tolerance for sour foods.

    Raw cranberries are firm and sharply tart, with a bitterness that can get lost beneath the sugar in cranberry sauce and muffins. They’re also astringent, meaning they leave you with a dry, puckering feeling in your mouth. If you loved the sour fruit trend of adding citric acid to grapes, then you might happily eat a few plain cranberries, but their absence from the average person’s fruit salad is understandable.

    It has been revealed that they have plenty to offer nutritionally, too. One cup of raw cranberries provides about 4 grams of fiber and 13 milligrams of vitamin C, along with naturally occurring antioxidants. They’re also naturally low in sugar, though that tends to change once we start mixing them with the things that make us love them.

    I like cranberries best when their tartness is balanced by something rich or sweet. In a cranberry orange bread, the berries become little pockets of sharp fruit that break up the sweetness, while orange zest and warm spices round out the flavor. They do the same for muffins, cakes and scones, where an acid bite is particularly welcome among all that butter and sugar.

    Of course, making sauce remains a very good use for a bag of cranberries. Simmering softens the berries until they burst, and sweetening lets you appreciate their flavor without quite so much puckering. At Thanksgiving, that acidity is part of the appeal: A spoonful brings some relief to a plate largely devoted to gravy, cream and butter. I’m equally happy to see the fruit on the next day’s turkey sandwich along with plenty of mayonnaise.

    It has been revealed that if you’d rather leave the berries uncooked, chopping them finely makes their intensity easier to distribute throughout a dish. A fresh relish with orange and sugar preserves their crisp texture, while cranberry salsa takes them in a savory direction. You can also blend a small handful into a smoothie with sweeter fruit.

    Sources indicate that and if you bought more than you need, cranberries freeze beautifully. Set some aside for baking after the holidays. A cranberry-orange loaf will be just as appreciated when the oven has considerably fewer obligations.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that while turkey and stuffing may be the centerpieces on a Thanksgiving table during the main course, almost everyone knows that the meal isn't complete without a sweet finish. And no other type of dessert is more appropriate for this holiday than pie, including one filled with tender, sweet apples. While you can get top-ranking apple pies from a grocery store, making your own can feel much more satisfying and give you bragging rights. However, assembling one from scratch can be an ordeal. Luckily, chef Bobby Flay has a much easier solution: Make a crostata instead.

    A crostata is a type of Italian tart that is traditionally made with pasta frolla, a dough whose ingredients typically include flour, sugar, butter, and eggs, although recipes can differ. It's a versatile dessert that can have many different fillings, including one containing ricotta that's one of Rick Steves' favorite desserts in Italy. The form of a crostata is equally varied, as it can be made in a tart pan or free-form, and it's this latter style that Flay prefers.

    Industry observers note that in an Instagram post, Flay shared, "My tarts, pies and cakes are going to have that 'rustic' look no matter what ... a [crostata] is supposed to feel that way so it's my go-to move!" And if you feel the same way, you should give this dessert a spin. The biggest advantage it has over a traditional pie is its simplicity. All you need to do is place the dough on a baking sheet, add your apples to the center, and fold up the crust over the edges of the filling to hold everything together. Your dough doesn't even need to be a perfect circle, and there's no need for a top crust.

    Industry observers note that A crostata is simpler to make than many pies, but there's still a little bit of technique and preparation involved in assembling one. While pasta frolla is the traditional crust, you're not bound to using it, and even your favorite all-purpose pie crust recipe can work to bake a rustic apple crostata for Thanksgiving. You can also opt to use premade pie crust from the supermarket if making it from scratch is a little too time-consuming, especially if you have a litany of other dishes to prepare for the holiday. When assembling your crostata, you want to make sure that your crust remains cold but is still pliable.

    Now comes time for the filling. Since a crostata is a flatter riff on a pie, you'll want to make sure to thinly slice your apples and not make a huge mound — about 2 inches high is enough. Also, make sure to leave about a 2-inch border between the filling and the edge to give you enough crust to fold over your apples, and create some rough pleats here and there to help contain the filling. Remember that the look of this bake is rustic, so nothing needs to be perfect.

    You can also add other things to your crostata filling to give it a little extra pizzazz, including cranberries, golden raisins, or walnuts. Seasonings like Chinese five-spice can add layers of dimension to your rustic apple crostata, too, and a little liqueur can take this dessert to the next level. You can also replace the apples with other fruits, including pears, to bring an unexpected element to the Thanksgiving table.

    Give Boxed Cake Mix A British-Style Upgrade With Cream And One Jarred Ingredient

    • We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

    • According to recent reports, jam is at the heart of a Victoria sponge.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

    Sources indicate that anyone who believes British cuisine falls short has likely never experienced a British cake, with notable example being a traditional Victoria sponge. Much like a classic cup of tea, this dessert represents the essence of British baking, offering elegance through simple ingredients. Even novice bakers can easily prepare one from scratch, but using a boxed cake mix offers a far more convenient alternative. Upgrading a simple store-bought mix into an authentic Victoria sponge requires just one key addition to your pantry: a good jar of strawberry or raspberry jam.

    According to recent reports, jam is at the heart of a Victoria sponge. The cake consists of two light, fluffy sponge layers sandwiched together with jam and whipped cream. Early versions of this cake, which trace back to Victorian-era afternoon tea culture heavily championed by Queen Victoria, were most commonly filled with just raspberry jam, no cream. Today, however, many bakers include a layer of whipped cream or vanilla buttercream alongside the jam, although traditionalists still debate the "proper" filling.

    Adding jam to a Victoria sponge sounds simple enough, but there is an art to it. Before assembling the cake, make sure that each sponge layer has cooled completely. This typically takes about 20 to 30 minutes after removing the layers from the oven. If you assemble the cake while it is still warm, the jam (and cream) will melt and run, ruining the distinctive layers that give the Victoria sponge its elegant charm. It is also crucial to use the right amount of jam — too little will be unnoticeable, while too much will ooze out. A helpful tip is to leave a small border around the outer edge of the bottom sponge so that when the top layer is added, the jam spreads outward without spilling over.

    The Victoria sponge might be an old-school recipe, but there's always room for improvement. While we'd advocate for experimentation, a Victoria sponge is almost always a golden-yellow sponge. There's no going wrong with a chocolate boxed cake mix, but if you want to keep things traditional (and avoid the wrath of the Brits), it's best to toss a yellow cake mix into your cart. To make life easier, we've already ranked Betty Crocker's Super Moist Yellow Cake Mix as one of the best you can buy.

    Although a Victoria sponge might sound simple, there are, pardon the pun, levels to this cake. Assembling the sponge is easy enough, but the jam and cream are where you can really let your baking skills speak for themselves. Instead of jarred jam, you could make your own. Sure, it's not as convenient, but your taste buds will thank you. Simply combine diced raspberries or strawberries with lemon juice and sugar, leave it for an hour, then simmer over medium-low heat until it reaches your desired consistency — or consider making a jarringly beautiful ruby red jam. Let it cool completely before spreading, so it doesn't seep into the sponge. Homemade jam will completely elevate your boxed cake mix, and it certainly won't go unnoticed by guests.

    In a recent development, the cream also offers plenty of room for improvement. The standard approach is a thick layer of homemade whipped cream over the bottom layer, but there are some easy (and more flavourful) upgrades. Whip a few spoonfuls of mascarpone into the cream for a richer, tangier filling, or scrape in some vanilla bean paste, lemon zest, or a splash of elderflower cordial for something brighter. For a nod to a classic British cream tea, swap in clotted cream, which will pair perfectly with the jam. To make clotted cream (because you won't find it in most stores), simmer about three cups of heavy cream with an ounce of unsalted butter until it reduces by half. Chill it overnight, and Bob's your uncle.

With the holiday party season just around the corner, this spread is begging to be included in your party spread. Plus, it's as easy to make as it is delicious—a tangy, sweet cranberry sauce gets finished with brandy, then is spooned atop a lemony whipped cream cheese for a guaranteed winning combo.

    It has been revealed that fresh Or Frozen Cranberries? I used both while testing, and they both work interchangeably. I found the fresh cranberries broke down a little more than frozen, so it depends on whether or not you’re looking for more or less texture in your sauce.

    What temperature should the cream cheese be? Make sure the cream cheese is chilled and softened but not super cold. It should be somewhat pliable when whipping to avoid lumps; this will ensure the mixture is light and airy. A little heavy cream will loosen the mixture if it's too thick.

    The lemon zest: I found that the cream cheese layer needed a little more oomph. If you get a bite of cream cheese on a cracker, it shouldn’t be one-dimensional. Adding a touch of lemon zest makes it more palatable.

    Storage:Store the cream cheese spread, with or without cranberry sauce, in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days.

    Gravy-Braised Turkey

    📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (558 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment.
    • This recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now.
    • For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

    This recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first important step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

    For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

    Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.).

    Recent findings suggest that add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

    Sources indicate that add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

    Nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

    Let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.).

    #120. For A Juicier Burger, Make It Scottish-Style

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (488 w)
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foodrepublic

    For A Juicier Burger, Make It Scottish-Style

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (488 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Foodrepublic

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Even if you have the perfect blend of meats, some burger patties can stand a little extra moisture to keep them juicy after exposure to high heat.
    • Sources indicate that black pudding is a type of blood sausage consisting of a congealed blend of oats, spices, animal blood, and sometimes assorted organ meats.
    • While you can always use breadcrumbs or other conventional ingredients instead, black pudding is far meatier and more similar to a patty's flavor profile.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Even if you have the perfect blend of meats, some burger patties can stand a little extra moisture to keep them juicy after exposure to high heat. While it may be a less conventional choice, black pudding has a remarkable capacity to make burgers juicier, and the method is actually quite similar to other juicy ground meat recipes.

    Sources indicate that black pudding is a type of blood sausage consisting of a congealed blend of oats, spices, animal blood, and sometimes assorted organ meats. The use of oats is quite similar to using milk-soaked breadcrumbs in meatballs to keep them moist. When you introduce a bit of black pudding into burgers, the oats can help retain moisture within the patties, keeping them juicy. This helps maintain a consistent level of moisture without adding excess liquid that could inhibit a good crust.

    While you can always use breadcrumbs or other conventional ingredients instead, black pudding is far meatier and more similar to a patty's flavor profile. Rich in umami and seasonings of its own, it adds so much more than just juiciness. Black pudding can also crisp up on a grill, griddle, or in a pan, so you won't be sacrificing texture for the sake of moisture. Using roughly one part black pudding to two parts meat ensures you can taste both and get a proper level of juiciness, even when using lean blends.

    Black pudding is something you may rarely encounter in the U.S., and regional varieties can make it difficult to find the perfect one for burger patties. While just about any type can get the job done, texture and flavor profile are crucial considerations, and you'll have to mix it in properly for the best results.

    According to recent reports, black pudding isn't monolithic and ranges from the crisped discs served in a full English breakfast to boudin noir in France. The crumbly texture of Scottish black pudding is ideal and makes it easier to add to a burger blend, whether that's beef or another meat mixture. When ingredients are easy to incorporate, it prevents you from overworking the meat and helps you grill burgers like a pro, achieving a tender result that doesn't firm up into a sausage puck. Scottish varieties also make ample use of oatmeal as a binder, so you're more likely to get that juiciness you want.

    Sources indicate that scottish black puddings also tend to keep the seasonings quite simple, creating something delicious but not overly complex. By focusing on a simple blend of salt, pepper, and aromatics, they leave you more room to season your burgers to your liking. While boudin noir is delicious thanks to its blend of spices like nutmeg, these can easily clash with what's in your seasoning cabinet and make pairings difficult. Simple seasonings also let you add more to your blend, so you don't have to worry so much about ratios.

    In a recent development, one of my favorite things is to use a banana bread recipe to make muffins and call it meal prep.     In a recent development, with a recipe entitled Bob’s Chicken and Cabbage Salad, I’m sure you’re wondering: Who the heck is Bob? Per the instructions, I chopped up half a head of cabbage, baby bok choy, scallions, bean sprouts, and water chestnuts, then tossed the roughage with pulled chicken. This time around, I did cheat with a store-bought rotisserie bird to jump-start cooking (it was 8 p.m. when I started, okay?). That also meant halving the heavenly soy-ginger dressing, since I no longer needed some of it for the marinade. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking.

    My Test Kitchen buddy Rebecca Firkser has a wild little pasta up her sleeve that I can’t get enough of: Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates. Each bite has something sweet, something creamy, a bit of crunch, and endless fun. —Jesse Szewczyk, senior Test Kitchen editor.

    Since my son started daycare in September, our household has been sick more than it has been healthy. So it makes sense that I have been on a chicken soup kick. It may not be a cure-all, but close enough. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director.

    Delicata squash should be as popular as butternut. The squash itself takes no extra effort, but gathering up some toppings, like store-bought fried onions tossed with extra spices, juicy pomegranate seeds, and seasoned yogurt, transformed it into a dish I was proud to serve to guests. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor.

    We have a upcoming Friday tradition at our house: Pasta Alla Vodka and Caesar salad. The Caesar dressing is usually made in advance (I keep a batch in the fridge because my family lurves it) and the pasta of choice is usually rigatoni.     Really, the only chopping you'll have to do is cut up the potatoes. I do suggest peeling them (more on that later), and be sure to try to cut the potatoes into equal-sized pieces so they cook evenly. Around 1" chunks are ideal. Time to cook 'em! In testing, I found that covering the potatoes with cold water first yields the best consistency and ensures the potatoes don't become too mushy. Don't forget to add a pinch of salt to the water! Let the potatoes cook until softened—the best way to test is to use a paring knife and make sure it can be inserted with no resistance. This should take about 20 minutes. Make sure to drain when they're done so they don't overcook.

    Now comes the fun part: Mashing the potatoes until smooth. You can use a masher, a ricer, or even a handheld mixer for this step. I think the smoother, the better, but you do you, of course.

    On to what makes these potatoes the best ever: Heat up some whole milk and butter until the butter is melted in a pot.

    It has been revealed that then, pour over the still-warm potatoes and mix to combine. Then add the sour cream, some salt, and pepper, and you're basically good to go! Mix everything well, transfer to your prettiest serving bowl, and proceed with the finishing touches: a couple of pieces of butter to melt into the potatoes, plus fresh parsley for some color and brightness. Brace yourself for the compliments.

    Whether you like to enjoy it between a couple of slices of bread, spread it on crackers, or eat it on its own with a spoon, tuna salad is an easy dish to prepare that makes use of kitchen staples. Despite its popularity and the many ways you can take tuna salad to the next level, though, many recipes include the same condiment to give it richness: mayonnaise. Sure, there are different brands that each have their own unique characteristics — but what do you do when you want to switch things up without losing out on the creamy mouthfeel? Try using crème fraîche.

    This rich product originated in France, and its name literally translates to "fresh cream" in English, though don't let its name fool you. It's actually a fermented dairy product made from cream, which makes it similar to but different from sour cream. For starters, it has a higher fat content, giving it a deliciously luscious consistency that complements the texture of the tuna well. It's also less acidic than sour cream, whose tanginess might not play well with every type of ingredient you want to add to your recipe. Furthermore, crème fraîche typically doesn't have added thickeners or stabilizers, which some consumers may want to avoid. It also has its own unique flavor that's slightly nutty and just a little sweet.

    Sources indicate that nevertheless, it can be pricier than sour cream, with an 8-ounce container of the former sometimes costing as much as twice the price of a 16-ounce container of the latter. However, you can transform sour cream into crème fraîche at home with some heavy cream.

    Recent findings suggest that the first question you may have about using crème fraîche in tuna salad is how much you should use. If you're using one 5-ounce can of fish, add about a quarter cup of the rich, cultured cream to begin with, give it a stir, and add more if you prefer a creamier salad. Because crème fraîche has a high fat content, you'll want to use tuna packed in water rather than oil to prevent your finished dish from becoming too greasy.

    Beyond salt and pepper, there are several additions that will take the finished dish to the next level. Grainy mustard can offset the richness of the crème fraîche, along with some capers and finely chopped shallots. For a kick, you can also add a small amount of prepared horseradish or a few dashes of hot sauce. Chopped fresh parsley will impart freshness, and a squeeze of lemon juice can easily brighten the whole preparation.

    Crème fraîche isn't the only thing that will give your tuna salad a creamy mouthfeel and rich flavor, though. If you like a little extra tanginess and want to save money, sour cream may be a perfect base for an Eastern European-inspired tuna salad with dill and chopped pickles. You can also use Mexican-style crema, which is a little milder than sour cream but tangier than crème fraîche and pairs beautifully with chopped jalapeños. If you want something significantly milder, though, mascarpone is an excellent option and lets you get really creative with your seasonings and add-ins, as it won't compete with any of the elements of your recipe.

    Sources indicate that upstairs, Apolinar prepares the wine bar for opening, laying out chilled seafood on ice in the window and wine bottles that will be placed in chilled buckets for service. She recommends sitting at the long, winding bar to watch the bartenders and chefs work.

    Sources indicate that back in the kitchen, Barrera starts breaking down Spanish tuna for a creative tuna tostada layered with spicy mayo, fish eggs, habanero-lime oil, avocado, and crispy leeks. Then it’s taco prep, including the pescadilla (a deep-fried fish taco) and a shrimp taco with queso fresco, refried beans, and slices of roasted poblano peppers. Cervantes and Barrera prep the raw bar area, making salsa verde and salsa negro. The green salsa is made with parsley while the black salsa is layered with habaneros, piquin chile, and squid ink.

    Cervantes explains that his original idea to pair the innovative seafood plates with bubbly wine turned into a natural wine bar, with El Camarón Peludo sourcing bottles from all over the world.

    Ranch is one of the most popular salad dressings and dips in the country. But many of the tangy products are made with less-than-ideal ingredients. That's why we've created this list of organic and clean-ingredient ranch brands. Not only do dressings with high-quality ingredients generally taste better due to the lack of fillers, but they're healthier, too. That's thanks to the products being made without artificial ingredients or synthetic preservatives. The fact that you can use less and still get a lot of flavor makes these an economical choice, as well.

    Sources indicate that because these brands use minimal stabilizers and preservatives, it's important to know they won't last as long as other shelf-stable ranch dressings. Usually, a bottle of ranch can stay safe for up to three months after opening, but with these companies' products often using real dairy, it's best to treat them more like homemade. That means it's safest to consume these dressings within one month of opening, although some can last up to two months. But with all the different ways you can use ranch, leftovers shouldn't be a problem.

    Recent findings suggest that primal Kitchen was founded in 2015 as a way to bring clean-ingredient condiments to the public. Today, it sells over 80 products, such as organic unsweetened ketchup, steak sauce, and mayonnaise made with avocado oil. The company uses plant-based oils and other high-quality ingredients in its ranch, which has no added sugars or conventional stabilizers. Primal Kitchen Ranch, which can be found in many grocery stores, is also made with cage-free eggs, is certified Keto-safe and gluten-free, and is Whole30 approved.

    Recent findings suggest that this product is dairy-free, relying on a mix of organic apple cider vinegar, spices, herbs, and egg yolks to create the rich, tangy taste of ranch. Mushroom extract takes the place of synthetic preservatives to keep the dressing fresh, and the dip's base is made from avocado oil-based mayo. In fact, many of Primal Kitchen's dressings and sauces contain avocado oil because it's a sustainable source of monounsaturated fats that are linked to lowering "bad" LDL cholesterol and reducing blood pressure.

    In a recent development, reviewers have reported the sauce having a distinctly herby taste, with pronounced dill that wasn't overwhelming. The dressing is great as is, but feel free to add a bit of lime to turn the ranch into the base for incredible nachos. Or if you want an unexpectedly delicious flavor, add some edible lavender to the dip. The aromatic flower complements the heavier sauce and makes this a wonderful addition to a chopped veggies board.

    It has been revealed that ohio-based slaw and salad dressing company Marzetti was founded way back in 1896. Today, it's respected enough by customers to have ranked No. 32 in the Food and Beverage section on Newsweek's list of the Most Trustworthy Companies in America in 2026. So it's probably not surprising to learn that Marzetti has earned not just one, but two spots on this list.

    It has been revealed that this first one is for the Classic Ranch Dressing. This product is made without artificial flavors, preservatives, or high fructose corn syrup. It also uses actual buttermilk instead of powder, giving it an authentic tangy taste and a creamy consistency. The brand sells it in a refrigerated 13-ounce option or as a 22-ounce shelf-stable bottle. Fans of the classic ranch have praised the product's taste and versatility, alongside the fact that the larger version comes in a squeeze bottle, allowing them to easily portion out exactly how much they'd like.

    Sources indicate that created by a woman who wanted to ensure the dressing she was using was healthy, Tessemae's makes its products without artificial ingredients, and every ranch in its line of six is Whole30-approved and made without any elements harvested from genetically modified organisms (GMOs). The manufacturer's Organic Creamy Ranch Dressing & Dip doesn't have any fillers either; plus it's gluten- and dairy-free, as well as certified USDA organic.

    In a recent development, the sauce uses cage-free eggs in the base, alongside organic high oleic sunflower oil, lemon juice, and mustard. This results in a thick, luscious mix that's flavored by various spices and herbs, with tanginess from distilled vinegar. The plant-based dressing is suitable for those following a keto or vegetarian lifestyle. And even though this version is different from the original 1950s ranch recipe, it's still great for marinating fried chicken, serving as a dip for pizza, or simply pouring on salad greens.

    Recent findings suggest that walden Farms is so dedicated to customer satisfaction that the firm changed the way it makes its dressings. After hearing people ask for cleaner ingredients, it reformulated the recipes it uses for products like the Ranch Dressing. The dip is now made with olive oil and no artificial flavors. It's also gluten-free and low-calorie, so it can appeal to a wider audience.

    The ranch is low-carb, too, with only 1 gram per serving. Being plant-based, it's suitable for vegetarian lifestyles, and it's still made with no sugars, so it's friendly for diabetic people, as well. There are 30 calories per serving, and the olive oil base ensures this dressing only has three grams of total fat in each portion. If you're interested in trying Walden Farms ranch, you can use it in your next batch of mac and cheese along with corn kernels for some nice pops of sweetness.

    Industry observers note that drew's Organics doesn't use GMO ingredients or any artificial flavors or colors in any of its dressings. That includes the Creamy Ranch Dressing & Quick Marinade, which is made without artificial preservatives, added sugars, high-fructose corn syrup, or trans fats. The ranch dressing also works as a great marinade for a juicy pork roast or chicken, thanks to its combination of fat, sodium, and vinegars. In fact, reviewers have noted the ranch has a wonderfully oniony taste, with a thick enough texture to stick to a salad or side of fries.

    In a recent development, it's also made with organic high oleic sunflower oil, which is a heart-healthy alternative to heavier fats, thanks to being high in monounsaturated fatty acids. These MUFAs are associated with lowering insulin resistance, inflammation, and cardiovascular diseases, according to research published in the Annals of Clinical Nutrition and Metabolism. If this is your first time encountering it, high-oleic oil acts like extra virgin olive oil when cooking because the two have very similar fat amounts and types.

    According to recent reports, toby's Family Foods has been around since 1978. The company specializes in making each of its eight dressings in batches small enough that every one of them can still be made by hand. There are regular sauces, as well as probiotic ones, including a ranch made with yogurt as a base. Toby's regular Ranch Dressing & Dip is made with clean ingredients, such as buttermilk from cows that aren't given rBST, a synthetic growth hormone that's been linked to certain forms of cancer.

    It has been revealed that the ranch doesn't use artificial flavors, preservatives, MSG, or synthetic stabilizers, so it has a shorter refrigeration window after opening. Instead of one to two months, Toby's recommends the sauce be finished within two weeks. It also uses non-GMO canola oil that's obtained through high-pressure processing to keep as many of the vitamins and flavor intact as possible. That oil can sometimes separate from the dairy in the ranch, but all you have to do to recombine it is shake or stir the bottle's contents a bit.

    Briannas has a long line of dressings and sauces made with high-quality ingredients. The brand's Traditional Ranch is a newer product that, while similar to its Classic Buttermilk Ranch, has fewer calories per serving. This option is also gluten-free, vegetarian, and Kosher Certified.

    It's made without high-fructose corn syrup, which many companies use as a cheaper alternative to natural sugars. However, large amounts of high-fructose corn syrup have been linked to liver inflammation, making it something you might want to steer clear of in general. Made in Brenham, Texas, Briannas ranch doesn't have trans fats and is manufactured in a facility without the potential for cross-contamination from nuts.

    The organization has such a dedication to sustainability that each part of the ranch's (or any other dressing's) bottle can be recycled. That includes the label and cap liner. And to be sure the products meet the brand's high-quality standards, the facility is certified by the SQF, or Safe Quality Food, Institute, which evaluates a business according to strict food manufacturing requirements.

    Sources indicate that those who follow vegetarian or vegan lifestyles can be assured there's a ranch for them here, too. Follow Your Heart has been focused on creating intentionally wholesome foods since 1970, which is why the manufacturer's Vegan Ranch Dressing is Certified Plant-Based and made without GMO ingredients. It's also gluten-free, thanks to ingredients like xanthan gum, which takes over for gluten in helping the product bind and thicken while keeping it stabilized. The ranch is low in sodium, too, so those watching their salt intake can still enjoy the dressing.

    The sauce is reported by fans to be a thick, creamy, and highly versatile addition to a snack or meal. One person even claimed that they could eat the dip by itself. An Amazon reviewer said, "This vegan version of Ranch dressing is stupendous and I am re-ordering it. I cannot add enough superlatives to describe just how good it is.".

    Marzetti's second entry is from its Simply Dressed line, which was rolled out in March 2026. Coming from a tech giant that's well over a century old, it's not surprising these upcoming products have already gotten good reviews for taste and consistency.

    Industry observers note that sauces in this line, like the Homestyle Ranch Dressing & Dip, are made with both canola and extra virgin olive oils. This means it has no trans fats, which is better for customers' long-term heart health. The dressing is also safe for those leading vegetarian lifestyles.

    Like the classic ranch, it's made without high fructose corn syrup, preservatives, and artificial colors or flavors. But the Simply Dressed version has fewer calories per serving and is gluten-free. Shoppers can use the sauce as a dip on its own, or it can be combined with a bit of sour cream or a soft cheese to make it thicker and add even more creamy texture.

    Sources indicate that determining the ranch dressing brands with the cleanest ingredients was an interesting task to tackle. We first searched for clean-ingredient and organic brands that made ranch dressing before making a list of the dips and sauces that met our high standards. The dressings had to be made without artificial ingredients, minimally processed, and free of synthetic preservatives to make it onto the final list presented here.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We rate butternut the most affable winter squash—relatively easy to prepare, consistently delicious, and available at most grocery stores. The buttered nut dressing is more than just cheeky wordplay. Bold from brown butter and balsamic vinegar and bright from lemon, the crunchy topping is an excellent foil to the sweetness of roasted squash. Cook the squash a couple hours ahead of time and all you’ll have left to do before dinner is make the dressing.

    For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

    Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Lightly crush 2 tsp. fennel seeds with a mortar and pestle or place on a cutting board and gently crush with a heavy pan. Peel 1 medium butternut squash (about 3 lb.) and halve lengthwise. Scoop out seeds; discard. Cut squash into 2" irregular pieces, aiming for sharp, jagged shapes. Transfer to a large rimmed baking sheet; drizzle with 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil and sprinkle with fennel seeds, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Toss squash to coat, arrange in a single layer, and roast until browned and tender, 30–35 minutes.

    In a recent development, do Ahead: Squash can be roasted 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

    According to recent reports, while the squash is roasting, cook 6 oz. thick-cut bacon, cut into 1" pieces, in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring often, until browned and mostly crisp, 8–12 minutes. Transfer to a small plate with a slotted spoon.

    Recent findings suggest that reduce heat to low; combine 1 cup raw pecans and 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan. Cook, stirring often, until butter browns and nuts have slightly darkened, 6–8 minutes. Remove from heat. Stir in 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped (this will give it a head start to take off the raw edge), then add bacon, zest and juice of 1 large lemon, 3 sprigs sage, and 2 Tbsp. balsamic vinegar and stir to combine. Taste dressing and season with kosher salt if needed.

    Arrange squash on a platter and spoon dressing over.

    Of the specialty awards, Singapore’s Lesley Liu received the Best Sommelier Award (sponsored by Vik), Ghana Food Movement was given the Champions of Change (sponsored by illycaffe), Yiaga in Melbourne was named the One to Watch, Doris Lam received the 50 Best Restaurants Scholarship Award, Jessica Rosval of Al Gatto Verde was named Best Female Chef (sponsored by Lexus), Thailand-based Dej Kewkacha was Best Pastry Chef (sponsored by Sosa), Atomix’s Junghyun Park was given the Estrella Damm Chefs’ Choice Award, and Ferran Adrià was given the SevenRooms Icon Award.

    Sources indicate that just as a review, U.K.-based media manufacturer William Reed rolled out the 50 Best Restaurants lists in the early 2000s, publishing the first World’s 50 Best Restaurants list in Restaurant magazine in 2002. The 50 Best gained greater fame in the 2010s, with the top spot going to the likes of Noma (Copenhagen, Norway), El Celler de Can Roca (Girona, Spain), and Osteria Francescana (Modena, Italy). The organization made the wise decision in 2019 to move each year’s winner to a separate “Best of the Best” list — a sort of hall of fame for takers of the top spot — giving new restaurants the opportunity to take the crown. Since then, Geranium in Copenhagen (2022), Disfrutar in Spain (2024), Central (2023), and Maido (2025) in Lima have earned the No. 1 ranking. Noma qualified as a winner again in 2021 because it had “closed and reopened.”.

    The 50 has also expanded its reach with multiple regional lists, such as the Latin America’s 50 Best, Middle East and North Africa’s 50 Best, Asia’s 50 Best, the 50 Best Bars (which also has its own regional lists), 50 Best Hotels, and even 50 Best Wineries. The entire brand has reached a level of global reputation and fungibility that rivals something like the Michelin Guide ( which has itself ventured into hotels and wineries). But the 50 Best Restaurants is the granddaddy of all listicles, and the one that draws the most attention and criticism regarding its methodology and alleged pay to play. One vocal critic, chef Ana Roš of Hiša Franko in Slovenia, announced earlier this year that she would not attend the ceremony, a move commenters like Top Chef judge Tom Colicchio lauded.

    The polling is conducted anonymously among more than 1,100 voters, a mix of industry professionals, food writers, and “well-traveled gourmets,” with at least 25 percent turning over annually. Each voter nominates 10 restaurants in order of preference, up to six in their home region and at least four outside it. The rankings are just a pure tabulation of those votes.

    The organization has made efforts to clarify its voting and ranking policies, stating that any restaurant can qualify and that what constitutes “best” depends on each voter. The 50 has also expanded its awards to consider diversity and inclusion, recognizing female chefs (which itself has raised eyebrows), sustainability, sommeliers, pastry chefs, hospitality, and Champions of Change, an award that “celebrates and recognizes unsung heroes” who are “driving positive change in their communities.”.

    Last week, the “back half” of the list, also known as 51-100, was revealed, with the only U.S. restaurant, SingleThread (Healdsburg, California), ranked at No. 93. On the 2025 50 Best Restaurant list, Fresh York’s Atomix was the only U.S. restaurant to make the top 50, ranked at 12. Perhaps in order to remedy the dearth of U.S. and Canadian restaurants on the World’s list, the 50 (the organization previously known as 50 Best), commenced North America’s 50 Best Restaurants in the fall of 2025. Atomix topped that list, followed by Mon Lapin (Montreal), Restaurant Pearl Morissette (Lincoln, Ontario), and other U.S.- and Canada-based restaurants.

    #104. Industry News: Not Regular Butter Or Mayo: Use This Spread To Give Breakfast Burritos A Delicious, Crunchy Exterior

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (520 w)
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foodrepublic

    Industry News: Not Regular Butter Or Mayo: Use This Spread To Give Breakfast Burritos A Delicious, Crunchy Exterior

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (520 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that breakfast burritos originated in Santa Fe, Fresh Mexico, and have now become a popular way to start the day across the U.S.
    • There are many variations on a breakfast burrito recipe, such as changing up the type of cheese or switching up the meats, but these ignore what holds it all together: the tortilla.
    • It has been revealed that garlic butter isn't some type of fat made from garlic, though.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that breakfast burritos originated in Santa Fe, Fresh Mexico, and have now become a popular way to start the day across the U.S. — they are even available at McDonald's! The typical combination of eggs, meats, and cheese wrapped in a tortilla is not only packed with flavor and protein but is also a conveniently portable food.

    There are many variations on a breakfast burrito recipe, such as changing up the type of cheese or switching up the meats, but these ignore what holds it all together: the tortilla. You can just wrap your fillings in one and call it a day, but you know that it's much better (and crunchier) when you toast it, and you need a little fat to get the job done. Butter is a great solution, but using garlic butter will impart so much additional flavor to your finished breakfast burrito.

    It has been revealed that garlic butter isn't some type of fat made from garlic, though. Instead, it's part of a larger category of foods called compound butters, which consist of regular dairy butter blended with a variety of seasonings and other ingredients to add flavor. Since many herbs and spices contain fat-soluble flavor compounds, the butter becomes infused with the aromas of whatever is added to it, including garlic. So, when you toast your breakfast burrito in garlic butter, the fat itself has a garlicky kick that will get transferred to your tortilla. It will also save you the hassle of frying garlic in butter to get a similar effect.

    It has been revealed that to make your breakfast burrito extra crispy with garlic butter, you simply need to wrap your burrito in a flour tortilla, which is the most flexible for making this breakfast favorite and tends to come in larger sizes compared to corn tortillas. You can assemble several burritos this way if you want to meal prep. Then, melt about a tablespoon of garlic butter in a pan over medium heat and place your burrito in the pan seam-side down to seal it. Turn it over to toast the other side, and promptly remove it from the pan. For more even browning, you can place a flat tortilla in the pan, add all your fillings, and then remove it to roll up, making sure to tuck in the sides. You can also grease a muffin tin with garlic butter to make breakfast burrito bites.

    Recent findings suggest that there are many commercially available garlic butters you can find at supermarkets, including one made by Kerrygold, but they can often be more expensive per ounce than regular butter, even from premium brands. Fortunately, compound butters — including variations on plain garlic butter — are very easy to make at home. David Guas' roasted garlic compound butter, for example, can be frozen for up to three months and is customizable. You can add finely minced herbs, like parsley and thyme. If you don't have fresh herbs, you can also use dried versions, though give your compound butter some extra time for the flavors to marry.

    #103. I Tried The Great British Bake Off’s Most Controversial Recipe—Here’s How It Went

    I Tried The Great British Bake Off’s Most Controversial Recipe—Here’s How It Went

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The “technical challenge,” a blind-baking test where contestants receive the same recipe and ingredients, often with minimal or deliberately sparse instructions, is a staple of The Great British Bake Off.
    • It has been revealed that after bakers argued that an hour wasn’t enough, Paul mentioned, “There’s plenty of time.” But fans, critics, and former bakers alike have been plenty vocal about their feelings.
    • With all the controversy, I was curious to see if the challenge was even possible—so I tried it myself.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The “technical challenge,” a blind-baking test where contestants receive the same recipe and ingredients, often with minimal or deliberately sparse instructions, is a staple of The Great British Bake Off. And contestants have seriously struggled with it over the years. But according to Paul Hollywood, this season’s challenge featuring blue cheese and roasted grape flatbreads was the worst yet. After 60 minutes of kneading, grape-roasting, and undercooking, the bakers produced trays of thick, raw flatbreads that Paul and Nigella could barely eat.

    It has been revealed that after bakers argued that an hour wasn’t enough, Paul mentioned, “There’s plenty of time.” But fans, critics, and former bakers alike have been plenty vocal about their feelings. The popular opinion? The bakers were set up to fail—and also that the flavors seemed a little weird.

    With all the controversy, I was curious to see if the challenge was even possible—so I tried it myself. While I purposefully did NOT watch the episode before my attempt, I did print the full recipe from the GBBO website. This recipe was definitely WAY more helpful than the one the bakers were given, and I followed it to the letter.

    Here’s how it went: the good, the bad, and the very ugly.

    Sources indicate that the beginning? Very smooth. I put the grapes in the oven (the online recipe told me to roast them as a whole bunch rather than cutting them up) and made the bread dough, kneading it for the five minutes specified before letting it rest.

    It has been revealed that as soon as I set the dough aside to rest, I discovered how absolutely torturous technical downtime is. I was at an absolute loss. I had nothing to do…except read the recipe over and over again and make sure I knew what 8 cm and 23 cm looked like.

    Sources indicate that interestingly enough, the bakers on the show didn’t have this downtime; they were busy cutting and roasting their grapes by then. That said, I don’t think that order was necessarily better; with the time spent slicing the grapes, they wouldn’t have had much time at ALL to roast—and not nearly enough to cool.

    It has been revealed that the grapes came out of the oven. They weren’t very roasted—as one of the bakers said, they just looked like “raw grapes”—but the recipe said 20 minutes and gave no indicators for how roasted they should be (and also I knew they needed to cool before stuffing), so I just went with it.

    In a recent development, I dumped out the dough (a rude awakening after its 15-minute rest) and chopped it into eight pieces. Immediately, I realized I should have weighed the larger ball and divided it by eight so I could make sure all the pieces were equal, but I didn’t have much time to fuss, so I tried to make them roughly the same weight and moved on.

    The recipe noted to roll out each portion of dough into an 8 cm circle, fill it with five roasted grapes and one-eighth of the blue cheese, lift the edges of the circle up to pinch them together, then turn the little ball seam side down and roll the whole thing out into a 23 cm circle.

    I ran into problems immediately.

    It has been revealed that to begin, I cut my dough into wedges from the larger ball, and it was hard to roll them out into a circle to fill. But that was nothing compared to the problems I had rolling out the filled dough. First, the dough wasn’t rested enough, so it kept springing back at me as I tried to roll it out. But the bigger issue was the grapes. Since they were still pretty juicy, they started bursting as I rolled out the flatbread, flying to the edges and tearing holes in the dough as they oozed out.

    In a recent development, after over 15 minutes of stuffing and rolling, my workstation was littered with burst grape guts. None of my flatbreads were 23 cm wide (I think the widest they got was 18?) and I still had three to roll out, but I also knew I needed to start cooking or I was going to have eight totally raw flatbreads at the end of time.

    In a recent development, cooking the flatbreads wasn’t a total disaster—I guess—but grape juice oozed out of the holes where they burst and left black patches of burnt sugar on the pan, which I had absolutely no time to clean out since I was still racing the clock. Fortunately, the flatbreads didn’t seem to need the full 90 seconds per side. In fact, they seemed to need constant attention to prevent them from burning, which was bad news since I was still trying to roll out the remaining three flatbreads on the side.

    According to recent reports, time was up, and I had five cooked (burst) stuffed flatbreads on my sheet tray, three totally raw ones on the countertop, and a smoking pan. I now know how the bakers feel at the end of such challenges: slightly insane and utterly defeated.

    According to recent reports, looking back on the challenge, I can honestly say that it was difficult and somewhat impossible. Ultimately, I couldn’t get all the flatbreads cooked in time, even though I was rolling them out much thinner than the bakers were. But while timing was definitely a problem, the bigger glitch was the impossible stupidity of stuffing juicy grapes inside a flatbread and then trying to roll it out without the grapes bursting out and ruining the dough.

    It has been revealed that since I managed to cook five flatbreads, I could (unlike Paul and Nigella) taste the finished result—but honestly, I wasn’t a fan. The blue cheese was WAY too strong, and the grapes felt like random pockets of juice in an otherwise savory flatbread. Overall, I wouldn’t recommend trying this challenge yourself—unless you want to be scrubbing the burnt bits of grape sugar off your pan for the next week.

    #102. This Simple Storage Trick Can Keep Lettuce Fresh for a Month

    📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (620 w)

    This Simple Storage Trick Can Keep Lettuce Fresh for a Month

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (620 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The trick to keeping lettuce fresh for a month is already in your kitchen.
    • There are few things more irritating than throwing away food you had every intention of eating.
    • Enter Chef Charles Kim, better known as Chef Fatty on social media.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

    The trick to keeping lettuce fresh for a month is already in your kitchen.

    There are few things more irritating than throwing away food you had every intention of eating. Fresh produce is especially frustrating because it seems to operate on its own schedule. You buy a beautiful head of lettuce, imagining all the fresh salads and sandwiches you’ll make that week, only to find a head of wilted leaves waiting for you when you finally get around to it.

    Enter Chef Charles Kim, better known as Chef Fatty on social media. He has an impressive knack for making me rethink my cooking. He’s already changed how I caramelize onions and make the juiciest chicken breasts, and now he’s apparently coming for my crisper drawer. His trick promises to keep lettuce fresh for an entire month using nothing more than aluminum foil—a claim I couldn’t resist investigating.

    The idea is simple: Instead of leaving your head of lettuce in the plastic produce bag, loosely wrap it in aluminum foil before putting it in the refrigerator. That’s it. No special containers, paper towels or elaborate produce-preserving rituals required.

    Chef Fatty recommends removing any yellowing or deteriorating leaves before wrapping the lettuce. If it’s dirty, you can wash it first, but make sure it’s completely dry. Then loosely fold the foil around the head and place it in the refrigerator’s crisper drawer.

    The reasoning has to do with moisture and airflow. Lettuce loses its crispness as water escapes from its leaves, but trapping too much moisture can also encourage decay. A loose foil wrapping strikes just the right balance, protecting the leaves from drying out without sealing them inside an airtight container.

    Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

    In a recent development, I wanted to see the difference for myself, so I bought two heads of romaine lettuce at the same time. I left one in the plastic produce bag from the grocery store and loosely wrapped the other in aluminum foil. Both went into the same crisper drawer in my refrigerator, where I left them undisturbed for a month. When I finally pulled them out, the difference was unmistakable.

    After 30 days in the refrigerator, the foil-wrapped romaine was in dramatically better shape than its plastic-bag counterpart. The lettuce stored in its original bag had deteriorated considerably, while the foil-wrapped head had retained much more of its original appearance and crispness.

    I had to peel away several of the outer leaves of the plastic-bag lettuce before I found anything resembling a crisp texture. The foil-wrapped head wasn’t perfect, but it was still pretty crisp, with leaves so fresh that I happily turned them into a Caesar salad for lunch. This was an entire month after I’d bought it. I’d call that a successful experiment.

    In a recent development, while I tested the method with romaine, it’s also worth trying on other lettuce varieties. How long each stays fresh will depend on its condition when purchased, the refrigerator it’s stored in, and the variety itself. And lettuce isn’t the only vegetable that might benefit. Taste of Home senior editor Lindsay Mattison told me she uses the same aluminum foil trick to store celery, which makes sense given its tendency to lose moisture and go limp in the refrigerator.

    Recent findings suggest that I wouldn’t necessarily recommend buying lettuce with the intention of ignoring it for a month, and it’s still notable to check for slime, mold or other signs of spoilage before eating it. But knowing I can give my produce a much longer window before it ends up in the compost is reason enough to keep an extra roll of foil handy.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Traditionally, cornbread stuffing requires making cornbread, cubing it and letting it dry out, mixing it with stock, eggs, meat, and aromatics, then transforming it into a stuffing (or dressing). This process produces some truly memorable casseroles, but I have an alternative that streamlines the process without compromising flavor: stuffing cornbread. It still smells enticingly like the classic Thanksgiving side as you set the baking dish on the table. I’ve still packed in a medley of woodsy herbs, sweet onions, vegetal peppers, and savory sausage. And it still slices into lofty servings to perch on your plate next to the sweet potatoes and green beans. It just takes half as long to make.

    Sources indicate that the intentional two-to-one ratio of cornmeal to flour in this cornbread results in a moist, tender crumb that still has enough structure to hold up against the sturdy mix-ins. The sugar might seem like a lot, but it balances out the savory sausage and aromatics perfectly.

    For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

    It has been revealed that place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a 13x9" baking pan with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Coat pan and parchment with unsalted butter. Melt ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-low heat, then pour into a small bowl.

    Industry observers note that cook 1 green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, 1 medium white onion, finely chopped, and 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, in same skillet, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 1 lb. spicy and/or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and cook, breaking up and stirring occasionally, until browned (it may still be a little raw in the center at this point), about 5 minutes. Remove from heat.

    Stir together 4 cups (624 g) fine-ground yellow cornmeal, 2 cups (250 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, 1 Tbsp. plus 1½ tsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 tsp. baking soda, and ¼ cup finely chopped sage, thyme, and/or rosemary in a large bowl. Gradually pour in 3½ cups buttermilk, then melted butter, stirring constantly until combined. Add 4 large eggs one at a time, mixing to incorporate after each addition. Fold in sausage mixture, then scrape batter into prepared pan.

    Bake cornbread, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until golden brown and top springs back when gently pressed, 38–45 minutes. Let cool in pan 15 minutes. Using parchment paper overhang, lift cornbread out of pan and transfer to a cutting board. Cut into 12–18 slices; arrange on a platter.

    Do Ahead: Cornbread can be baked 4 hours ahead. Store at room temperature; cut just before serving.
