    It has been revealed that our harvest cabbage salad with date dressing was inspired by a viral recipe that happens to be perfect for fall. London-based cook and writer Natalie Chassay created her original recipe as an homage to the celery salad served at The Four Horsemen in Brooklyn, New York. The true star of the show—in both her recipe and in ours—is the date dressing: a sweet and savory mixture of thinly sliced Medjool dates, shallots, lemon juice, grated Parmesan and extra virgin olive oil. The ensemble of sweet, sour, tangy and savory flavors is the perfect complement to a simple salad, whether it’s made with finely sliced celery like Natalie’s, or finely shredded cabbage like ours.

    In a recent development, in our salad, we’ve combined finely shredded green cabbage with red cabbage for an extra pop of color. Shredded carrots add a touch of sweetness, while a topping of crunchy toasted pecans turns the crunch up to 11. Whether shared at a fall potluck, served alongside a warm and cozy autumn dinner, or tossed as a quick and easy lunch, this crunchy cabbage salad is sure to hit the spot.

    It has been revealed that in a large bowl, stir together the dates, shallots, olive oil and lemon juice. Season the mixture with flaky sea salt to taste.

    In a recent development, editor’s Tip: Allow the dressing to sit for at least 10 minutes before adding it to the salad. Allowing the dressing to rest softens the dates and allows the flavors time to meld together.

    In a large bowl, toss together the finely shredded green cabbage, red cabbage and carrots.

    Sources indicate that editor’s Tip: To easily core the cabbage, first slice the cabbage head in half. Then make a diagonal, V-shaped cut on each side of the core to separate and remove it.

    Recent findings suggest that pour the salad dressing over the shredded cabbage and carrots and toss to combine them. Top the salad with toasted chopped pecans.

    Leftover harvest cabbage salad with date dressing should be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator.

    It has been revealed that harvest cabbage salad with date dressing will last up to four days when stored properly in the fridge. However, over time its texture may become a bit soggier and the green cabbage may take on a pink hue from the red cabbage. It will still be quite tasty.

    Letting the shredded cabbage and dressing sit together lets the flavors meld, so making the salad a few hours in advance is perfect—but any longer is not ideal. You could also prepare the shredded veggies and dressing up to a day in advance. Store them in separate containers in the refrigerator.

    In a recent development, you don’t need to salt the cabbage before making cabbage salad. However, salting the cabbage beforehand can reduce bitter flavors and enhance its crunch factor. To do so, toss the cabbage with salt and allow it to sit for about an hour. Use a clean kitchen towel or paper towel to wring out the excess moisture.

    In a recent development, this recipe calls for a half-head each of green cabbage and red cabbage. Alternatives include savoy and Napa cabbage, both of which have a more tender texture.

    According to recent reports, crunchy apples like tart Granny Smith or sweet Honeycrisp, diced or julienned, would make a tasty addition to this harvest cabbage salad. Other fruits that would work well with this recipe include diced pear, halved red or green grapes, and dried fruits like cranberries or tart cherries.

    In a recent development, add to bowl with beans, stir to combine, then transfer to a 13" x 9" baking dish. Spread in the dish, then bake until everything is bubbly, which should take just 30 minutes.

    Time for the fried onions! Return to the oven and bake until the onions are just warmed through, about 5 minutes more.

    The full list of ingredients and directions can be found in the recipe below.

    Save some time (and oven space) on the busy holiday by making this Thanksgiving side ahead of time. Simply assemble the casserole (without the fried onions), cover tightly with plastic wrap, and refrigerate for up to 4 days or until you're ready to bake!

    #77. Skip Butter And Milk: The Canned Ingredient That Makes Burgers Juicier

    📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (512 w)
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foodrepublic

    Skip Butter And Milk: The Canned Ingredient That Makes Burgers Juicier

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (512 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, juicy burger patties are all about nailing the perfect ratio of fat, moisture, and protein for something that isn't wet or greasy but also isn't dry and crumbly.
    • Cream of mushroom soup may be billed as a shelf-stable meal in its own right, but the condensed version is a canned soup hack for many recipes thanks to its texture and flavor.
    • According to recent reports, chopped mushrooms for extra-juicy burgers is an increasingly common tactic, but evenly mixing all the little bits without overworking the meat is challenging.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, juicy burger patties are all about nailing the perfect ratio of fat, moisture, and protein for something that isn't wet or greasy but also isn't dry and crumbly. While butter and milk can certainly help, condensed cream of mushroom soup is a far better and easier alternative that perfectly strikes the balance when you use the right amount.

    Cream of mushroom soup may be billed as a shelf-stable meal in its own right, but the condensed version is a canned soup hack for many recipes thanks to its texture and flavor. It's had much of its moisture removed and therefore has a higher ratio of fat. While wet enough to infuse proteins with a bit of juiciness, its fat content helps preserve the tenderness and protect the existing moisture, all with the delicious umami of mushrooms. Condensed varieties also tend to be more potent, so the small amount you'll use for juiciness translates into a subdued but still noticeable taste.

    According to recent reports, chopped mushrooms for extra-juicy burgers is an increasingly common tactic, but evenly mixing all the little bits without overworking the meat is challenging. While wet ingredients are far easier to thoroughly disperse, they come with a caveat. You need a starch to hold and release the moisture unless you want it to drip out right away. Breadcrumbs are a common choice in meatballs and other ground beef recipes, and a ratio of half a cup of starch to one 10.5-ounce can to one pound of protein gets the job done quite well.

    It has been revealed that burger patties made with condensed cream of mushroom soup are pretty forgiving and more difficult to dry out, but that doesn't mean you can just chuck them on the grill willy-nilly. To preserve the juiciness and keep them easy to work with, you need to know when to leave them alone, whether that's while they're raw, cooking, or resting.

    Immediately cooking a burger infused with condensed cream of mushroom soup leaves a lot of surface moisture. This ends up steaming it, so it doesn't develop a good crust and robs it of much of the juice you were attempting to preserve. Letting any patty chill in the fridge helps it firm up and makes it easier to manipulate on the grill, but it also allows the breadcrumbs to absorb the moisture to release later. Similar to marinating, it also helps to let the flavors mix a bit, so you don't end up with pockets of intense mushroom-ness that can ruin an otherwise good bite.

    While exact timing varies based on your method, the 5-6-7 rule when cooking burgers is a reliable starting point. Five minutes on one side, six on the other, then seven minutes resting helps you balance enough heat to create a crust with enough time to ensure that the insides are not still raw. The resting is particularly important, as you don't want to release all your juice onto your plate or as steam and make your subsequent bites drier.

    #76. Spinach Artichoke Baked Potatoes

    Spinach Artichoke Baked Potatoes

    📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (454 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Epicurious

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This baked potato stuffed with spinach-artichoke dip is the ultimate solo comfort meal.
    • The rich, velvety filling that melts over top comes together in moments while your spud cooks.
    • According to recent reports, most recipes serve multiple people.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This baked potato stuffed with spinach-artichoke dip is the ultimate solo comfort meal. Classic twice-baked potatoes require two trips to the oven to deliver a pillowy, gussied-up filling and crispy skins all in one bite. Here, I’ve streamlined the workflow with a microwave. By zapping your spuds to start, you can reduce the overall baking time without sacrificing texture. Pick a large russet (or Idaho) for the best results; their relatively high starch and low moisture content helps them bake up airy and light, not gummy.

    The rich, velvety filling that melts over top comes together in moments while your spud cooks. Cream cheese and mozzarella pack in enough dairy richness for a satisfying cheese pull and mellow out the subtle bitterness of baby spinach and nutty tang of artichoke hearts. (It’s crucial that your cream cheese is room temperature before you mash it in with the veggies. If it’s still got a chill from the fridge, it won’t fully incorporate.) The Worcestershire sauce is optional, but just a few shakes from the bottle bring instant savory depth to the filling.

    According to recent reports, most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

    Preheat oven to 425°. Poke 1 large russet potato (about 12 oz.) all over with a fork; rub with avocado or vegetable oil to coat and sprinkle with kosher salt. Microwave potato on a microwave-proof plate on high 5 minutes. Turn potato over and microwave on high until fork-tender, about 5 minutes more. Let potato sit until just cool enough to handle.

    While potato is cooling, microwave 5 oz. baby spinach with 2 Tbsp. water in a medium microwave-proof glass bowl until wilted, about 2 minutes. Carefully press leaves to release as much liquid as possible, then drain off liquid. Coarsely chop spinach.

    Mix 2 Tbsp. cream cheese, room temperature, in a medium bowl until smooth. Add spinach, 4 quartered artichoke hearts (from a 14-oz. can), coarsely chopped, 2 Tbsp. finely grated Parmesan, 2 Tbsp. coarsely grated mozzarella, ½ tsp. garlic powder, and ¼ tsp. Worcestershire sauce (if using) and fold to combine; season with salt and freshly ground pepper.

    Slice potato in half lengthwise and lightly fluff flesh in each half. Set on a small foil-lined rimmed baking sheet. Divide spinach mixture between potato halves, piling high (don’t pack too tightly). Sprinkle more Parmesan over. Bake potato halves until very tender when squeezed and skin is wrinkled and crisp, 20–25 minutes. Let cool slightly before eating.

    Breaking: Cranberry Brie Pull-Apart Bread

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, this cranberry Brie pull-apart bread recipe is bursting with melted cheese and sweet-savory cranberry butter.
    • According to recent reports, I may be a year-round cranberry fan, but it’s hard to deny just how right it feels to feast on the ruby-colored fruit during the holiday season.
    • Cranberry Brie pull-apart bread is what happens when you make a mashup of party cheese bread and cranberry butter.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recipe by Taste of Home Test Kitchen.

    Tested by Taste of Home Test Kitchen.

    Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

    In a recent development, this cranberry Brie pull-apart bread recipe is bursting with melted cheese and sweet-savory cranberry butter. It's an interactive joy to eat.

    According to recent reports, I may be a year-round cranberry fan, but it’s hard to deny just how right it feels to feast on the ruby-colored fruit during the holiday season. Fresh and frozen cranberries are perfect for cranberry sauce and not-too-sweet cranberry desserts, but I also love using dried cranberries in everything from muffins to party appetizers. And my new favorite way to use dried cranberries is in cranberry Brie pull-apart bread, where they transform a loaf of cheesy bread into a holiday masterpiece.

    Cranberry Brie pull-apart bread is what happens when you make a mashup of party cheese bread and cranberry butter. A crusty, round loaf of sourdough is cut in a grid pattern and stuffed with half a pound of cubed Brie. The cheese-stuffed loaf is then coated in a dried cranberry-honey butter (bolstered by orange zest, garlic and rosemary) and baked until it’s hot, crispy and melty. It’s hearty, decadent, sweet, salty and impossible to stop eating.

    Preheat the oven to 350°F. In a small bowl, beat together the softened butter, finely chopped dried cranberries, honey, grated orange zest, minced garlic and salt until they’re blended.

    Cut the bread into 1-inch slices to within 1/2 inch of the bottom of the loaf. Repeat cuts in the opposite direction. Insert the cubed Brie into the cuts.

    Editor’s Tip: If your sourdough is crusty, a serrated bread knife will get the job done without too much elbow grease. The best bread knives slice cleanly without tearing the fluffy interior.

    Spread the cranberry butter over the top of the bread. Wrap the loaf in foil and place it on a baking sheet.

    According to recent reports, bake the bread for 20 minutes. Unwrap it and continue to bake it until the cheese is melted, about 10 minutes longer. If desired, drizzle it with hot honey before serving it.

    Ellie Crowley For Taste Of Home.

    Wrap leftover cranberry Brie pull-apart bread tightly, or transfer it to a food storage bag and refrigerate it for up to four days. To reheat it, wrap the bread in foil and bake it at 350º until it’s warm. Unwrap it and continue to bake until the cheese is melted and the bread is crisp. If the bread got pulled apart enough that it’s not really holding its shape anymore, transfer it to a baking dish, bake it until it’s melty, and eat it like stuffing.

    In a recent development, cranberry Brie pull-apart bread tastes best hot and crispy right out of the oven, but you can assemble the bread a few hours ahead of time, wrap it in foil, and refrigerate it until it’s ready to bake. You can also make and refrigerate the cranberry butter up to four days in advance and soften it at room temperature before using it. If you want to bring it to a party or Friendsgiving, follow good party etiquette and check with the host about whether the oven will be available to bake it when you arrive.

    Ellie Crowley For Taste Of Home.

    If your pull-apart bread is soggy, it might need to be baked longer or at a slightly higher temperature—especially if your bread is really fresh and soft. I use kitchen timers and oven thermometers to track my bakes and ensure my oven isn’t running cooler or hotter than I’d like. Don’t be afraid to bake the bread for a little longer than the recipe suggests if it hasn’t crisped on the outside or if the cheese isn’t fully melted.

    It has been revealed that sourdough’s structure (and slightly sharp flavor) is perfect against the richness of the Brie and cranberry butter, but if sourdough isn’t for you, try a round, crusty loaf of rustic white bread. Get a loaf that weighs about 1 pound. Whole wheat and multigrain loaves can work as well, but they tend to have a denser texture and tighter crumb that won’t pull apart as easily. If you can’t find a round loaf, an oval-shaped loaf is the next best choice, but steer clear of sandwich loaves, which can’t be cut as easily into the necessary grid pattern.

    Set cranberry Brie pull-apart bread out as a party appetizer next to a crudite platter, cocktail meatballs, and a selection of festive cocktails and mocktails. You can also add it to the holiday table as part of the main course, alongside a holiday ham, roast turkey or standing rib roast.

    #73. Keeping the Diwali Flame Burning in Fresh York City

    📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1270 w)
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Saveur

    Keeping the Diwali Flame Burning in Fresh York City

    📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1270 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, the akhand diya, the continuously burning flame, has one purpose: to stay lit.
    • Industry observers note that as a teenager, I remember feeling that I had crossed an invisible threshold into womanhood.
    • In many ways, this transition is happening outside of me.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, the akhand diya, the continuously burning flame, has one purpose: to stay lit. It is a small but enduring presence, tended to around the clock, its care passed from one person to the next so that the light never goes out. I’ve often thought about how much of life is like this, how we are constantly passing the torch from one version of ourselves to another.

    Industry observers note that as a teenager, I remember feeling that I had crossed an invisible threshold into womanhood. I was becoming someone different from the girl I had been, carrying parts of her with me but beginning to understand the world through a upcoming lens. Now, years later, I find myself at another such transition: I am becoming a different version of a woman, one I am still getting to know.

    In many ways, this transition is happening outside of me. Thirteen years ago, I moved away from my family in Mumbai and the home where Diwali had always been celebrated. For all those years, the rituals continued, even as I participated in them from thousands of miles away, mostly over video calls. Back in Mumbai, Diwali meant a house full of family and friends, kitchens bustling with cooking and frying, and the warm glow of diyas illuminating the mandir. I was no longer physically there, but I remained part of it. This year, for the first time, I hosted my parents for Diwali in the home I’ve built for myself in Latest York City.

    It felt cataclysmic, or at least I was making it feel that way in my head. As I welcomed a different version of myself, I was also taking on a newly introduced role within my family. I was no longer simply the daughter returning to their house for Diwali; I was the one opening my home, preparing the food, tending to the rituals, and making space for the people who first taught me what this celebration means. There is perhaps no greater joy than watching the people I love receive and experience care. And yet, this was a responsibility I had chosen to take on, and one that felt particularly daunting as the eldest daughter. I wanted to get it right.

    Sources indicate that for me, that care has always found its way to the table. Food is how my family celebrates, how we mark occasions, and, perhaps most importantly, how we look after one another. So naturally, much of my energy went into planning the meal. Despite my best efforts, my dad promptly assigned himself the task of making the goat kari—apparently, even after 13 years away, some things hadn’t changed. We headed to our local butcher in Brooklyn to buy fresh goat meat, and almost immediately, his attention turned to the spice tolerance of my guests.

    According to recent reports, “How much spice can your friends tolerate?” he kept asking me. “Should I keep it at a level six? But our level six might be their level ten. What do I do?” he lamented. “Relax, they’ll be able to handle it! Just make it our level five,” I told him.

    It has been revealed that I gave in and handed over part of the kitchen to my mother, too. She took charge of the paneer, cooking generous chunks in a luscious onion-tomato gravy and making the chapatis. Selfishly, I didn’t mind relinquishing that responsibility: This would be my one chance for the year to eat chapatis fresh off the tava, puffed up and piping hot, and made by my mother.

    As the days drew closer, I found myself loosening my grip on the intends I’d made. My parents had their own ideas about what needed to be cooked, and while I was initially resistant to them taking over (any immigrant will tell you how hard it is to get our parents to just relax!), I was learning that hosting didn’t necessarily mean doing everything myself. It also meant making room for everyone to contribute and allowing new rituals to form.

    In a recent development, the evening began with freshly fried moong vadas. My mother, of course, insisted on frying them for everyone, right before serving. Made from soaked and ground mung lentils, these little fritters are crisp and golden on the outside, with a soft, almost creamy interior. They have a naturally earthy, nutty flavor from the lentils, sharpened with green chiles, ginger, and spices.

    It has been revealed that moong vadas are best eaten immediately, still hot out of the oil, with a tangy green chutney. The scene reminded me of Diwalis back in Mumbai, when the vadas rarely even made it to the serving platter: Everyone would gather around the kitchen, waiting for the next batch to come out of the kadai, reaching for them before they had a chance to cool. I saw the same thing happening in my kitchen in Newly introduced York.

    Recent findings suggest that in the meantime, my friends Leanne and Christina took charge of the tamarind margaritas, my ode to the soft, sweet-tart tamarind candies I grew up savoring as a kid. The tangy cocktails were a welcome counterpoint to the savory fritters, the perfect way to wake up our taste buds (and made exercising some restraint with those moong vadas before dinner particularly difficult). My brother helped set the table and move furniture around, just as we used to do for our parents back in Mumbai. There was something deeply comforting about watching us fall into these old rhythms.

    The table eventually came together with a mix of dishes that felt both familiar and celebratory. There was chana masala from my cookbook, East to East, alongside my dad’s goat kari, slow-cooked with spices until the meat was tender. My mother’s saucy tomato-onion paneer was accompanied by a pile of chapatis that disappeared almost as promptly as they came off the stove. We served everything family-style, laying out the dishes on kansa thalis, traditional Indian plates made from bronze or bell metal, an alloy of copper and tin. They reminded me of the way my grandparents served meals, and I wanted to bring a little of that into our Diwali celebration.

    Sources indicate that at the center of the spread was a vegetable pulao, fragrant basmati rice cooked with carrots, cabbage, cauliflower, and whole spices. Alongside it, I placed bowls of pickled onions and mango achaar, whose sharp, tangy bite cuts through the richness of the karis. There was also cucumber raita, cool and creamy, offering a welcome respite from the heat of the spices. These accompaniments might seem like small additions, but they are essential to the balance of an Indian meal. Every bite can be a little different, depending on what you bring together on your plate.

    Recent findings suggest that for dessert, I made homemade gulab jamun, my brother’s favorite. The soft dumplings are made from milk solids and fried until golden, then soaked in a warm saffron-and-cardamom-scented sugar syrup.

    In a recent development, as I sat cuddled among both my families, I realized that while it wasn’t the perfectly orchestrated dinner I’d imagined when I first started planning, it was something better. The family I was born into celebrating Diwali alongside the family I’d chosen and built in New York, all gathered around the same table and enjoying every minute of it. Perhaps keeping the flame alive was never about re-creating the past exactly as it was but about allowing it to illuminate whatever comes next.

Here are some early contenders on our radar — places we’re thrilled to have in the conversation no matter how the scene shakes up as 2026 wraps and we continue into 2027.

    Our New York team is excited to see the full spectrum of what pastry chef Camari Mick has in store with her own new venture, Afro-Caribbean brasserie and bakery Calabash, which opened in the West Village in early October.

    Also in the West Village, the Taqueria Ramírez team debuted this Mexican-seafood-focused wine bar, which translates to “the hairy shrimp.” The tiny convivial space opened in mid-September.

    Sources indicate that alex McCoy’s resurrected Thai restaurant, which opened in early September, is dishing up some of the spiciest Thai food the D.C. area has seen since the much-lamented closure of Little Serow. Thanks to its moody, candlelit atmosphere, it’s also becoming a favorite tucked-away date spot.

    Recent findings suggest that chicago’s tavern-style pizza has been having a moment outside of the Midwest; in D.C., it’s a menu centerpiece of La Merna, which has been one of the city’s tough-to-get tables since its August opening. Co-owner Bradley Shorten used to run a few tavern-style pizzerias in Chicago, and his wife and partner Meg Schmitt, who has a background in cheese distribution, is topping pastas with cheeses she makes fresh. The wood-paneled dining room with red leather-covered booths resembles a Midwest supper club with its laid-back, old-school atmosphere.

    We had high hopes that this coastal Italian Pittsburgh restaurant — from the team behind Lilith, Jamilka Borges and Dianne DeStefano — would open in time for 2026 Eater Awards consideration, but the opening date kept continually getting pushed back. The most recent estimate is “late fall.”.

    Atlanta already knows the team behind Lucian can combine a fantastic wine list with thoughtful food and a carefully curated retail experience; they’ve started doing it again at Sargent, the combination bistro and bookstore that hadn’t yet opened when our scouts hit the city in early August. The classic menu and gorgeous space are already catching attention in the city; we’re also keeping our eyes on the upcoming opening of Thai-style bar Some Luck from the Talat Market team, slated to open any day now.

    Sources indicate that this new modern Mexican restaurant was only a few days old when our correspondent Matthew Kang stopped by in early September. Our LA team has high standards for tacos, and Kang notes the top-notch Chihuahuan food here could already hold its own even when competing with standout California options. Kang appreciated Chiwas’s delicious seafood and short ribs, and approachable, homey vibe; we’ll be back to see how the restaurant matures.

    October brought the debut of this ambitious restaurant from chef Jonathan Granada, and editor Dianne de Guzman is ready to try the tableside duck, laminated brioche, and a gougeres-like Parmesan tart — all set inside an Art Deco-style former post office.

    We thought this long-in-the-works, highly anticipated Filipino cocktail bar might open in time for us to visit Detroit and check it out this year, but the project from Tyler Olivier and Marcee Sobredilla is still wrapping up construction.

    In a recent development, this Evanston, Illinois, project is the first full-service restaurant from Chicago barbecue royalty D’Andre Carter and Heather Bublick. The restaurant is a true celebration of their community, decked out with local art and paired with a steakhouse-esque menu. It opened just outside our 2026 cutoff, and it’s looking like an exciting time for barbecue in the Windy City in general, as Chicago also awaits the opening of Sanders BBQ Prime in Hyde Park.

    In a recent development, lielle was a hit with the Eater LA team when it opened this year, and our team might even be more enamored with follow-up Marée, which just missed our window with its early September opening. At a recent visit, Matthew Kang noted the creamy mussels au gratin and Instagram-worthy squab, and says the au poivre burger earns its $42 price tag.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foodrepublic

    Breaking: The Creamy Ingredient That Makes PB&J Sandwiches 10x More Delicious

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (477 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Foodrepublic

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When you want to upgrade your peanut butter and jelly sandwich, you don't have to splurge on high-priced bread or get particular about the jam like Ina Garten.
    • It has been revealed that toasting the exterior of your sandwich with butter in a pan gives you a golden-brown outside packed with richness and flavor.
    • While the heat won't caramelize the sugars in the jelly or toast the peanut butter fats, it does make them taste more delicious.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When you want to upgrade your peanut butter and jelly sandwich, you don't have to splurge on high-priced bread or get particular about the jam like Ina Garten. How you prepare it can make all the difference, and treating it like a grilled cheese with a bit of butter on the outside can give you a serious result with even more serious flavor.

    It has been revealed that toasting the exterior of your sandwich with butter in a pan gives you a golden-brown outside packed with richness and flavor. It brings out the best in your bread and warms the peanut butter and jelly for something as gooey as melted cheese but infinitely creamier. This is especially true if you use a top-ranked store-bought butter brand, since even a small amount acts like a seasoning and truly upgrades the whole thing. The toasted bread and melted insides create a dichotomy of textures that transforms one of the simplest recipes in the world into something more decadent and complex.

    While the heat won't caramelize the sugars in the jelly or toast the peanut butter fats, it does make them taste more delicious. Smell is just as notable as taste when enjoying a meal, and heat releases those aromas so you can enjoy them more. This is especially nice if you work with higher-end, complex ingredients like artisan jellies, as it lets you better experience each little nuance.

    A fresh preparation method means new opportunities for better flavor. While simple toasting alone is enough to make any mixture of ingredients delicious, taking inspiration from other recipes and choosing the right type of bread maximizes that effect.

    Industry observers note that while you should avoid crusty bread for a PB&J because it tends to be a bit dry, this trick is a great way of getting around that. Even older bread gets a texture boost, transforming it from stale and brittle to crispy and delicious. If you're focusing on the rich, buttery flavor, using something full of dips and ridges, like sourdough or a rustic country-style loaf, only lets you use more butter for a thoroughly flavored exterior. Just be sure not to use something with deep holes that your filling can leak through, as it may burn in the pan and foul the flavor.

    If you want to take things even further, you can make the most decadent PB&J French toast with this method. It's especially great if you dip a soft, fluffy white bread or brioche in the egg mixture, giving you something that's pillowy on the inside and crispy on the outside. Butter alone can toast the bread, but the addition of milk and eggs adds binding proteins and delicious fats that create a stronger, but still crispy, structure that holds its shape well and prevents the liquidy insides from oversaturating the bread.

    Recent findings suggest that also in today’s Open Tab: How much more ridiculous can advent calendars get? Was this NYC gay bar actually designed by AI? And how is Andy Baraghani thinking about his first restaurant?

    Gone are the days when advent calendars were essentially manufactured cardboard inside of which you could find some of the most unfortunate tasting chocolate ever produced. These days we’ve moved beyond chocolate. Some advent calendars open to reveal tinned fish, others jewelry, and still others skin-care products. Google Trends data shows search interest for advent calendars has grown steadily for the past five years, and as writer Emily Bloch reported for Bon Appétit, the global advent calendar market is expected to grow to $2.47 billion by 2033.

    Part of the appeal, as Bloch mentions, is the little-treat-culture of it all. It’s nice to open up a little surprise each day. But another element, surely, is the content that’s made around advent calendars. There are the unboxings—tailor-made for the short-form vertical video format which rewards reveals—and there are the scandals. Who could forget (everyone except me, realistically) the backlash against Chanel’s $825 advent calendar in 2021 when customers declared the included products decidedly lackluster? This year Skims faces a similar backlash for its $148 advent calendar for which it is now offering refunds.

    But drama and outrage gets attention, which in turn fuels more content. And as the Kardashian clan knows better than most, no matter what the public is saying, at the end of the day they’re still talking about you. Thus, the advent calendar cycle continues for another year, growing ever greater. Will we ever summit the peak of the advent calendar craze? So far, the data say no.

    If you’ve read—or even skimmed—this column in the past, you’ve likely gleaned that I often point out the many fumblings of AI—one could argue I make a sport of it. That’s why, when I saw grumblings online that a new gay bar in New York City’s Hell’s Kitchen looked like it had been designed by Chat-GPT, I felt a morbid curiosity begin to bubble. The bar, commenters said, was so deeply on-the-nose gay-bar-coded, it simply couldn’t have been made by a human brain. It was named Pride Bar x Lounge (a bit first thought, right?), and its decor is essentially just rainbow flags. It kind of looks like how they’d design a gay bar in a Netflix show, which is to say: almost impressively bland.

    In a report from The New York Times, the two co-owners say that they did not in fact use any AI in designing the bar, which has cost about $5 million so far to come to fruition. On the other hand, the posters released to promote the bar, which had also received some heat, were in fact made using AI.

    The saga is an interesting data point in the public’s perception of what is an appropriate way to use this tech: making a grocery list? Sure. Using it to help you figure out what exactly you like about your own child? Absolutely not. Asking AI to help you strategy a trip? I guess. Using it to design a gay bar? Hard no.

    I Tried Taco Bell’s New FLAMIN’ HOT Menu Items To See If They Really Bring The Heat

    I'll try just about anything Taco Bell puts on its menu, and whatever I order usually ends up drenched in hot sauce. So when I heard the chain was adding a upcoming FLAMIN' HOT offering (and bringing back a punchy fan favorite), I was curious whether they'd finally give me enough spice to leave those packets alone. I like my food hot enough to get a few beads of sweat forming on my nose, and with a name like FLAMIN' HOT, I don't think that's asking too much.

    According to recent reports, there were two contenders: the returning FLAMIN' HOT Grilled Cheese Burrito ($5.49), which I'd missed during its first run, and the brand-new FLAMIN' HOT Mini Taco Salad ($2.49). Both feature Fritos FLAMIN' HOT, so I figured I was in for some decent spice. Here's how that worked out.

    Recent findings suggest that I love a good taco salad, especially when the bowl itself is edible. But my first impression of this mini version was that it looked like a pretty ordinary Taco Bell salad. And after a few bites, I wasn't finding much to convince me otherwise.

    Sources indicate that you've got seasoned beef, refried beans, lettuce, tomatoes, cheddar, and Creamy Chipotle sauce tucked into a crispy flour tortilla bowl. Beneath everything was a layer of reddish rice, which Taco Bell says is seasoned with FLAMIN' HOT Fritos. I could definitely see the color, but whatever was making that rice spicy wasn't doing much for my taste buds.

    In a recent development, and speaking of Fritos, I'm still trying to figure out where mine went. They're supposed to be in there, but I genuinely couldn't tell whether they'd been included in my particular serving. I would've loved more of the chipotle sauce, too, because the other ingredients seemed to overpower whatever heat was hiding underneath.

    The shell itself was fine, although a little bland and greasy. I’m still pro-taco salads, but I just wish the spice had been more noticeable—especially with a name that makes such a big promise.

    The returning burrito is stuffed with seasoned beef, spicy rice, crunchy FLAMIN' HOT Fritos, nacho cheese sauce, sour cream, and Creamy Chipotle sauce. And because Taco Bell clearly believes there's no such thing as too much cheese, the entire thing gets a three-cheese blend grilled onto the outside of the tortilla.

    According to recent reports, I took a pretty substantial first bite, making sure to get into those Fritos and all its FLAMIN’ HOT components. There's a lot happening inside this thing, and I was enjoying every bit of it.

There was a satisfying punch of spice, followed by that little tickle at the back of my throat that tells me something's doing its job. I wasn't desperately reaching for a drink, but the burrito had enough kick to make me happy.

    Industry observers note that I even went back for another bite of the mini taco salad afterward, and it tasted better with the burrito's lingering heat still in my mouth. Who knew it needed a little help from its menu companion?

    Ultimately, the burrito is the one I'd order again. The mini taco salad has potential, and for $2.49, I wouldn't be opposed to giving it another shot. But next time, I'm bringing the extra hot sauce packets it should've saved me from needing.

    #66. Puppy Chow Balls

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (513 w)
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tasteofhome

    Puppy Chow Balls

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (513 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Puppy chow is our favorite Midwestern snack, and it’s the inspiration these holiday-ready truffles.
    • Industry observers note that like puppy chow, Chex cereal (crushed for easier rolling) and peanut butter are melted together to make the crunchy truffle filling.
    • According to recent reports, in a large microwave-safe bowl, heat the peanut butter in 30-second increments until it’s completely melted, stirring occasionally.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recipe by Margaret Knoebel, Milwaukee, Wisconsin.

    Tested by Taste of Home Test Kitchen.

    Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

    Puppy chow is our favorite Midwestern snack, and it’s the inspiration these holiday-ready truffles. You’ll find all the same ingredients—peanut butter, Chex, chocolate and confectioners’ sugar—but with a truffle redesign that’s sophisticated enough for a Christmas dessert table (and that keeps hands considerably less messy!).

    Industry observers note that like puppy chow, Chex cereal (crushed for easier rolling) and peanut butter are melted together to make the crunchy truffle filling. Each truffle is enrobed in a thick layer of melted chocolate then coated generously with confectioners’ sugar. These puppy chow truffles are a two- to three-bite affair and totally remind me of those significant puppy chow clusters everyone fights over.

    According to recent reports, in a large microwave-safe bowl, heat the peanut butter in 30-second increments until it’s completely melted, stirring occasionally. Add 2 tablespoons of confectioners’ sugar and stir until smooth. Add the crushed Chex and stir until everything is well combined.

    It has been revealed that scoop the puppy chow truffles by the tablespoonful onto wax-paper-lined baking sheets. Freeze them until they’re firm, about 30 minutes.

    In a microwave-safe bowl, melt the semisweet chocolate and shortening at 50% power, and stir until they’re smooth. Dip each puppy chow ball into the melted chocolate and shake off the excess. Place the puppy chow truffles on a waxed paper–lined baking sheet.

    According to recent reports, place the confectioners’ sugar in a large airtight container or resealable bag. In batches, add the puppy chow balls and shake them in the bag until they’re well coated in confectioners’ sugar. Store the puppy chow truffles in an airtight container.

    Ellie Crowley For Taste Of Home.

    Store puppy chow truffles in an airtight container at room temperature for up to four days. They can also last in the fridge for up to one week.

    According to recent reports, yes, you can freeze puppy chow truffles, but wait to coat them with confectioners’ sugar until after they’ve thawed. To freeze the puppy chow truffles, place them on a parchment-lined baking sheet and freeze them for one hour. Transfer them to a zip-top bag or airtight container, and freeze them for up to two months. Thaw them overnight in the fridge before enjoying them.

    Ellie Crowley For Taste Of Home.

    Your chocolate may not be smooth for a few reasons. The first is you may have burned it in the microwave. When you burn chocolate, it will seize and become clumpy. Unfortunately, this is unfixable. It’s also possible that you left out the shortening. Shortening makes the chocolate slightly less viscous, which makes it easier to evenly coat the truffles. It also makes it smooth and glossy. Don’t skip this ingredient!

    To help puppy chow balls hold their shape, be sure to use a no-stir creamy peanut butter. It’s much thicker than the natural peanut butters you have to stir. Because their oils separate so easily, natural peanut butters will make the mixture softer and more malleable.

    #65. This Chain Was Dunkin's Bitter Rival In The '50s — Now It's The Most Popular Donut Spot In Japan

    📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (609 w)
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foodrepublic

    This Chain Was Dunkin's Bitter Rival In The '50s — Now It's The Most Popular Donut Spot In Japan

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (609 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, dunkin' is one of America's favorite spots to grab a quick donut and one of its famous syrup-infused iced coffees — which we ranked from worst to best.
    • Sources indicate that what makes this feud particularly fascinating is that it was a family affair.
    • As is often the case, feuds rarely end with a clear winner.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, dunkin' is one of America's favorite spots to grab a quick donut and one of its famous syrup-infused iced coffees — which we ranked from worst to best. Today, the chain boasts more than 10,000 stores in the U.S. alone and sits comfortably at the top of the country's donut hierarchy. However, it wasn't always the undisputed heavyweight. In a rivalry that gives McDonald's and Burger King a run for their money, Dunkin' spent decades going head-to-head with Mister Donut. Ultimately, Dunkin' came out on top — at least, if we're talking strictly about the USA. Over in Japan, Mister Donut reigns supreme.

    Sources indicate that what makes this feud particularly fascinating is that it was a family affair. Dunkin', originally known as Dunkin' Donuts, was founded in 1950 by William Rosenberg. The simple combination of donuts and coffee proved to be a huge success. Naturally, Rosenberg wanted to expand the business through franchising. So far, so good, right? Well, not everyone was happy with the idea, including Harry Winokur, Rosenberg's brother-in-law. In a move that would spark a decades-long rivalry, Winokur left the business and opened Mister Donut just a few miles from Dunkin's original location. He even embraced franchising, with Mister Donut employees reportedly being prohibited from saying the word "dunk" in their stores.

    As is often the case, feuds rarely end with a clear winner. In 1990, Dunkin' acquired Mister Donut and rebranded nearly all of its American locations as Dunkin' stores (ouch). Today, just one Mister Donut location remains in the U.S. That must have been a hit on Winokur's pride, but while Dunkin' was busy making cereal in the '80s, Mister Donut was thriving on the other side of the world. Today, Mister Donut is Japan's leading donut chain, with more than 900 locations in operation.

    In a recent development, japan has embraced plenty of Western-style foods with open arms. Think of the juicy, hamburger-inspired hambāgu, or comforting pizza toast with its wide array of toppings. Mister Donut also happens to fit comfortably into this category. However, one thing worth knowing about Japan's take on Western staples is that they're rarely direct copies. Instead, the country has a knack for putting its own spin on imported dishes. That's exactly how Mister Donut managed to carve out a place for itself in the market.

    In a recent development, the first Mister Donut opened its doors in Japan in 1971, after business executive Seiichi Suzuki acquired the exclusive rights to operate the brand in the country. The original menu featured familiar American favorites, but Suzuki also introduced items and adjustments designed to appeal to local tastes. These included reducing the sugar content of certain products, serving more modest portions, and creating a cozy, sit-down atmosphere. The approach proved successful, and Mister Donut quickly expanded across Japan. Dunkin', meanwhile, had also tried its luck in the Japanese market, opening its first location in 1970. While Mister Donut continued to grow, Dunkin' struggled to gain a foothold and eventually left Japan altogether in 1998.

    According to recent reports, in 1989, Suzuki's manufacturer Duskin acquired full ownership of Mister Donut's Japanese operations, giving it greater freedom to develop the brand's distinctly Japanese identity. From there, the chain continued to expand, eventually bringing its donuts to markets including Thailand, Australia, Taiwan, and Singapore. Today, Mister Donut is best known for its playful, distinctly Japanese creations, particularly the Pon De Ring, a chewy, ring-shaped donut made up of small dough balls, and Mocchurin, its mochi-inspired donut line that is so soft, they require paper trays to keep each donut from losing its shape.

    #64. A Chef’s Guide to Eating and Drinking in Santo Domingo

    📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1881 w)
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Saveur

    A Chef’s Guide to Eating and Drinking in Santo Domingo

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1881 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, on a Friday night in July, Nidia Evangelista walked with her arms crossed over the Puente Flotante toward East Santo Domingo.
    • On the other side, we turned a corner and found hundreds gathered around a dance floor in the undercroft of a bigger bridge.
    • It has been revealed that bur normally walks (or bikes) everywhere.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, on a Friday night in July, Nidia Evangelista walked with her arms crossed over the Puente Flotante toward East Santo Domingo. Six lanes of traffic jockeyed inches from her left shoulder, while the black waters of the Río Ozama coursed below. “Oh my God, Oli, what are we doing?” she said. “Nobody does this.” Evangelista is the communications manager for Santo Domingo’s most intriguing restaurant, Casarré. Her boss, Swiss Dominican chef Olivier Bur, was leading Evangelista, photographer Clay Williams, and me beyond the fortified walls of the Zona Colonial, where few travel on foot.

    On the other side, we turned a corner and found hundreds gathered around a dance floor in the undercroft of a bigger bridge. Live bachata drowned out the traffic overhead. Bur procured a major bottle of Presidente and plastic cups from a vendor, poured, and raised a “Salud!”.

    It has been revealed that bur normally walks (or bikes) everywhere. Moving slowly, he’s learned the textures of the city. Still, for the next six days, he took Williams and me to his most beloved restaurants by car. We visited a string of chimi stands where hawkers compete for clientele through the night; a chicharrón spot where couples dance shoeless on the cool tile floor; and a cafeteria where boys shuffle stewed eggplant, beets, and goat to bus drivers en route. Places like these are the “infrastructure for life,” Bur said. “Thirty years ago, there was nothing else.”.

    Industry observers note that over the last couple of decades, however, another dining scene has sprouted. Dominican chefs have returned from kitchens in Mexico, Japan, or Switzerland to explore the forgotten and sometimes shunned ingredients of their (or their parents’) homes. They served us conch, cassava, breadfruit, and djon-djon mushrooms in sashimis, foams, tostones, and surprising dessert creams. The dishes were fresh and exciting, but local and global traditions have always mingled—as such, the cuisine is not “New Dominican,” it’s simply “Dominican,” fully expressed.

    Calle Andrés Julio Aybar 13+1 829 545 7503.

    In a recent development, the Piantini neighborhood was once verdant and sleepy, according to Bur. Now it’s a bustling business district. Most of the remaining vegetation decorates the façades of restaurants, like Ajualä’s. Brushed palm thatch and a bushy barba de Fidel (Fidel’s beard) tree greet you at the tall aged-steel door.

    According to recent reports, venezuelan chef Saverio Stassi is a leader among the culinary new guard. His treatment of local ingredients is virtuosic. He confits guinea hen in cocoa butter and tops breadfruit tostones with local yellowfin and Cambita avocado; and over two days, his team bathes the succulent goat from the northwest—where they famously graze on wild oregano, self-infusing their meat—in Seville orange juice before roasting it in a barbacoa pit.

    Calle Max Henríquez Ureña 14+1 809 547 3592.

    Chef Erik Malmsten has cooked at his parents’ cabaret in Gothenburg, Sweden, at Aquavit in Upcoming York, and at Bocuse d’Or competitions around the world. But to take his career to the next level, he returned to his mother’s homeland to open a Nordic-Japanese restaurant.

    Sources indicate that “You’ll see, it’s really good,” Bur told us. The meal starts with “lobster chicharrón,” with a reduced crustacean bisque, fried into airy orange sheets of bubbly crackling and served with tōgarashi Kewpie. Then, a parade of sashimi, like king fish, served with brown butter soy emulsion, ikura, and lemon zest. It ends with Dominican chocolates, molded, painted, and plated to look like koi fish on a synchronized swim.

    Calle Caonabo 35+1 809 584 9481.

    If, like me, you come from a pizza region, you might not be inclined to use one of your Santo Domingo meal slots on a pie. But I urge you: Make time for Casa Gazcue. Spanish Dominican chef Francis Pena’s 48-hour-fermented crust comes blistered and sometimes covered in honeyed sesame seeds. Iterations are variously laden with spicy Dominican oxtail, chimi sandwich sauce, pistachio, and jamón ibérico, but you don’t have to choose: For groups, he serves a rosca (a round with an open middle) of six sections arranged like floral pizza petals.

    Calle Pablo Casals+1 809 562 6060.

    Industry observers note that in 1954, the Bonarelli family opened the legendary Italian restaurant Vesuvio. For decades, it was the place—the only place—to go out for a formal sit-down meal around here. Vesuvio closed over 20 years ago, but the founder’s grandson, Giancarlo Bonarelli, now runs Bottega Fratelli in a sleek modern building in Naco (Piantini’s equally upscale neighbor).

    Sources indicate that you’ll notice a great variety of beet dishes in the Dominican Republic. Farmers harvest them year-round in the cool, pine-forested Costanza Valley. Try them here, roasted and served with blue cheese, chèvre, candied nuts, and honey. Also try a carpaccio of king mackerel, caught off the eastern coast, or any of the risottos, an emblem of the family’s enduring Italian culinary influence.

    Calle del Seminario #57+1 809 565 1621.

    Hideyoshi Tateyama’s parents opened Samurai in 1990. The restaurant joined Vesuvio, along with one or two others in that era’s small restaurant scene. It still stands out today among the many dozens.

    Be sure to order the guatapaná con coco. A tried-and-true combo of shrimp and coconut imbued with native guatapaná leaf, tobiko, sesame seed, and scallion—it’s been on the menu for two decades. Also, don’t miss the chance to sample a sashimi of the meter-long “calamar diamante” from the Samaná region. It’s simply brightened with lemon zest. Meals are capped with a green tea amaro. Once a month, Tateyama personally runs a chef’s-choice omakase service.

    Avenida Independencia 312+1 809 682 1433.

    On the day we visited Villar Hermanos, lines formed around the block for each of two buffets. Women balanced towers of takeout containers tightly wrapped in plastic. It was the World Cup Final, and people were rushing to get some of the city’s best comfort food to their coffee tables. “This is the place to come for all the Dominican classics,” Bur told us.

    Sources indicate that we found a large table under the sprawling canopy of a banyan tree and ordered mofongo. It was moist, punctuated with crisp chicharrón crackling. The sancocho, the classic Domincan stew thick with potato and yuca starch, assumed extra body when alternating spoonfuls of broth and rice. While I didn’t have my coveted mangú and tres golpes (salami, queso frito, and eggs), I would trade my house and car to live next door and eat breakfast there every morning under the filtered sun.

    Avenida San Vicente de Paúl, Santo Domingo Este 11504+1 809 244 8906.

    In a recent development, on Avenida San Vicente de Paúl in East Santo Domingo, scooters zip down the busy street all through the night, many popping over a curb into the Plaza Del Chimi. The “plaza” is a stretch of  10 to 15 “chimi” sandwich stalls outfitted with griddles and prep stations heaped with roasted pork shoulders. Dealers rapidly slice the meat, lay it on the griddle, flip it onto a squishy pan de agua roll, and top it with cabbage, tomato, and tangy pink sauce before sliding it into your mitts. The stalls are open till 6 a.m. When they run out of beer, a man runs bottles from a cooler at his house and serves them in paper bags.

    Avenida Independencia KM 8+1 809 532 2580.

    Across from a shopping mall on Avenida Indepencia, about a dozen cars cram into five parking spaces for the lunch or late-night staple pica pollo. Behind a crowded serving station, a woman slides eight pounds of chicken into a hotel pan, and the picking begins. Six sets of tongs compete for room, like bird beaks, snapping the chicken into styrofoam containers before barely holding them shut with strained rubber bands. Another eight pounds comes out less than two minutes later.

    In a recent development, pica pollo is one of the lasting influences of Chinese immigrants in Santo Domingo. Usually cooks marinate it in bitter orange, garlic, and oregano before coating it in flour and spice (in this case we detected Chinese five-spice) and deep-frying it to golden brown.

    Avenida Cayetano Germosén+1 809 286 2141.

    It has been revealed that at Parque Mirador Sur, teens and whole families perch along concrete walls and hilltops eating fried yuca and succulent mojo-dipped chicharrón with long toothpicks. It comes from the crowded, steel-barred serving window across the street: Chicharrones Light de la Cayetano.

    Sources indicate that among all the chicharrón we ate in the city (there was a lot), theirs stood out. There’s a small covered seating area where you can order beer to share. Bachata plays loud over a hanging speaker. Women take turns kicking off their heels to do the four-step shimmy with their jevos (boyfriends).

    Calle Ciriaco Ramirez 70+1 809 689 5544.

    The Colmado, Bur indicates, “is essential to Dominican life. Everything happens there.” For 70 years, Colmado La Venganza has anchored a prominent corner in the Don Bosco neighborhood. It’s hosted thousands of late-night domino games and sports viewing parties. We were there during the World Cup.

    Recent findings suggest that at the entrance, a man with a crisp-edged haircut, major sunglasses, and a pressed floral shirt parked his shoe on a milk crate while a boy polished it with a rag. Inside, groups spanning all ages gathered at high-tops and around the bar. Folks shared triple-stacked ham, pickle, and cheese sandwiches, pressed, cubed, and spiked with toothpicks: the “sándwich especial.” Leaving the bar, chef Raniel Cruz (part of our party) texted his mom in Montreal. She responded: “Wait, you’re at Venganza? I used to drink there.”.

    Calle Luperón 52+1 849 460 5600.

    Sources indicate that one couldn’t understand the Dominican Republic’s vast culinary splendor in a lifetime, but if you had just one night to try, you’d want to dine at Casarré. Every Tuesday, the team takes excursions. We accompanied them to meet the countryside cooks, who wrap guáyiga root masa in leaves from the almond trees on Najayo beach and bake it in coal-covered pots. We visited a produce market, where vendors passed fruit samples, like little red “frutas milagrosas” that, when chewed beforehand, make bitter limes taste like sweet limeade.

    At night, in a candlelit, contemplative room in the Zona Colonial, Bur and his team showcase their findings in a series of sublime, thoughtful dishes. On our visit, they presented djon-djon mushrooms from the Haitian borderlands in a sweet, guáyiga-thickened foam and in the broth of a citrusy okra and fish soup. Chef Isabella Sánchez explained: “The broth is murky, like the current state of the Río Ozama. It represents the negative aspects of our water—contamination and conflict—and the beautiful: the fish, the beaches, and our grandmother’s tea.”.

    Avenida Lope de Vega 44+1 809 816 7200.

    Smoke from an open Uruguayan-style parrilla floats in the soft light over two stories. Our waiter said, “We want this to feel like a Sunday asado.” Indeed, the smoke, the char, and the Malbec are there. This asado, though, also has Negronis smoked tableside and poured from a glass goose. As we awaited a perfect aged rib eye, we enjoyed paper-thin beef carpaccio with foie, and a paella-esque rice with soft leeks, cilantro, and pork trotters.

    Recommendations on where to dine, shop, and stay, wherever you’re headed next.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Five U.S. chefs making waves in their communities with compelling menus.

    If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

    Sources indicate that each of the chefs featured in our upcoming national Chef of the Year category made news in a major way. But their most recent projects are just one part of their story.

    In a recent development, this year we celebrate five chefs who are making an impact both on the city where they cook and on the larger culinary conversation. — Missy Frederick, editorial director.

    Learn more about this year’s Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, and how editors selected them, here.

    Industry observers note that san Francisco diners became acquainted with powerhouse couple Laura and Sayat Ozyilmaz through their championing of Eastern Mediterranean cuisine at Dalida. That restaurant told the story of Sayat’s upbringing and influences in Istanbul, Turkey, opening in 2023 inside a historic building within the lush environs of the Presidio and earning critical acclaim for the duo’s cooking.

    In a recent development, in the years since, diners came to know Laura outside of Dalida. She completed an impressive run on Top Chef in 2024, where viewers saw her deftly plant one foot in Mediterranean food and another in Mexican cuisine, showcasing her skill in both fields throughout the season. With the 2026 debut of the Ozyilmazes’ restaurant Maria Isabel, the food feels like an even fuller expression of Laura’s heritage and personal history.

    Named after Laura’s sister (Maria) and her mother (Isabel), the restaurant steeps in Mexican matriarchy, highlighting female winemakers, ceramics made by Mexican producers, and indigenous Mexican ingredients. The menu channels Laura’s upbringing in Guerrero and her family’s Sinaloan roots, as recounted through mariscos and maiz, moles and salsa macha. The ceviche Acapulqueño reimagines the Fanta- and ketchup-laden version instead with marigold flowers and preserved Seville oranges dressing tender shrimp and raw scallop; petals — and three fried shrimp heads — adorn the top. Duck enmoladas showcase the power of mole negro against a seasonal mole (sometimes a peach manchamanteles, other times a rhubarb rendition, but always compelling). Chochoyotes, a lesser-seen dish in San Francisco, demonstrates the restaurant’s ability to apply masa in different ways — in this case, dumplings — while harnessing the earthy flavor of huitlacoche. Maria Isabel is both a conduit for diners to connect with complex Mexican flavors and a view into Laura’s vision of the Mexico of her past and future. — Dianne de Guzman, editor, Eater SF.

    Chef Carlos Delgado’s meteoric rise in D.C. began in 2022 with the opening of tiny tasting room Causa, located in Shaw, where he sends diners on a seafaring voyage along the Peruvian coastline and into the Andes he grew up around, and its accompanying upstairs pisco destination Bar Amazonia. His meticulous sourcing and culinary skills quickly drew critical acclaim.

    2026 might be the Lima native’s biggest year yet: His breakout project, Maru San, commanded instant Capitol Hill buzz upon opening in February for its orchestra of Nikkei-style hand rolls, sashimi, and other polished seafood plates he and fellow José Andrés alum Simon Lam pass across a 25-seat black marble counter under a major pink octopus mural, as his favorite tropical house blasts in the background. A rare few get to sample the restaurant’s elaborate tasting menu full of ingredients like high-end uni and dry-aged fish; reservations for the 15-course feast are nearly impossible to get.

    Sources indicate that the ambitious chef, at 36, isn’t afraid to stretch in many directions. He linked up with the Eaternity Group last year to give the Mediterranean-themed La Vie a needed menu makeover at D.C.’s Wharf development — meanwhile, at least one more Maru San is in the works elsewhere in D.C.

    Sounds a lot like his former mentor: Before Causa, Delgado honed his craft under José Andrés as the longtime executive chef at Penn Quarter’s Peruvian mainstay China Chilcano. They still text frequently. — Tierney Plumb, Northeast editor.

    While Amir Hajimaleki has had American-leaning restaurants in Austin for well over a decade, he hasn’t had the opportunity to fully express himself as an Iranian-born, Texas-raised chef. That is until he opened Roya, his most personal restaurant and a project that has been in the works for more than eight years. Here, he manifests the depth and diversity of Persian cuisine, a bold feat for the middle of Texas. The space, designed with his brother Ali Hajimaleki, feels transportive with intricate tile mosaics, burnished gold and dark blue hues, and delicate chandeliers.

    There’s been an electric energy to the Philly restaurant scene in recent years. The city, ever the underdog, has long punched above its weight; now, the rest of the world has come to the same realization. Amid this buzz, two newer restaurants have outrun the shadow cast by the city’s substantial names: Cambodian noodle house Mawn, which opened in 2023, and Southeast Asian oyster house and raw bar Sao, which opened last September.

    Sources indicate that at their helm is the slick, stylish Phila Lorn. The restaurants he runs with his wife Rachel feel singular, blending the influences of his Philadelphia upbringing with his Cambodian background in food that feels playfully free and emboldened by a lack of boundaries between cuisines. At Mawn, funnel cake meets coconut macaroons, and vinegar peppers enhance scallops in red curry. At Sao, the crispy rice in the nam khao salad, which features Italian sausage, feels analogous to arancini. Tuna carpaccio is served with crispy shallots and jalapeños, then cured in lime until it picks up the aura of the bowls of beef pho on Washington Avenue.

    Hear Lorn talk, with his South Philly-bred bravado (and requisite uses of “jawn”) giving him a commanding presence, and it’s clear that the city’s culinary community is listening, rallying, and getting stoked to eat more of his food. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

    Tucson-based chef Aaron Lopez had a vision that started in his small California city of El Centro, an agricultural city near the U.S.-Mexico border. There, he hatched a initiative to create a menu imbued with the techniques and flavors of the Sonoran Desert that spans northern Mexico, Arizona, and southeastern California. Trained at top kitchens in Los Angeles and beyond, Lopez researched by going deep into the desert, armed with a camera and his wits. A year later, he and his wife June Chee carried the project to Tucson, a larger venue still deeply embedded in the desert, but with a upcoming audience.

    Inside the high-ceilinged, brick-walled downtown space, Ursa serves as a hushed gallery for Lopez and his team’s $150 tasting menu, which merges Indigenous cooking techniques with foraged and locally farmed ingredients. Barrel fruit (a yellow cactus) topped with the tang of pickled chiltepin leaves is the first bite, a luscious treat you may never see on a European plate. Quail breast arrives on a metal skewer dressed in pickled yucca, hovering over a jujube broth like a quiet offering. Goat roasted in agave, pit barbacoa-style, is unveiled tableside and served over softened tepary beans.

    At every turn, with no extraneous adornments, the kitchen lets the produce and meats boast their innate nature. Lopez eschews conventional comfort, reimagining a meal of cactus, corn, sunflower tea, and beans as true luxuries, and the results are evocative and powerful. His message — seeing the value and beauty of this landscape, its people, its ingredients, and the way it all comes through the cooking — is the luscious pith of the cactus you find beneath the surface of the American Southwest. — Matthew Kang, correspondent.

    #59. Thanksgiving Leftovers Nachos

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (673 w)
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tasteofhome

    Thanksgiving Leftovers Nachos

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (673 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • These Thanksgiving leftovers nachos are piled high with turkey, Brie, stuffing and squash before being finished with gravy, cranberry sauce and French-fried onions.
    • Scouring the internet in search of ideas for what to make with your Thanksgiving leftovers?
    • If you spend any time on social media, this likely isn’t the first recipe for Thanksgiving leftovers nachos you’ve seen.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recipe by Lauren Habermehl, Pewaukee, Wisconsin.

    Tested by Taste of Home Test Kitchen.

    Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

    These Thanksgiving leftovers nachos are piled high with turkey, Brie, stuffing and squash before being finished with gravy, cranberry sauce and French-fried onions.

    Scouring the internet in search of ideas for what to make with your Thanksgiving leftovers? While turkey potpie and the infamous Moist Maker sandwich from Friends are always solid choices, I implore you to try Thanksgiving leftovers nachos this year.

    If you spend any time on social media, this likely isn’t the first recipe for Thanksgiving leftovers nachos you’ve seen. But I promise it’s the best. Our rendition begins with a pile of corn tortilla chips layered with leftover roast turkey and a secret ingredient: creamy Brie cheese. Next, leftover stuffing and roasted butternut squash (or candied sweet potatoes) are piled on before the nachos bake to crispy, cheesy perfection. Once finished with turkey gravy, cranberry sauce, and a shower of French-fried onions and herbs, this mountain of Thanksgiving glory is a feast for the senses.

    It has been revealed that serve these Thanksgiving leftovers nachos after a day of Black Friday shopping, or invite friends over for the big game on Sunday afternoon. Absolutely no one will complain about a second Thanksgiving in nacho form.

    Recent findings suggest that preheat the oven to 400°F. In separate microwave-safe containers, reheat the leftover turkey, squash and stuffing until they’re warmed through.

    On a 15x10x1-inch baking sheet, arrange a layer of tortilla chips. Top them with half of the cubed Brie and shredded turkey. Repeat with another layer of chips, Brie and turkey.

    Crumble the stuffing over the nachos, then top with the roasted butternut squash. Bake the nachos until the cheese is melted and the toppings are heated through, about 10 to 12 minutes.

    While the nachos bake, warm the gravy in the microwave or on the stovetop until it’s heated through.

    Drizzle the nachos with warm gravy, dollop small spoonfuls of cranberry sauce on top, and sprinkle them with fresh herbs and French-fried onions. Serve the nachos with additional cranberry sauce and gravy on the side.

    ELLIE CROWLEY FOR TASTE OF HOME.

    It has been revealed that thanksgiving leftovers nachos are best enjoyed immediately. Since they’re piled high with toppings and warm gravy, the chips will get soggy when stored. For best results, make only what you intend to eat in one sitting.

    ELLIE CROWLEY FOR TASTE OF HOME.

    It has been revealed that tortilla chips will almost always soften a bit when they’re baked as nachos. You can slow the process, however, by selecting thicker, sturdier chips that hold up to the weight and moisture of the nacho toppings. Here are our favorite tortilla chip brands that will stand up to the task.

    In a recent development, you may also wish to bake the chips briefly for three to five minutes before piling on the toppings. Warming the chips first drives out any residual moisture and boosts their moisture resistance.

    Not really. While the ingredient amounts in the recipe offer the best ratios of flavor and texture (in our opinion), you can wing it and use whatever leftovers you have on hand. These nachos will taste sublime no matter what.

    In a recent development, these nachos are pretty spectacular—so much so that you may find yourself craving them long after Thanksgiving has passed and there are no leftovers in sight. While you would have to prepare a miniature holiday dinner to make these nachos, you can simplify things by using a box of stovetop stuffing, precut butternut squash (for easy roasting), canned cranberries and rotisserie chicken instead of turkey.

    This an all-in-one meal that doesn’t need any sides. That noted, there’s always room for a fun cocktail. Cranberry margaritas are another great Mexican-Thanksgiving mashup. Looking for dessert? If you have leftover pumpkin puree, make pumpkin bars for a quick and easy treat. Of course, you may also have leftover Thanksgiving desserts to continue chipping away at, too.

    #57. Drinking Tea Too Hot Could Be Bad For Your Health—Here's What To Know

    📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (430 w)
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Delish

    Drinking Tea Too Hot Could Be Bad For Your Health—Here's What To Know

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (430 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Delish

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • There’s more than one reason to brew your tea at the right temperature—and one of those reasons could affect your health.
    • Recent findings suggest that according to the study, drinking extremely hot tea was associated with a 16 percent higher relative risk of vascular disease.
    • Chelsea Azarcon is similarly cautious about drawing conclusions from the findings.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    There’s more than one reason to brew your tea at the right temperature—and one of those reasons could affect your health. A recently published study followed nearly half a million adults in China for almost a decade, examining how tea-drinking habits related to their health. Researchers found that regular tea drinkers had a lower risk of vascular disease than non-tea drinkers. But one major caveat emerged: Those who reported drinking their tea “burning hot” had a higher risk of vascular disease.

    Recent findings suggest that according to the study, drinking extremely hot tea was associated with a 16 percent higher relative risk of vascular disease. But don't give up your daily tea habit quite yet. “This study is interesting, but we don't have a proven biological explanation yet,” Dr. Niraj Patel, medical director at Clara, states.

    Dr. Chelsea Azarcon is similarly cautious about drawing conclusions from the findings.

    Recent findings suggest that “It doesn’t look like this study has any proposed mechanism for why burning hot tea would increase the risk of cardiovascular disease,” she explains. “However, we do know that drinks that are too hot can increase the risk of esophageal cancer by creating local injury and damage.”.

    That concern is supported by the World Health Organization's cancer research agency, which has classified drinking beverages hotter than 149°F as probably carcinogenic to humans. The classification specifically concerns esophageal cancer, though, so it doesn't explain the connection to vascular disease identified in the upcoming study.

    In a recent development, the study didn’t identify a specific temperature at which drinking tea becomes detrimental to vascular health. And although researchers found an association between drinking extremely hot tea and vascular disease, that doesn't necessarily mean one causes the other.

    ScienceDaily also notes that drinking tea at extremely high temperatures may diminish some of the health benefits associated with regular tea consumption.

    Azarcon believes further research into tea's chemical makeup and how it may change at different temperatures could help answer some of the remaining questions.

    Sources indicate that "I'd say enjoy your tea, but don't feel like you need to drink it while it's scalding hot,” Patel suggests. “There's a difference between brewing tea with hot water and actually drinking it at that temperature. Letting it cool for a few minutes is an easy precaution and doesn't require giving up something you enjoy.".

    So while I don’t plan on giving up my tea habit any time soon, I am definitely making extra sure that I let my cup sit out a little longer before taking that first sip.
