    #54. The Best Nontoxic Cookware Trusted by BA Editors (2026)

    📅 02 Dec 2024 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2950 w)
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bonappetit

    The Best Nontoxic Cookware Trusted by BA Editors (2026)

    📅 02 Dec 2024 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2950 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

    ⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that if you’ve shopped for nonstick pots and pans in the past decade, you’ve had the term nontoxic cookware thrown at you with increasing velocity.
    • The answer begins with a class of synthetic chemicals known as PFAS, short for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances.
    • According to recent reports, whether you’ve never heard of PFAS or you’re already familiar with their nearly 100-year-old history, you’re in the right place if you want to avoid them.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that if you’ve shopped for nonstick pots and pans in the past decade, you’ve had the term nontoxic cookware thrown at you with increasing velocity. As you've thought about getting fresh pans you may have even searched for the best nontoxic cookware without being totally sure what “toxins” they supposedly do not have in them. So what exactly makes cookware “toxic,” and why do these “safe” or “healthy” pans claim to be better?

    The answer begins with a class of synthetic chemicals known as PFAS, short for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances. These chemicals, which repel liquids, have been used in everything from waterproof jackets to nonstick cookware coatings, and after decades of use, the health concerns raised by scientists started to break through to the public more broadly in more recent years.

    According to recent reports, whether you’ve never heard of PFAS or you’re already familiar with their nearly 100-year-old history, you’re in the right place if you want to avoid them. We’ve tested dozens of nonstick and “nontoxic” pans to find the best options to help you keep PFAS out of your cookware. Read on for the lowdown on all things nontoxic cookware.

    When companies label their cookware “nontoxic,” it’s a marketing move as much as anything, designed to position it as a safer alternative to traditional nonstick, which is typically coated in a chemical called polytetrafluoroethylene, or PTFE. And to understand why people began to colloquially refer to old nonstick pans as “toxic,” we need a little history of PTFE.

    Discovered accidentally in 1938 and trademarked by chemical tech giant DuPont as Teflon in the early 1960s, PTFE was an earthquake in the home cookware market during the second half of the 20th century because it provided consumers with a completely nonstick, no-oil-needed cooking surface. By the turn of the century, Teflon had become ubiquitous, finding its way into a staggering number of American kitchens in the form of PTFE-coated skillets, muffin tins, baking dishes, and more.

    PTFE, though, is just one of thousands of a class of chemicals in PFAS family mentioned earlier. Around 1951, DuPont started using another PFAS called PFOA (short for perfluorooctanoic acid) in its Teflon manufacturing process. Over time, it became clear that PFOA could enter the human body by way of gaseous fumes or chipped coatings and have detrimental effects on human health and the environment, including increased risk of certain cancers, birth defects, ulcerative colitis, and thyroid disease. Under mounting pressure from public health and environmental advocacy groups, manufacturers phased out PFOA by 2013.

    These days traditional nonstick cookware is made using PFOA-free PTFE (which is also typically free of PFOS, another harmful PFAS). You’ll see it marketed under names like T-fal, Dura-Slide, or hard-anodized aluminum. While PTFE itself is considered less harmful than other PFAS, there is still a broader concern. Thousands of PFAS compounds remain unregulated, and there is ongoing research into the class of chemicals as a whole. A label that states “PFOA- and PFOS-free” does not necessarily mean the product is free of all potentially risky chemicals in the PFAS family.

    While not necessarily the first recorded use of the term, the idea of “nontoxic” cookware was largely introduced to consumers when GreenPan released the first PFAS-free ceramic nonstick frying pans in 2007. Since then, “nontoxic cookware” has come to mean “PFAS-free nonstick cookware.” While there’s nothing inherently incorrect about this characterization, it’s key to recognize the degree to which it has become a marketing buzzword.

    While “nontoxic cookware” typically refers to ceramic nonstick, which is made from silica using a method called the sol-gel process, any cookware that’s made without the use of harmful chemicals like PFAS can be considered “nontoxic.” That includes some tried-and-true options you probably already know and love: stainless steel, cast iron, and carbon steel.

    Industry observers note that ceramic nonstick comes closest to mimicking the ease of traditional Teflon, but like any coating, it will degrade over time and can chip (more on that below). That’s why we recommend getting comfortable with uncoated stainless, cast iron, and carbon steel. With the right technique, your food won’t stick to them either, and they’ll last a lot longer.

    Valencia Pro Ceramic Nonstick 12" Frypan.

    Available sizes: 8", 10", 12"Induction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: Yes, but hand-washing recommendedMetal-utensil-safe: Theoretically, but wood or silicone recommendedOven-safe: Up to 600ºFWarranty: 1 year.

    About ceramic nonstick: I have to be honest here, I've personally sworn off coated nonstick pans for good, because no matter which one you buy, it will only last you a few years tops before the coating starts to degrade and you need to replace it. That noted, I understand why people gravitate towards them—and if you're dead-set on buying one, ceramic nonstick is the way to go. These pans are typically made of stainless steel or aluminum and lined with a silica-based coating that makes them nice and slick—for a few years, at least. The exact makeup of that coating varies brand to brand, which is why we’ve spent years testing lots of ceramic nonstick pans to find the ones that best deliver on their nonstick promise.

    According to recent reports, our top pick: GreenPan’s ceramic nonstick pans were the first to hit the market in 2007, and the brand’s products have consistently come out on top in our best nonstick pan testing. Its Valencia Pro line is our favorite for a few reasons: It’s hefty enough to feel durable while remaining lightweight enough to be easily maneuverable. It’s also affordable enough that you won’t have to break the bank when you inevitably need to replace it in a few years, and more scratch-resistant than some earlier GreenPan iterations we've tried. Oh, and it's induction compatible too.

    A budget option: If you don’t cook on an induction stovetop and are looking for a cheaper option, you can go with GreenPan’s Paris Pro line, which performed similarly to the Valencia in our testing.

    Read more about our favorite nonstick pans.

    Deeper Carbon Nonstick Frying Pan & Glass Lid.

    Available sizes: 8", 10", 12"Induction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: NoMetal-utensil-safe: YesOven-safe: Up to 1,100ºFWarranty: Lifetime.

    About carbon nonstick (or nitrided carbon steel): At the outset, these pans act like traditional nonstick but can hold up to high heat, metal utensils, and years of use because they aren’t coated. Instead the carbon steel is nitrided, a process that infuses nitrogen into the metal to make it tougher, slicker, and both corrosion- and rust-resistant.

    Industry observers note that our top pick: When we first got a hold of Misen’s Carbon Nonstick pan it seemed like the holy grail for anyone trying to quit Teflon without giving up easy-release eggs. Unlike traditional carbon steel pans, Misen’s version has an aluminum core that heats rapidly and evenly, and its surface repels oil straight out of the box. In testing, fried eggs, chicken thighs, and sautéed onions all slid right off with minimal oil (food director Chris Morocco said it was “practically allergic” to eggs). The pan is lightweight and durable and will develop a terrific nonstick seasoning. However, as our lead cookware tester Wilder Davies continued cooking with the Misen, he noticed the initial corn oil seasoning layer started to wear, and the miraculous oil repelling characteristics decreased. Once that happened we assigned four more people, myself included, to work with these pans and we all noticed a reduction in the nonstickiness as time went on. However, the nonstick curve on these has proven to be more U-shaped, as we've continued to cook on and season them, food release started to become easier again.

    Read our full review of the Misen Carbon Nonstick Pan.

    D3 Stainless 3-ply Bonded Cookware; Saute Pan with lid; 3 quart.

    D3 Stainless Steel 14-in Skillet with Lid.

    Available sizes: 10", 12", 14"Induction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: NoMetal-utensil-safe: YesOven-safe: Up to 600°FWarranty: Limited lifetime.

    According to recent reports, about stainless steel: Stainless-steel cookware is a staple in home and professional kitchens because of its versatility, durability, and low maintenance needs. Use it on the stovetop, in the oven, or with metal tools—unlike shorter-lived ceramic pans, a stainless-steel skillet can serve you well for a lifetime. And here’s the thing: With the proper technique, stainless steel can release almost as easily as ceramic nonstick. The key in guaranteeing your food slides right off instead of becoming a stuck-on mess is using sufficient fat and heat. Make sure to wait until your oil is shimmering before adding whatever you’re cooking, give it enough time in the pan to let the maillard reaction do its thing, and you should have no concerns with stickage.

    It has been revealed that our top pick: We’ve tested many types of stainless-steel cookware throughout the years here at BA, and one brand has repeatedly stood out time and time again for its consistently well-made, durable, high-performing products. That brand is All-Clad.

    In our testing of stainless-steel frying pans and sauté pans, product testers and Test Kitchen editors alike lauded All-Clad’s D3 Everyday line as the best mix of value and performance for home cooks. The “3” refers to these pans’ 3-ply construction, which features an aluminum core sandwiched between two layers of stainless-steel cladding. That aluminum allows the pan to conduct heat swiftly and evenly, and it makes the pan more lightweight than solid stainless-steel cookware. In our testing, we found that those promises held true, and that the D3 pans were easy to clean (just hand-wash with a little soapy water, plus some Bar Keepers Friend if you need a hand getting any remaining bits off) and have continued to perform well over the many years we’ve been using them.

    According to recent reports, about cast iron: If you’re willing to put just a bit of work into caring for your cookware, a cast-iron skillet will easily fill the nonstick pan-size hole in your kitchen. Cast-iron cookware will never quite reach the level of nonstick that a Teflon-coated piece offers, but in our testing, we’ve found that a properly seasoned cast-iron pan is on par with ceramic nonstick—plus it only gets more slick over time as you continue to use it.

    Sources indicate that our top pick: After testing more than 20 cast-iron skillets over several years, our current top pick is the Lancaster No. 8 because it’s lightweight, it has a smooth pre-seasoned surface that’s nice and slick right out of the box, and it provides even heat distribution. The one downside is that it’s quite pricey compared to something like Lodge’s iconic cast iron, which we recommend as a great budget alternative. The Lodge is probably the pan most people think of when they hear “cast-iron skillet,” and at around $20, depending on where and when you buy it, it’s one of the best values in the cookware world—particularly because you can keep it forever rather than replacing it every few years. In our testing, it performed just as well as many more expensive pans.

    Read more about our favorite cast-iron pans.

    It has been revealed that about enameled cast iron: You may have also heard of enameled cast iron, which is frequently seen in products like our favorite Le Creuset and Staub Dutch ovens. Many people expect enameled cast-iron pots and pans to be nonstick because the ones with light-colored interiors sort of resemble the kinds of ceramic nonstick coatings we wrote about above, but in reality, that’s not the case. That doesn’t mean you can’t cook food in these things without it sticking, but you’ll need to use sufficient fat and heat to make that happen, as you do with a stainless-steel pan. The benefit of enameled cast iron is that it provides superior heat retention and distribution, and protects the cast-iron core from rust and acidity. It's become one of my favorite types of cookware to use at home over the past few years.

    Recent findings suggest that our top pick: The Staub Round Cocotte is my personal top pick when it comes to Dutch ovens, and tied with the Le Creuset in our official product testing. I prefer the Staub’s dark textured enamel interior, which is less prone to showing discoloration. In addition to the round cocotte, I also own the braiser and a deep skillet, both of which I find myself pulling out constantly.

    Read more about our favorite Dutch ovens.

    Available sizes: 8", 10.25", 11", 12.5"Induction compatible: YesDishwasher-safe: NoMetal-utensil-safe: YesOven-safe: Up to 500ºFWarranty: Limited lifetime.

    About carbon steel: Carbon steel is sort of the Goldilocks cookware because it affords you the nonstick qualities and lightweight feel of a coated nonstick pan and the durability of a cast-iron or stainless-steel skillet. The one caveat is that in order to achieve those nonstick qualities, you’ll need to spend some time properly seasoning your latest pan, just as you would with cast iron. But with a bit of work at the outset and occasional maintenance, you’ll be rewarded with an heirloom-worthy piece of cookware that has a well-earned nonstick patina.

    Our top pick: De Buyer is one of those famed, old European cookware brands that lots of American home cooks may not be that familiar with. Its “blue” frying pan comes pre-seasoned and will just get better and better as the seasoning improves. As senior writer Wilder Davies notes, you can take specific steps to season it—use a thin layer of oil (as thin as you can possibly get) and put it in a hot oven for an hour—but you can also just keep cooking with it and that seasoning will develop on its own. Another nice feature of this pan in particular, and one that has nothing to do with its seasoning, is its welded-on handle. That means there are no rivets to clean around when you’re done.

    Read more about our favorite carbon steel pans.

    What types of kitchen gear is PTFE found in?

    Sources indicate that A skillet may be the first thing you think of when you think of nonstick cookware, but PTFE coatings show up in a host of other items in the kitchen and beyond. On top of skillets, pots, saucepans, and Dutch ovens, you'll also find PTFE in rice cookers, waffle irons, baking sheets, and grill baskets.

    What is ceramic nonstick cookware?

    In a recent development, you may recognize ceramic nonstick as the material of choice of many of the aesthetically-pleasing, Instagram-viral cookware companies that started popping up in the late 2010s (I’m looking at you, Our Place and Caraway). Ceramic nonstick pans are made without any PFAS. Instead, a gel made from silica is applied and then dried onto the cookware’s metal body to create a nonstick surface.

    It has been revealed that sounds great, right? Well, there are a few caveats, the main one being that ceramic nonstick coatings are not built to last. That means you’ll want to be sure to avoid using metal utensils when cooking with them, opting instead for wood or silicone. You’ll also want to avoid exposing them to extremely high temperatures: Even though ceramic cookware is technically more heat tolerant than cookware made with PTFE, high heat will wear down the pan’s ceramic coating. Many manufacturers claim their pans are oven-safe up to certain (often high) temperatures, but we’d recommend using one of our other recommendations above for any stove-to-oven cooking, as those trips to the oven will only further degrade that ceramic coating over time. Similarly, despite any of being dishwasher-safe, hand-washing your pans will prolong their lifespans.

    What is the best nontoxic cookware?

    In a recent development, even if you treat your ceramic nonstick cookware with the utmost care and attention, you still shouldn’t expect it to last you more than one to three years before it starts to lose its nonstick properties. That’s why the best nontoxic nonstick cookware is not necessarily a coated piece of PFOA- or PFAS-free gear—in fact, we’d argue the best nontoxic “nonstick” pans money can buy are made of cast iron, or carbon steel. While these materials are not actually manufactured or marketed as nonstick, each has nonstick properties that can be achieved with proper use and care. .

    It has been revealed that the bottom line here is that no one needs a coated pan in their life. There is no recipe on this website (or in this world) that requires you to use one, and we tend to think you’re better off investing some time in learning to cook with a more durable type of cookware than spending you money on a full nonstick cookware set. That mentioned, we’re recommending a range of cookware options here for those who are looking for alternatives to traditional PTFE-base nonstick, including a ceramic option for people who aren’t quite ready to kiss coated nonstick goodbye.

    #51. Industry News: The 2026 Restaurant Dishes of the Year

    📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1303 w)
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Eater

    Industry News: The 2026 Restaurant Dishes of the Year

    📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1303 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eater

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • From an earthy curry crab callaloo dip to a plate of pickled walleye cheeks, these were editors’ most memorable bites.
    • Our editors ate in hundreds of restaurants across the country this year, but certain dishes left a lasting impression, and we’re recognizing them in this new national Eater Award category.
    • It has been revealed that from a textbook execution of the ubiquitous 2026 entree — roast chicken — to an innovative fish preparation offering Midwestern diners a upcoming way to experience a familiar ingredient, these dishes are all worth celebrating.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    From an earthy curry crab callaloo dip to a plate of pickled walleye cheeks, these were editors’ most memorable bites.

    Our editors ate in hundreds of restaurants across the country this year, but certain dishes left a lasting impression, and we’re recognizing them in this new national Eater Award category.

    It has been revealed that from a textbook execution of the ubiquitous 2026 entree — roast chicken — to an innovative fish preparation offering Midwestern diners a upcoming way to experience a familiar ingredient, these dishes are all worth celebrating. — Missy Frederick, editorial director.

    Learn more about this year’s Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, and how editors selected them, here.

    Recent findings suggest that when experiencing a five-course tasting menu ($145), I wasn’t expecting toast to be a main attraction. But even with competition from luxurious courses featuring everything from a complex Hokkaido scallop to an assertive charred rib-eye with peaches, All Well’s puffed grain toast left a lasting impression.

    After three years at two-Michelin-starred Oriole, Larry Feldmeier partnered with Noah Sandoval, fellow Oriole alum and James Beard winner for Best Chef: Great Lakes, to open the ambitious West Loop restaurant All Well, which offers both a la carte bar options and the aforementioned tasting; the toast is only available as part of the latter experience.

    The dish arrives to the table amplified with nutty buckwheat butter sweetened with honey, the backdrop for a pasta stuffed with triple-cream Délice de Bourgogne and a cauldron of salty chicken brodo. You’ll dive into the pasta, of course, using the bread to sop up the rich beurre blanc. Like a performer waiting in the wings for their monologue, the puffed grain toast takes center stage. The toast effectively offsets the creaminess and saltiness of the rest of the dish, but can stand on its own even without the accompanying pasta. Its subtle sweetness almost acts as a mid-meal dessert, a distinctive break in a seamless dinner you don’t quite want to end. — Isaiah Reynolds, audience editor.

    The only thing about Oklahoma City that feels even vaguely reminiscent of the Caribbean is the sheet-pan-flat horizon. And yet inside a gaping industrial dining room downtown, there’s Dougla Kitchen, where diners sip fruity rum drinks out of plastic bags and acclaimed chef Andrew Black digs deep in his past to bring OKC locals a taste of his Indo-Jamaican upbringing. I fully admit this Midwestern-born, California-raised girl doesn’t encounter ruddy callaloo greens as often as she’d like (my hunch is neither do most Oklahomans). No matter. What Black manages to do with this deceiving pile of greenish-brown mush, dank with hand-picked crab and sparkling with curry spices, translates the soul of Caribbean home cooking in a single scoop. I didn’t know it was possible to be overwhelmed by a sense memory from a life that’s not your own, but this heady appetizer does that, served with a side of crisp taro chips and worth lingering over all afternoon with a couple of Red Stripes. — Lesley Suter, brand director.

    To understand California cuisine in 2026, look no further than Henrietta, a neighborhood bistro that has struck a just-right balance of precision and ingenuity while imbuing a feeling of nostalgia that begs locals and travelers alike to return. The restaurant’s intentions come across most clearly in its roast chicken, served as a just-salty-enough half chicken hunked into handheld pieces with deep, smoky char marks. The prize chicken pile gets tucked onto a plate alongside a scorched lemon half and a heaping, chicory-heavy Caesar panzanella blanketed under a layer of Parmesan that could be a snowcap on a stretch of the San Gabriel Mountains. With the chicken, Henrietta nods to forebears (namely San Francisco’s Zuni), while making the dish its own with a Baja-born Caesar salad that feels distinctly Los Angeles, dotted with torn fistfuls of bread from the neighboring local Clark Street Bakery. Of course, 2026 continues to be the year of the Great Chickening, where roast chicken has become many a restaurant’s calling card — and an easy way into the cultural cache. In Los Angeles alone, Sqirl (with its upcoming dinner menu) and Pasjoli have both put out progressive, near-intoxicating spins on the dish, but Henrietta’s has lodged itself into the collective imagination with its brazen simplicity. — Rebecca Roland, deputy editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest.

    The striking cantaloupe and verjus terrine at Nashville’s Junior offers a glimpse into the minds of chef Philip Krajeck and chef de cuisine Brian Mejia, the duo behind the high-technique kitchen. A “terrine” slice arrives with pieces of cantaloupe suspended in a clear gelatin made with verjus, the pressed juice of unripened grapes. One corner is covered in tiny, diced cubes of cantaloupe dressed in citrus-forward turmeric oil; another gets draped in chamomile-steeped cream. The mix of textures and flavors comes together in a dynamic symphony: the bright, acidic cubes of summer-ripened fruit against the calming mellowness of chamomile and gelatin layers that meld cantaloupe juice sweetness with crisp verjus.

    Sources indicate that the dessert’s structural elegance, which highlights a French variety of melon grown by a local farmer, may not immediately reveal its full complexity: Clear gelatin features a layer of clarified cantaloupe juice with encased melon slices, stacked between two layers of verjus gelatin. The melon gets compressed to intensify its flavors. Somehow, Junior managed to make Jell-O cool again — and dare I say, even sophisticated? — an example of Junior’s steady confidence that makes the restaurant an irresistible experience. — Dianne de Guzman, lead editor, Eater SF.

    In a recent development, though people outside the Midwest may not be familiar with freshwater whitefish walleye, there it’s a classic comfort food, a staple of Lenten fish fries, state fair booths, and Lake Erie fishermen’s freezer stashes. At Rosy, chef Vinnie Cimino leans on that familiarity to help convince his customers to experience a beloved ingredient in an entirely upcoming way. Pickled walleye cheeks ($17) have been a recurring staple — if a fleeting one — on Rosy’s Eastern European-leaning menu since the restaurant opened in February 2026. Kate’s Fish in Cleveland’s historic West Side Market provides walleye filets for sister restaurant Cordelia; when breaking down and fileting each fish, the fishmongers save the cheeks until they have a formidable stash. About every three weeks, Rosy can offer pickled walleye cheeks for around four days at a time. It’s a thoughtful move for sustainability, but also for succulence, as fish cheeks are a prized cut for their luscious texture.

    Cimino conceived the dish as a nod to Jewish fish-pickling practices (for me, the results also brought to mind a tender ceviche). Seasonal vegetables are pickled with lemon — an earlier version invoked German-style potato salad, spring brought asparagus, and, when I went in June, bell pepper, carrot, and dill were in the mix. They’re then combined with the cheeks, which get a separate hot-pickling treatment involving red wine vinegar, salt, sugar, bay leaf, peppercorns, and coriander. “People really gravitate toward it,” Cimino says. “We’ve built up a great trust with our diners.” While the dish won’t be replacing fried walleye at area fish fries anytime soon, Cimino feels proud that when at Rosy, diners have been more than willing to go along with him for the ride. — MF.

    Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

    It has been revealed that I'll give you Mr. Scrooge, the Founder of the Feast! Here are all the foods Charles Dickens wrote about in A Christmas Carol.

    Sources indicate that charles Dickens’s A Christmas Carol occupies a particularly notable place in my heart. My grandma gifted me her copy when I was in junior high, and I’ve returned to it nearly every Christmas since, each year finding something in the story that speaks to me in a new way.

    And although I’m generally suspicious of film adaptations of the books I love, there are two versions I treasure every bit as much as the original story. I fell in love with them as a child, probably around the same time. The first was The Muppet Christmas Carol, which combined two of my favorite things: the Muppets and jaunty show tunes. I watched it incessantly throughout the Christmas season, and the tradition has carried on with my own children, who now know every song and every word of dialogue.

    According to recent reports, the other was the 1984 adaptation starring George C. Scott. I love its surreal, slightly unsettling atmosphere, the magnificent strangeness of the Ghost of Christmas Present and the genuinely frightening revelation of Ignorance and Want. And after all that darkness, Scrooge’s redemption is almost unbearably moving.

    Industry observers note that with another film adaptation arriving this year (Ebenezer), it’s clear that Dickens’s masterpiece has kept its hold on us. And because the food is an enormous part of what makes the story’s celebrations so memorable, I wanted to take a closer look at the happy commotion of the Cratchits’ kitchen, Fezziwig’s Christmas party and the astonishing abundance surrounding the Ghost of Christmas Present. Nearly two centuries later, those descriptions still give us a remarkably complete picture of what Christmas tasted like in Dickens’s world.

    Recent findings suggest that the Cratchits’ Christmas goose is one of the most eagerly anticipated meals in literature. As the family busies itself with the accompaniments, the younger children can hardly contain their excitement. When Mrs. Cratchit finally brings the bird to the table, Dickens describes it arriving with a great flourish and the stuffing spilling out as it’s carved.

    Goose was a traditional Christmas centerpiece in Victorian England, particularly for families who couldn’t afford a turkey. Its rich, dark meat was well-suited to roasting, and sage-and-onion stuffing was a familiar accompaniment.

    Recent findings suggest that bob declares that no goose has ever been so tender and delicious, and the family agrees wholeheartedly. The bird may be small for so many people, but the family’s excitement is anything but.

    Recent findings suggest that while the goose roasts, the Cratchit household is busy! Peter tends to the mashed potatoes, Belinda sweetens the apple sauce, and Mrs. Cratchit prepares the gravy. Nearly two centuries later, the menu would look perfectly at home on a modern Christmas table.

    In a recent development, apple sauce was an especially good companion to roast goose, with its tart sweetness balancing the bird’s rich, fatty meat. The mashed potatoes and gravy rounded out the meal, providing plenty of comfort alongside the centerpiece.

    For all his considerable literary talents, Charles Dickens also had a good understanding of the anxiety that comes with serving a dessert you’re not entirely sure has turned out.

    While Mrs. Cratchit retrieves her Christmas plum pudding from the kitchen, the family imagines every possible disaster. Perhaps it isn’t cooked through, or perhaps it will break when she turns it out. The younger children even worry that someone might have stolen it. Fortunately, Mrs. Cratchit returns triumphant with a pudding Dickens describes as a “speckled cannon-ball,” blazing with brandy and decorated with holly.

    In a recent development, traditionally, plum pudding was a dense mixture of dried fruit, suet, spices and other ingredients, boiled for hours in a cloth. Despite the name, it didn’t necessarily contain plums; the term was historically used for dried fruits such as raisins.

    Bob declares the pudding Mrs. Cratchit’s greatest success since their marriage, and nobody dreams of disagreeing. The pudding may be modest in size, but to the Cratchits, it’s a triumph, and Mrs. Cratchit deserves every word of their praise.

    It has been revealed that few characters in A Christmas Carol embody the spirit of Christmas quite like old Mr. Fezziwig. When the Ghost of Christmas Past takes Scrooge back to the Christmas party hosted by his former employer, we’re treated to a lively evening of dancing, music, laughter and an impressive assortment of refreshments, including mince pies.

    Sources indicate that these little pastries had been associated with English Christmas celebrations for generations. Earlier versions of mincemeat often contained actual meat alongside dried fruit, suet and spices. By Dickens’s time, sweeter fillings were increasingly common, though meat hadn’t disappeared from every recipe.

    In a recent development, I rather like imagining Fezziwig presiding over the festivities, dispensing good cheer as generously as the food. His party is one of the few memories that briefly softens Scrooge, and it’s easy to understand why.

    According to recent reports, after the Cratchit family finishes dinner, apples and oranges are brought out, chestnuts are placed on the fire, and Bob serves a warm drink of gin and lemon. With the excitement of the goose and Christmas pudding behind them, the family settles in for the evening.

    Sources indicate that roasted chestnuts were a familiar winter treat in Victorian London, sold hot by street vendors and enjoyed at home. Oranges were especially welcome during the winter months, when fresh fruit was less readily available.

    According to recent reports, dickens mentions that the family has only two tumblers and a custard cup without a handle, a detail I love for its specificity. The bustle of dinner has given way to the quieter pleasure of sitting together, and Dickens allows us to linger with the family a little longer before the evening draws to a close.

    Christmas celebrations in Dickens’s England didn’t necessarily end on Dec. 25. Twelfth Night, traditionally observed on Jan. 5 or 6, marked the close of the Twelve Days of Christmas, often with a party and an elaborate cake. Twelfth cakes were rich with dried fruit and spices, beautifully decorated and sometimes baked with a hidden bean. Whoever found the bean in their slice might be crowned king or queen of the festivities, an arrangement that presumably made everyone a little more attentive to their dessert.

    Sources indicate that dickens details “immense twelfth-cakes” among the extraordinary foods surrounding the Ghost of Christmas Present. The tradition was already evolving by 1843, but the cakes were still familiar enough to belong on his magnificent collection of Christmas indulgences.

    Dickens includes entire barrels of oysters among the Ghost of Christmas Present’s holiday foods, which may seem an extravagant addition to modern readers.

    In Victorian London, though, oysters were commonly eaten, including by working-class people. They were sold by street vendors, served in taverns and prepared in everything from pies to stews. Britain’s oyster fisheries were once enormously productive, although overharvesting and pollution eventually led to their decline.

    Dickens’s Ghost certainly had no shortage of delights surrounding him, but the barrels of oysters wouldn’t necessarily have struck his readers as the most impressive things in the room.

    When Scrooge wakes on Christmas morning and realizes he’s been given another chance, one of his first acts is to purchase an enormous turkey for the Cratchits.

    In a recent development, he sends a boy to the poulterer’s shop for the prize bird, giddy at the thought of how surprised the family will be. Dickens describes Scrooge’s delight so vividly that it’s difficult not to share his excitement.

    Roast turkey was becoming fashionable for Christmas dinner in Victorian England, particularly among wealthier households. Compared with the Cratchits’ modest goose, Scrooge’s gift is a magnificent extravagance.

    In a recent development, I especially love that he arranges for the bird to be delivered anonymously. He’s discovered the joy of doing something generous without expecting anything in return, and he can barely contain himself.

    Recent findings suggest that at the end of the story, Scrooge promises Bob Cratchit a raise and suggests they discuss the particulars over a bowl of smoking bishop. It’s a peculiar name for what was essentially a warm, spiced wine punch.

    Smoking bishop was traditionally prepared with red wine or port, roasted citrus, sugar and spices. The ingredients were warmed together to make a fragrant cocktail similar to modern mulled wine. It belonged to a family of similarly named punches, including smoking cardinal and smoking pope. Victorian drinkers evidently enjoyed a little ecclesiastical creativity with their beverages.

    I love that Dickens saves this particular drink for the end. We’ve seen the Cratchits gather around their modest dinner and the Ghost of Christmas Present preside over a feast of extraordinary abundance. Now Scrooge, who once wanted nothing to do with either, is inviting Bob Cratchit to share a bowl of punch. Of all the wonderful things on Dickens’s Christmas menu, that invitation may be the most satisfying.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that fast food chains aren’t exactly famous for their salads. They usually fall into two categories: a sad bowl of lettuce added to menus as an afterthought, or a vehicle for fried, calorie-dense ingredients that offset any nutritional upsides. But some chains do make an effort to sell salads worth ordering.

    It has been revealed that to identify the best better-for-you fast-food salads, we asked three nutrition experts to weigh in. Here are the menu items they recommend, along with some tips and tricks for maximizing their nutrition.

    Sources indicate that first, we need to debunk salad’s diet-friendly reputation. “A salad isn't automatically the healthiest choice on a fast food menu,” indicates Kathy Levin, RDN, CDCES, dipACLM, LDN. “Once you add fried chicken, bacon, cheese, candied nuts, crunchy toppings, and a creamy dressing, some salads land in the same calorie and fat range as a burger and fries.”.

    In a recent development, taking all of those components away isn’t always a solution either. A sad salad with just lettuce and a smattering of vegetables is more like rabbit food than a satisfying meal for humans. According to Briana V. Reamer, MS, RDN, LDN, the secret is getting enough fiber, which she notes “will keep you satisfied and full until your next meal.” Take advantage of the restaurant's add-ons—like beans, avocado, and more vegetables—to make your salad more substantial.

    In a recent development, experts also recommend watching your saturated fat intake, specifically with your protein and dressing. Grilled chicken generally has fewer calories and less saturated fat than deep-fried alternatives. Consider your dressing options, too. “If you’re not sure what to pick, look for a vinaigrette or olive-oil-based dressing,” claims Tina Sergi, MS, RD, CSSD, CSCS, TSAC-F.

    Recent findings suggest that and, as a rule of thumb, order your dressing on the side. It keeps your salad from getting soggy on the drive home, for one, but it also gives you more portion control. “Using only part of the packet cuts saturated fat and sodium, especially when they're already on the higher end,” Sergi adds.

    According to recent reports, of course, the dressing is only part of the equation. With those tips in mind, here are the five salads that made the cut.

    According to recent reports, this regional chain is known for its fire-grilled chicken, and this salad packs plenty of it. Each portion contains a double serving of citrus-marinated chicken breast, sliced avocado, cotija cheese, salsa fresca, and tortilla strips over a bed of greens. It's served with a creamy Mexican-inspired Caesar dressing.

    El Pollo Loco strikes the right balance between substantial and light with this dish. Before you add dressing, the entire salad contains 420 calories and 52 grams of protein. “The fire-grilled chicken makes it very filling, the avocado adds heart-healthy fat and fiber, and the salsa fresca adds flavor without much sodium or sugar,” Levin claims.

    Sources indicate that like with most salads, the dressing significantly raises the calorie count—in this case, it adds 440 calories if you use the entire serving. If you're closely monitoring your daily intake, Levin advises going easy on the dressing.

    Culver’s may be best known for its ButterBurgers, but experts say you shouldn’t sleep on its salads. The Chicken Cashew Salad in particular is a great choice. It starts with a bed of mixed greens, topped with cheddar, grape tomatoes, cucumbers, and roasted cashews. You can also choose from several dressings to finish it off.

    With grilled chicken, the salad comes in at 430 calories and 41 grams of protein before adding dressing. Culver’s also offers six dressing varieties ranging from 50 to 260 calories.

    “This is a great fiber- and protein-packed option,” indicates Sergi. “Plus, the cashews add healthy fats, copper to support energy production, and magnesium for optimal nerve and muscle function.”.

    This Lone Star staple sells a Cobb salad that’s a lighter alternative to its lineup of burgers and sandwiches. It comes loaded with all of the essentials: greens, bacon, a hard-boiled egg, grape tomatoes, carrots, and shredded cheese. You can also choose from three chicken options (the grilled chicken filet is, naturally, lighter than the fried options).

    Sources indicate that without dressing, Whataburger's Cobb with grilled chicken has 430 calories and 44 grams of protein. It's also a source of fiber and is low in sugar, according to Reamer. “Salads high in fiber help with weight management and satisfy hunger.”.

    Some of Whataburger's creamier dressings add 200 to 280 calories, while the balsamic vinaigrette has 180.

    Sources indicate that for a fried chicken chain, Chick-fil-A makes some surprisingly stellar salads. The Market Salad starts with mixed greens and is topped with strawberries, blueberries, red and green apples, blue cheese, roasted almonds, and the chain’s Harvest Nut Granola. Chick-fil-A also has the most protein options on this list. The grilled chicken can come in nugget or filet form, warm or cold, and spicy or regular. Talk about variety!

    Sources indicate that the different grilled chicken options provide between 26 and 32 grams of protein, according to Chick-fil-A's nutrition guide. Levin also says you can forgo chicken entirely for a meatless meal that doesn't feel like an afterthought. “Berries and apples bring fiber, antioxidants and natural sweetness, which makes it one of the most plant-forward options on the list.”.

    The Market Salad is typically paired with Chick-fil-A's Zesty Apple Cider Vinaigrette Dressing, which contains 230 calories per packet. But the chain is known for its sauces, after all, so you can swap it out for another option. There's a Light Balsamic Vinaigrette with 80 calories, Fat-Free Honey Mustard with 90, and Light Italian Dressing with just 25.

    It has been revealed that zaxby's is the third chicken chain on this list, and it stands out by offering a salad with Asian-inspired flavors. The Asian Zensation Zalad (not Salad) adds shredded carrots, cabbage, wonton strips, and Asian Slaw to mixed greens, along with a drizzle of teriyaki sauce. It also comes with a vegetable egg roll on the side.

    This salad is loaded with plant-based toppings, which is why Levin also recommends the garden version as a vegetarian option. Zaxby's lists that version at 390 calories, while the grilled chicken version comes in at 530 calories and 39 grams of protein, before adding dressing.

    In a recent development, alongside the teriyaki drizzle, Zaxby's offers Citrus Vinaigrette with the salad, which has 110 calories per packet. It's one of the chain's lighter options. But if you're watching your calorie intake, you can swap in Lite Vinaigrette, which contains just 30 calories.

    #44. Easy Eggplant Bolognese (1 Pot!)

    Easy Eggplant Bolognese (1 Pot!)

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that when we add another bolognese to the blog (Yes, we already have versions 1, 2, 3, and 4), you know it’s something special!
    • It has been revealed that even better?
    • Bolognese is an Italian sauce that gets its name from the Italian city of Bologna.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that when we add another bolognese to the blog (Yes, we already have versions 1, 2, 3, and 4), you know it’s something special! This newest version is made with EGGPLANT, meaning it’s the perfect bolognese for late summer. It’s light yet satisfying, creamy yet bright, and full of bold Italian-inspired flavor — everyone will be asking for seconds!

    It has been revealed that even better? It’s a breeze to make — just 1 pot required! What are you waiting for? Get that pasta water boiling!

    Bolognese is an Italian sauce that gets its name from the Italian city of Bologna. It’s typically made with meat, soffrito (onions, celery, and carrots), white wine, milk, and tomato paste or sauce, all simmered to create a rich, flavorful sauce.

    Our eggplant version strays from the traditional as it excludes meat (and includes eggplant) and incorporates dairy alternatives. But the rest of the dish is very similar to traditional bolognese and feels so hearty it might convert even the most adamant veggie skeptics!

    Sources indicate that this 1-pot eggplant bolognese is everything you want for a cozy pasta night, minus the fuss! It starts with sautéing onion and carrots to create a simple, savory-sweet base. Next, we add eggplant (cut into very small cubes) and let it sauté until it has softened and browned (hello, flavor!).

    In a recent development, build the flavor even further with garlic and red pepper flakes and by deglazing the pan with wine. Crushed tomatoes and tomato paste ensure a bright, tomato-forward sauce, and a small amount of dairy-free milk (we like homemade cashew milk) gives it a gentle creaminess and richness. The final flavor touches include dried Italian herbs (basil + oregano), sea salt, and maple syrup to balance the acidity of the tomatoes.

    It has been revealed that once all the ingredients are in your pan, it’s time to let the heat do its magic. Simmering for at least 20-30 minutes allows the sauce to thicken and concentrates the flavors as liquid evaporates away. If you have the time, you can let it continue simmering for up to an hour for even more flavor!

    Industry observers note that when it’s done simmering, you’ll be left with an oh-so delicious, plant-powered sauce perfect for serving with your favorite pasta! It would also be lovely over polenta and is elevated by garnishing with fresh basil and our homemade vegan parmesan cheese.

    Recent findings suggest that we think you’ll LOVE this eggplant bolognese! It’s:RichSavoryCreamy yet brightLight yet satisfyingEasy to make& SO delicious!

    Sources indicate that it’s the perfect dish for a late summer pasta night! While quick enough for a weeknight, it’s also impressive enough to serve to dinner guests, especially paired with our Simple Vegan Meatballs, Pesto Turkey Meatballs, or Chickpea Caesar Salad (30 Minutes!).

    In a recent development, if you try this recipe, let us know! Leave a comment, rate it, and don’t forget to tag a photo @minimalistbaker on Instagram. Cheers, friends!

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Precision pastries are sweeping the nation. These bakers are leading the charge.

    If there’s one thing we’ve noticed over the past several years, it’s how much bakeries have stepped up their game.

    Some embody a personal expression of a baker’s identity, while others push the envelope beyond expected flavor combinations; all excel at a time when “little treat” culture is at its peak. — Missy Frederick, editorial director.

    Learn more about this year’s Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, and how editors selected them, here.

    If one latest place in Chicago needs no further hype, it is Bad Butter. You’ll know you’re there when you spot the line cascading out of the whitewashed storefront along West Cortland Street, a queue that doesn’t let up until the pastry case is empty. Formerly a head baker at Soho House Chicago, Dan Koester was stuck at home like the rest of us in 2020, handing off excess home-baked sourdough loaves to friends and family and making some available for free pickup. After he was officially laid off that summer, he launched his own online bakery business, earning a massive following along the way.

    One residency at the Emily Hotel later, Koester debuted his Bucktown bakery, demonstrating the full range of his skill. Still warm, charred, and dimpled flats of focaccia showered with scallion furikake rest on its shelves. Impossibly crisp and exquisitely laminated twice-baked almond croissants burst with subtle, aromatic almond paste. A spicy harissa monkey bread with a cloudlike texture is cooled by a pool of creamy labneh drizzled with silky olive oil.

    According to recent reports, the bakery’s menu has breadth and also manages to arc with the season. Customers snake along the floor waiting their turn to claim a towering cruffin, dusted in fine grains of sugar and piped full of ginger plum jam, or a seasonal tart piled with plump, lacquered blueberries. A pastry box filled with these confections is well worth the wait. — Brenna Houck, dining editorial manager.

    According to recent reports, born as an underground dinner party operated out of Karla Subero Pittol’s Echo Park garage, Chainsaw finally got its own digs in November 2025 in the form of a lively cafe in Melrose Hill, an unquestionably gentrifying neighborhood that has become home to some of Los Angeles’s best independent restaurants. At the cafe, Subero Pittol channels her Venezuelan heritage through a menu of arepas plump with beans, limey guasacaca, and cheese; a Venezuelan hot dog (“perro caliente”) buoyed by an acidic slaw; and her bracingly tart passionfruit-lime icebox pie, which commands a cult following all its own.

    Stepping into Chainsaw feels like you could be in Subero Pittol’s own kitchen as she greets regulars and newcomers as if they are old friends. Customers study a handwritten menu that changes daily — it doesn’t help to come in too attached to any one dish (save the ever-present icebox pie) when you may get tempted by another. The cafe’s impact on Los Angeles feels clear in the near-constant crowds that hover outside, reading their newspapers over an espresso or tucking into the latest of Subero Pittol’s ideas, such as a full English breakfast served for a single day. In a city lacking in untamed Venezuelan cooking, Chainsaw offers a home for Subero Pittol to celebrate the cuisine in a way that feels distinctly Los Angeles. — Rebecca Roland, deputy editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest.

    With both Afghan and Latin American influences, Diljān gives New Yorkers a bakery with a point of view and innumerable reasons to become a regular. Ali Zaman and Mohamed Ghiasi, owners of Astoria’s Little Flower Cafe, teamed up with Bryan Ford, Honduran American baker and cookbook author, to conceptualize the bakery, now perched on a corner near Atlantic Avenue in Brooklyn Heights.

    According to recent reports, their combined talent makes for some of the city’s most compelling baked goods. For the Saffron Shah, laminated pastry holds delicate saffron cream in the shape of a crescent, an key Islamic symbol. Halwa tops the sticky bun, while a swirl of samosa pastry wraps halal lamb under a dusting of powdered sugar. Don’t miss the enormous Afghan flatbread crowned by toppings such as halal beef bacon with scallions or sour cherry cream cheese. The team has also branched into pizzas topped with cheese and Afghan cumin, kofta kebabs, or beef pepperoni. Look for specials like the flan with cardamom-poached apricots and conchas stuffed with firni, a rice pudding. — Nadia Chaudhury, deputy editor, Eater New York.

    San Francisco’s pastry game is stronger and more competitive than ever before, and Parachute Bakery steps to the forefront of a crowded field with a mix of patisserie standards and seasonal standouts. At his Ferry Building bakery, pastry chef Nasir Armar marries his fine dining training, honed at Michelin-starred Sorrel and Saison, with flavors that make everyone sit up and take notice (and snap a food photo or two for their socials).

    It has been revealed that vegetables and savory complements are given their own footing on the menu. Stalks of grilled asparagus shine in a baton-shaped croissant shell, with fennel jam, sheep’s milk ricotta, and ramp pesto alongside them; one brief, bordering-on-gimmicky croissant got piped with clam chowder, a reference to the soup in a bread bowl famously served on the city’s wharf. Even potato-laden samosas and bright tomato shakshuka get interpreted into pastry form. Parachute succeeds with its experimental vision, a hype well-earned that leaves fans clamoring for what they’ll come up with next. — Dianne de Guzman, editor, Eater SF.

    #36. 5 Restaurant Chains With Troubling Food Safety Records

    📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (863 w)
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Delish

    5 Restaurant Chains With Troubling Food Safety Records

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (863 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Delish

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Not every day can be a home-cooked meal kind of day.
    • Admittedly, fast food chains don’t always have the best reputation, especially when it comes to health concerns.
    • Cleaning protocols differ from chain to chain—and even from location to location.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Not every day can be a home-cooked meal kind of day. Sometimes, going out really pays off. It saves you time in the kitchen, cuts down on effort, and most importantly, lets you relax while someone else does the heavy lifting. Many families turn to fast food when they want an easy, quick meal or when time is of the essence. But where you go can really make a difference.

    Admittedly, fast food chains don’t always have the best reputation, especially when it comes to health concerns. But beyond the macros, another factor to consider is cleanliness.

    Cleaning protocols differ from chain to chain—and even from location to location. You may have seen headlines concerning less-than-stellar hygiene reports stemming from certain fast food locations over the years. Kitchen cleanliness is paramount to food safety (just look at this year’s Cyclospora outbreak), and some chains have faced more than their share of troubling headlines. Here are five fast food chains with a disappointing history of food safety complications.

    Industry observers note that I hate to break it to burrito-with-extra-guac fans, but Chipotle has a history of high-profile food safety challenges. The organization paid $25 million to resolve criminal charges related to a series of foodborne illness outbreaks between 2015 and 2018. According to the documents, Chipotle was charged with "adulterating food in violation of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act," resulting in the largest criminal fine ever imposed in a food safety case at the time.

    According to recent reports, records cited at least five foodborne illness outbreaks across several states, including incidents involving norovirus, that sickened more than 1,100 people. These outbreaks "primarily stemmed from store-level employees' failure to follow organization food safety protocols." Personally, I'd rather have a side of hot sauce than a side of stomach flu.

    Industry observers note that in February 2025, a Massachusetts store was cited for nine core health code violations—including insufficiently cleaned ice machines, improperly stored produce, and missing thermometers in a walk-in cooler—along with one priority foundation violation. Such issues can raise concerns about food safety and sanitation.

    In 2022, a health inspector described another location in the state as "very unclean." A year before that, workers at a Springfield, Missouri, location staged a walkout over poor working conditions. A subsequent health inspection found that "the floors in the food preparation area (especially under equipment and near drains), walk-in refrigerator and freezer, and dry storage areas were not clean," leading to a follow-up inspection. (Don't even get us started on some of the problems found overseas!).

    Sorry, chalupa lovers. Taco Bell has also faced its share of food safety concerns over the years. Reports include an E. coli outbreak along the East Coast in 2006 resulting in 71 illnesses (53 of whom were hospitalized), two Salmonella outbreaks in 2010 affecting at least 155 people across 21 states, and a hepatitis A outbreak in 2000 that sickened 23 people and hospitalized 15.

    More recently, a customer’s viral video appeared to show a Taco Bell kitchen strewn with food, garbage, and old boxes near food prep areas. Some commenters suggested that it was filmed during rush hour while the restaurant was understaffed and that employees were too busy to clean. Still, it's not a great look for in-store hygiene.

    Significant Mac lovers, look away. The Golden Arches have faced numerous lawsuits over food safety problems over the years, including a class action suit (plus several personal injury suits) filed in 2024 following a multistate E. coli outbreak linked to Quarter Pounders. The outbreak ultimately sickened 104 people and killed one, with investigators identifying slivered onions as the likely source of contamination.

    The Boston City Department of Inspectional Services found nearly 125 violations at seven different McDonald's locations between 2018 and 2019—everything from mismanaged storage to mold, rat droppings, and even live cockroaches. Complaints and lawsuits have also alleged undercooked meat and foodborne illnesses caused by cross-contamination.

    According to recent reports, wendy's locations have racked up numerous health code violations, too (one Las Vegas restaurant in particular drew 27 demerits in a 2019 inspection for dirty soda nozzles, food left on the floor, raw food cross-contamination, and more). A 2023 "Dirty Dining" segment called out a Fort Lauderdale, Florida, location with an inspection that found insects all over the restaurant.

    Perhaps most concerningly, a Michigan family filed a lawsuit in 2024 alleging their daughter developed hemolytic uremic syndrome following an E. coli infection they attributed to food from Wendy's. According to the lawsuit, the illness caused permanent brain damage, kidney failure, a seizure disorder, and other lasting health problems. Inspectors had found the location in violation of 17 different health and food codes just days before the family's visit, including moldy food, spoiled produce, dirty surfaces, and water leaks.

    Even with these histories of violations, not every location should make you rethink your dining options—many restaurants are up to code and clean. While all this information is enough to convince me to stick to home-cooked meals for the rest of my life, I suggest checking your local restaurant's latest health inspection report before deciding whether or not to visit your chain of choice.

    #35. Industry News: The Exiled Thanksgiving Dishes You Forgot Were Once on the Table

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1498 w)
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tasteofhome

    Industry News: The Exiled Thanksgiving Dishes You Forgot Were Once on the Table

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1498 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • There was a time when Thanksgiving dinner involved gelatin—and lots of it.
    • Recent findings suggest that thanksgiving is a holiday that doesn’t take kindly to change.
    • Some were beloved family favorites that gradually fell out of fashion.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

    There was a time when Thanksgiving dinner involved gelatin—and lots of it.

    Recent findings suggest that thanksgiving is a holiday that doesn’t take kindly to change. Suggest replacing the mashed potatoes or leaving the stuffing off the menu, and you’re likely to hear about it until Easter. Yet for all our devotion to tradition, the Thanksgiving table has changed quite a bit over the years. Somewhere along the way, entire dishes disappeared, and most of us barely noticed.

    Some were beloved family favorites that gradually fell out of fashion. Others were products of an era when gelatin was considered an essential ingredient, even in dishes that had no business holding that much shape. Looking through old Thanksgiving menus, cookbooks and holiday advertisements reveals a rather wonderful assortment of foods that once had a place alongside the turkey. A few deserve to come back. Others might be better left to history, although I would very much like to meet the people responsible for them.

    “Aspic” is a lovely word. It’s French, sophisticated, and just mysterious enough to suggest that whatever arrives at the table will be very impressive. You could put it on a formal dinner menu and nobody would think twice. But what you’re actually discussing is meat Jell-O.

    And not some unfortunate kitchen experiment, either. Savory aspics were perfectly respectable additions to holiday meals well into the 1950s, with suspensions of meat, vegetables, seafood and even hard-boiled eggs presented in elaborate molds. The finished creations could be sliced into neat portions, allowing guests to admire every carefully arranged ingredient through a translucent wall of solidified broth.

    There’s something almost admirable about the confidence required to make one of these. Imagine spending hours arranging shrimp and vegetables in a decorative mold, then carrying it proudly to the dining room as though everyone had been waiting all year for a slice of cold, wobbly meat.

    Diana Chistruga for Taste of Home.

    Not every gelatin creation merits as harsh a judgment as aspic. I have a certain affection for the brightly colored Jell-O salads that used to appear at holiday gatherings. There was something cheerful about a ruby-red cranberry gelatin salad or a fluffy lime concoction studded with pineapple, even if calling either one a “salad” required a fairly generous interpretation of the word.

    These dishes were enormously popular in the mid-20th century, when molded gelatin desserts offered home cooks an opportunity to get creative with fruit, nuts, cream cheese, whipped topping and whatever else happened to be in the refrigerator. Some combinations were genuinely delicious. Others involved shredded carrots, celery or mayonnaise, at which point the distinction between salad and practical joke became rather difficult to maintain.

    I’d happily make room for a cranberry Jell-O salad at Thanksgiving. The ones made with canned tuna can remain in retirement.

    There was a time, particularly in the 1890s, when mincemeat pie was every bit as deserving of a place on the Thanksgiving dessert table as pumpkin or apple pie. Its rich filling of dried fruits, spices and citrus had a long history in English cooking, and early versions also contained actual meat—often beef or mutton—along with suet.

    The meat gradually disappeared from many recipes, leaving behind the sweet, deeply spiced filling that became a holiday tradition in its own right. Even so, the name has never done the pie any favors. Tell someone you’re serving mincemeat for dessert, and there’s a reasonable chance they’ll assume you’ve been sampling too many Thanksgiving cocktails.

    Industry observers note that that’s a shame, because a well-made mincemeat pie has plenty going for it, particularly for anyone who loves the warm flavors of cloves, cinnamon and nutmeg. It may be a harder sell than pumpkin pie, but I wouldn’t object to seeing it make a modest comeback.

    Sources indicate that waldorf salad has much more glamorous origins than most other dishes on this list. It was created at Latest York’s Waldorf Hotel in the 1890s, originally as a simple combination of apples, celery and mayonnaise. Walnuts became a familiar addition later, and by the 1960s, the salad had found its way onto holiday tables across the country.

    I can understand why. The crisp apples and celery provide a welcome contrast to the rich, heavy dishes that make up Thanksgiving dinner, while the walnuts add enough substance to make it feel like more than just a bowl of chopped fruit. It’s refreshing, pleasantly crunchy and especially good alongside roasted turkey.

    Recent findings suggest that of all the dishes that have slipped off the Thanksgiving menu, Waldorf salad might be one of the easiest to bring back. It requires very little fuss, and a fresh, crisp side is hardly unwelcome at a table already crowded with casseroles.

    At some point in the ’50s, we became convinced that nearly every food could be improved by pressing it into a loaf pan.

    The holiday vegetable loaf was one expression of that enthusiasm, turning assorted vegetables into a tidy, sliceable centerpiece with the help of binders like eggs, breadcrumbs or gelatin. Some versions were baked, while others emerged cold from the refrigerator, ready to be unmolded and presented with considerable ceremony.

    I understand the practical appeal of preparing a dish ahead of time, particularly for Thanksgiving. What I struggle to understand is the insistence that vegetables should be made to resemble meatloaf. Carrots, peas and green beans are perfectly capable of sharing a serving dish without being pressed into a rectangular block.

    Mackenzie Williams For Taste of Home.

    Recent findings suggest that hot Dr Pepper sounds like something you’d find in a cookbook published during a national shortage of good judgment. But it was a genuine promotional idea, introduced by Dr Pepper in the 1960s as a way to enjoy the soft drink in colder weather.

    It has been revealed that the instructions were simple: Heat Dr Pepper, pour it into a mug and add a thin slice of lemon. The tech giant promoted it as a warming drink for winter gatherings, making it an intriguing candidate for the sort of holiday refreshment that now seems to have vanished almost completely.

    According to recent reports, I can’t decide whether this is a terrible idea or one that deserves a fair trial. Dr Pepper already has a distinctive blend of sweet and spicy flavors, and warm spiced drinks are hardly unusual during the holidays. The lemon is an interesting touch, too. I wouldn’t necessarily replace the hot apple cider, but curiosity might get the better of me.

    According to recent reports, there are questionable vintage recipes, and then there are the recipes that suggest the author had finally snapped. Cranberry mayonnaise candles belong firmly in the second category.

    Recent findings suggest that the idea was to turn cranberry sauce and mayonnaise into a molded holiday creation resembling a candle, complete with a decorative wick or flame effect depending on the version. It was the sort of elaborate presentation that food companies once promoted with an entirely straight face, apparently confident that a candle-shaped mixture of fruit and mayonnaise was just what the Thanksgiving feast had been missing.

    I have several questions, beginning with why the cranberry sauce needed to look like a candle and ending with why mayonnaise was invited to the party. There’s also the matter of placing something resembling a candle in the food and expecting guests to understand they’re supposed to eat it.

    If you’ve ever wondered what to do with leftover turkey, the sensible answers include sandwiches, soups, potpies and perhaps casseroles. Vintage recipe developers, however, were not always interested in sensible answers.

    Enter frozen jellied turkey vegetable salad, a 1970s creation that manages to combine several questionable ideas into a single dish. Turkey, vegetables and a gelatin-based mixture were assembled into a cold, molded preparation that was perhaps more ambitious than necessary.

    It has been revealed that it’s difficult to imagine anyone looking at a plate of leftover turkey and deciding that what it really needed was to become a frozen, sliceable salad. Yet recipes like this reflect a period when casserole popsicles made perfect sense.

    Jonathan Melendez for Taste of Home.

    Industry observers note that creamed pearl onions were a familiar sight on Thanksgiving tables in the 1920s, and I think we may have been too quick to let them go. Tender little onions in a rich, buttery cream sauce are exactly the sort of thing that belongs alongside roast turkey, mashed potatoes and stuffing. They’re comforting, a little old-fashioned, and wonderfully suited to a holiday when nobody is particularly concerned about their butter intake.

    It has been revealed that they also have the advantage of feeling special without requiring an elaborate presentation. Peeling a mountain of tiny onions is admittedly nobody’s idea of holiday fun, but frozen pearl onions make the whole business much easier. If your family has never had creamed onions at Thanksgiving, this may be a tradition worth borrowing from an earlier generation.
